World.title: Feira Constituency Receives Ballot Papers
World.content:
Feira Constituency in Luangwa District has received ballot papers ahead of the General Election taking place on Thursday, 13thAugust, 2026.

Acting District Electoral Officer Paul Siyanga confirmed receiving one pallet of ballot papers at 21:53 hours yesterday, whose delivery was witnessed by stakeholders before the materials were secured in the strong room upon arrival.

Mr Siyanga, who is standing in for District Electoral Officer Greyson Sakala, explained that the ballot papers were received intact without any breakage on the seals and locks.

“I can assure the public that all stakeholders witnessed the arrival of the ballot papers and that they have been secured amidst tight state security of the Zambia Police until 13th August, 2026,” he explained.

Mr Siyanga thanked the stakeholders for a peaceful process of receiving the ballot papers and urged them to maintain this peace and order exhibited before, during and after the elections.

Socialist Party District Campaign Manager Canaan Mukanka appreciated the professionalism exhibited by the Electoral Commission of Zambia during the exercise.

Mr Mukonka explained that the tight security by the Zambia Police played a key role in ensuring that the ballot papers are not tampered with during transportation from Lusaka to Luangwa.

And National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) District Chairperson Obert Tembo expressed satisfaction with the way the Electoral Commission of Zambia handled the stakeholders at the civic centre.

Mr Tembo explained that the stakeholders were given ample time to inspect anything they felt needed to be checked for transparency purposes.

“We just had a concern as stakeholders on the safety of the strong room provided for the safe keeping of the ballot papers but we have been assured that tight security will be provided,” he expressed.

Meanwhile, United Party for National Development (UPND) District Youth Chairperson Kelly Kasongole said his party has confidence in the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

“We are not worried about the safety of the ballot papers because we believe in a transparent and professional process where no one can tamper with the election materials,” Mr Kasongole explained.

World.title: Luangwa Political Players Commended for Peaceful Campaigns
World.content:
Luangwa District Commissioner Luke Chikani has commended political players for maintaining peace and order during the campaign period in the district.

Mr Chikani says no violence has been recorded since the commencement of the campaigns, citing unity and love being promoted by government.

Speaking when a team of Election Observers who are in the country from the European Union paid a courtesy call on him, Mr Chikani emphasised that Zambia is a peaceful nation that does not promote violence.

“I must confess that the country has never had peaceful campaigns such as these since Zambia gained its Independence from the colonial masters and we are happy as a country and of course as a district that each political player has a fair playing ground,” he explained.

Mr Chikani further explained that the institution mandated to handle the elections at district level was doing everything possible to ensure that the process was transparent and professional from the voter education component to the actual voting day.

He said political players in the district have strictly adhered to the laid down guidelines by the Electoral Commission of Zambia leading to a safe political environment in the district.

The DC called on the public and all political players to maintain the love, peace and unity that has been exercised from the beginning of the electoral exercise.

European Union Long Term Observer, Milan Kuksa explained that the role of the European Union was to follow the electoral process in the field until the Election Day on 13th August, 2026.

Mr Kuksa said the observers meet key stakeholders and report regularly to the core team.

“My colleagues Claudia Kamariza and Suzen Mwape are part of the team that is monitoring and observing the electoral process in Chongwe, Rufunsa and Luangwa Districts and therefore, you will be seeing us quiet often,” he explained.

World.title: ZYAFAC Urges Monitors to Remain Neutral
World.content:
The Zambia Youths Association in the Fight Against Corruption (ZYAFAC) has urged its election monitors to remain neutral, professional and non-partisan during the August 13 General Elections.

ZYAFAC Board Chairperson Rickson Kanema says the monitors have a responsibility to observe and document the electoral process without supporting any political party or candidate.

Mr Kanema noted that the 250 monitors accredited by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) should act as the eyes of communities at polling stations and promote the integrity of the electoral process.

He was speaking in Lusaka during a ZYAFAC Election Monitoring Training Workshop at Ndeke Hotel.

He added that the organisation expects the monitors to contribute to peaceful, free, fair and credible elections through responsible and non-partisan monitoring.

“You are not here to campaign, you are here to observe, document and promote integrity.” he said

Mr Kanema also said ZYAFAC has also engaged the Electoral Commission of Zambia, Anti-Corruption Commission, Drug Enforcement Commission and the media as resource persons.

He emphasized that ZYAFAC expects the training to strengthen its monitoring and reporting system and enhance public confidence in the electoral process through credible and non-partisan youth-led election monitoring.

Mr Kanema further reminded the monitors that their participation in the elections should be guided by national interest and the desire to contribute to a peaceful and credible electoral process.

World.title: HH, UPND favoured for first-round win, new analysis shows
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema is favoured to retain the presidency in Thursday’s general election, with the United Party for National Development handed a 70 to 80 percent chance of securing an outright first-round victory, a new pre-election analysis has found.

The briefing, titled Zambia’s 13 August General Election: Assessing the Route to the Presidency, puts the likelihood of a run-off at 15 to 25 percent. It is authored by Southern Africa Coalition for Democracy and Accountability executive director Blessing Vava and Masosote Institute for Political Economy director Tamuka Chirimambowa, and was published by the Public Affairs Research Institute in Africa on 8 August.

The analysis finds that Hichilema is favoured to cross the mandatory 50 percent threshold required to avoid a second round. It cautions, however, that the reasoning behind the projected outcome is not as simple as incumbent popularity.

“A first-round UPND victory is the most likely single outcome,” the briefing states.

Ballot access emerges as the clearest structural advantage identified in the report. UPND has fielded candidates in all 226 National Assembly constituencies, compared with 156 for the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity. The ruling party is also contesting 115 of the 116 mayoral and council chairperson positions nationwide.

“Ballot access is the clearest measurable difference between the two campaigns. The UPND contested effectively every seat available. The NRPUP did not,” the report states. “The gap is not a matter of interpretation, it is recorded in the nomination returns, and it compounds downward, widest at ward level, where the machinery of election day actually sits.”

That gap widens further down the ballot. UPND has fielded candidates in wards countrywide, while NRPUP is contesting fewer than two-thirds of Zambia’s 1,858 wards.

The disparity matters beyond vote counting, the authors argue, because ward-level candidates are central to placing polling agents and monitoring the counting and aggregation of results on election day itself.

“The NRPUP’s decisive weakness is organisational rather than rhetorical,” the report says.

Opposition fragmentation stands out as the single biggest factor working in the incumbent’s favour, according to the analysis. Fourteen presidential candidates appear on Thursday’s ballot, splitting the anti-incumbent vote across a crowded field rather than consolidating it behind a single challenger.

Even so, the authors caution against reading the projected UPND victory as a sign of overwhelming popularity. The report points to an underlying anti-incumbent sentiment that persists among a segment of voters, suggesting the ruling party’s advantage rests more on organisational depth and opposition division than on broad public enthusiasm.

Zambians go to the polls this Thursday to elect a president, members of parliament and local government representatives.

World.title: ECZ Praises Siavonga Parties for Peaceful Campaigns
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has commended political parties and their supporters in Siavonga District for conducting peaceful campaigns ahead of the August 13 General Elections.

Siavonga District Electoral Officer Kennedy Shombo, speaking at Lake View Lodge when he opened a Poll Day briefing meeting for political parties, Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs), Civil Society Organizations (CSOs), church representatives and members of the media, said the district has so far recorded no cases of political violence since the commencement of the election campaigns.

Mr Shombo urged political parties and their supporters to continue adhering to the Electoral Code of Conduct and maintain peace before, during and after polling day and called on the media to verify information before publication and help promote peace and prevent the spread of misinformation.

Mr Shombo also reminded voters that political regalia will not be allowed at polling stations on polling day.

Meanwhile, Siavonga District Returning Officer Steven Mbita reaffirmed the ECZ’s commitment to delivering a credible election.

In a presentation, Assistant Returning Officer Mutinta Mutoloki highlighted key electoral processes and procedures, including the deployment of poll staff, timelines, conflict resolution mechanisms, verification of ballot papers and account forms, as well as results management.

Mr Mutoloki said the Commission was fully prepared and that all necessary arrangements were being put in place ahead of polling day.

The briefing was aimed at equipping stakeholders with information on Poll Day activities, operational arrangements, electoral procedures and their respective roles in ensuring a smooth, peaceful, transparent and credible electoral process.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 10, 2026
World.content:
Nigeria Army Rescues 33 Kidnapped Victims in Zamfara

The Nigerian army has said that it has rescued 33 people who were kidnapped by armed men while travelling through Zamfara state in the northwest. Troops and police responded to the abduction in Tsafe. They intercepted the kidnappers as they moved the hostages, forcing the gunmen to flee into nearby bushes. All 33 victims were rescued without casualties. Security forces are tracking the abductors. The rescue comes amid a recent series of successful operations, with more than 300 kidnapped people reportedly freed in separate incidents. Ransom kidnappings continue to be a major security and political problem in northern Nigeria as the country prepares for the 2027 elections.

DR Congo Hands 15 Prisoners to M23 in Peace Deal Move

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Democratic Republic of Congo authorities have released 15 prisoners and handed them over to the AFC/M23 rebel movement in the first known prisoner transfer under a 2025 peace deal. The deal is aimed at ending fighting in eastern Congo. The transfer, facilitated by the International Committee of the Red Cross and with Uganda's assistance, follows months of stalled negotiations over a larger exchange involving nearly 500 detainees. The ICRC described the operation as a potential step towards further releases and a "glimmer of hope" for families affected by the conflict. However, fighting between government forces and M23 has continued despite the peace agreement.

Ivorian Drum Looted by France Goes on Display at Home

Côte d'Ivoire has welcomed home the Djidji Ayokwe, a sacred "talking drum" looted by French colonial troops in 1916. It was returned to the country earlier this year. More than three metres long and weighing 430kg, the drum was used by the Ebrie community to send messages, warn of danger and summon villagers. It was paraded through Abidjan before being taken to its home village of Adjame, where traditional leaders and residents held ceremonies to mark its return. The drum is expected to go on display at the Museum of Civilisations in Abidjan as France faces growing pressure to return African artefacts taken during the colonial era.

Nigeria Holds Mass Wedding for 1,500 Couples

Around 1,500 couples have married in a two-day mass wedding organised by Kano State Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf in northern Nigeria to support low-income families and promote social stability. Each bride received a 200,000-naira dowry, business support and household items. Couples underwent screening and counselling before the ceremony. Among those married was a widower who lost his wife and six children in an attack earlier this year. The initiative comes as northern Nigeria continues to face widespread insecurity, including attacks and kidnappings by armed groups.

Africa's UN Secretary-General Bid Struggles for Support

Close 

The United Nations is set to name António Guterres's successor in October, whose second five-year term ends on 31 December. Africa's two candidates, former Senegalese president Macky Sall and Ugandan diplomat Olara Otunnu, are struggling to gain support in the first Security Council vote. Analysts said that Africa's chances are further weakened by the informal regional rotation system, which favours Latin America and the Caribbean this year. Neither African candidate has received backing from the African Union. Three women are also in the race, with UN Trade and Development chief Rebeca Grynspan emerging as the early frontrunner after receiving the most support in the first straw poll.

World.title: South Africa: Ramaphosa Calls on Men to Fight GBV - South African News Briefs - August 10, 2026
World.content:
Ramaphosa Urges Men to Stand Against GBV

President Cyril Ramaphosa has called on men and boys to take a stronger stand against gender-based violence, reports EWN. He said that they must reject violence against women and girls. Speaking at the Women’s Day commemoration at the Union Buildings, he also highlighted women’s achievements in education. He called for more women to enter science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields.

11 Killed in Three Cape Town Mass Shootings

Eleven people have been killed in three separate mass shootings in Cape Town, reports EWN. Three men were killed in Khayelitsha, and five people were killed in Langa. Three others died in a shooting at the Barcelona informal settlement in Gugulethu, where two additional people were wounded. Police have reinforced deployments in the affected communities, but no arrests have been made. The motives remain under investigation.

Malema Faces Prosecution Over 'Rapist' Remark

Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) leader Julius Malema is set to face criminal prosecution for crimen injuria after allegedly calling former Bergview College principal Jaco Pieterse a "rapist", reports EWN. The case stems from allegations that a seven-year-old girl, publicly known as Cwecwe, was raped at Bergview College in Matatiele, Eastern Cape, in October 2024. The NPA initially declined to prosecute anyone over the alleged rape, citing a lack of concrete evidence. However, it has now decided to prosecute Malema following a complaint pursued by AfriForum’s private prosecution unit. The case has been referred to the Johannesburg Magistrates Court.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Investigation Raises Alarm Over Uranium in DR Congo Cobalt Shipments to China
World.content:
An investigation by Lighthouse Reports, The Financial Times and Le Monde traces the possible export of uranium from the Democratic Republic of Congo back to a confidential International Atomic Energy Agency memo obtained in 2024. Chinese mining group CMOC, which owns the main site examined in Katanga, disputes the findings.

Lighthouse Reports obtained a previously undisclosed internal memo from the International Atomic Energy Agency in 2024 and began investigating its contents.

The 2009 document cited credible information indicating that uranium was present in "significant quantities" in most cobalt ores from Katanga, in the southeast of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and was "effectively exported as a cobalt by-product".

Lighthouse Reports conducted the investigation in partnership with The Financial Times and Le Monde.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Uranium in mineral-rich Katanga

The Katanga region - part of Central Africa's Copperbelt - has increasingly turned towards cobalt extraction as demand has grown for the metal, which is used in lithium-ion batteries and aerospace alloys.

But the region's mines have also long been known to contain uranium. A significant proportion of the uranium used in the Manhattan Project, which developed the first atomic bombs, came from Katanga's Shinkolobwe mine.

The mine was closed after independence and later placed within an exclusion zone. In 2004, then president Joseph Kabila declared the area a prohibited mining zone, citing national security, public safety and the presence of uranium, which Congolese law classifies as a reserved mineral substance.

"There are always by-products in Congolese mining exports - particularly cobalt - and these by-products are effectively monitored by the Congolese authorities. All except one: uranium," Tomas Statius, a Lighthouse Reports journalist and co-author of the investigation, told RFI.

Unchecked mining waste taints DR Congo communities

Mining professionals say uranium, copper and cobalt frequently occur together in the Congolese and Zambian Copperbelt.

"It is not limited to specific locations; it is a constant feature," Statius said.

Steve Muanza, head of the DRC's nuclear energy agency, told The Financial Times that it was "technically possible" and even "probable" that Chinese companies were extracting uranium from cobalt ore exported from the country, although he said there was no direct evidence.

He said his agency had requested funding to install radioactivity detectors on trucks travelling from the DRC into Zambia.

Up to 5,000 tonnes exported

To estimate the amount of uranium potentially exported, Lighthouse Reports worked with Sébastien Philippe, then a senior researcher at Princeton University, and geologist Ryan Manzuk.

Their calculations drew on previous analyses of uranium concentrations in Katanga ores, mine production data and geological samples held by the AfricaMuseum in Belgium.

A paper by Manzuk and Philippe, published on 30 July in Nature Communications, estimated that between 2,000 and 5,000 tonnes of uranium were exported from the DRC to China in cobalt hydroxide shipments between 2000 and 2024.

According to the researchers, even the lower estimate would be sufficient to fuel a one-gigawatt nuclear reactor for at least a decade.

The investigation did not establish whether the uranium was subsequently extracted or used in China.

DRC takes on Apple: can conflict mineral mining be stopped?

The most extensively documented site was Tenke Fungurume Mining (TFM), one of the DRC's largest cobalt producers.

The mine was owned by US company Freeport-McMoRan until it was acquired by Chinese group CMOC in 2016.

Internal company documents reviewed by the investigators recorded uranium-rich cobalt samples, including a peak concentration of 1,100 parts per million in December 2016 - around 15 times the export limit cited by the investigation.

Further documents indicated that significant uranium concentrations remained in cobalt produced at TFM in June 2021.

"There is an established, known method for removing uranium from cobalt exports," Statius said, adding that it had not been used.

"We have been unable to determine whether CMOC intends to retain the uranium for economic or strategic reasons," he added.

Doug Alexander, a former senior metallurgist at Eurasian Resources Group, suggested there could be two supply chains in the region - one in which contamination is addressed once detected, and another in which lower-quality products containing greater levels of impurities are shipped directly to China.

CMOC rejects findings

CMOC has categorically disputed the investigation. The company said all cobalt hydroxide currently produced by TFM complied with Congolese regulations and international customer standards, with no recorded breaches of permitted limits or trade rules.

Close 

It said it did not know the source of the investigation's historical data and maintained that uranium levels were below the relevant threshold, making a dedicated removal process unnecessary.

CMOC denied carrying out uranium separation or extraction in either the DRC or China. It also challenged the use of 75 parts per million as a universal limit, citing alternative thresholds of up to 100 parts per million.

Freeport-McMoRan did not respond to requests for comment, while the investigators said they stood by their findings.

"Our investigation is based on internal documents from the mine and its owners, spanning nearly a decade, that reveal both the contamination and attempts by certain metallurgical engineers to address the issue," Statius said.

"It also draws on a peer-reviewed scientific paper published in one of the world's top journals."

The investigation also found that a refinery in Kokkola, Finland, had received Congolese material containing uranium.

This has been adapted from the original article in French by RFI's Patient Ligodi

World.title: Senegal: Sall's Chances At UN Secretary-General Role Weakened After First Vote
World.content:
Antonio Guterres's successor as United Nations secretary-general will be named in October. So far, two candidates from the African continent - Senegal's Macky Sall and Uganda's Olara Otunnu - have failed to win sufficient support.

The UN is entering the final stages of choosing a successor to Guterres, whose second five-year term ends on 31 December.

Under the UN Charter, the selection is led by the 15-member Security Council, which holds a series of confidential, non-binding "straw polls" to test support for candidates.



In these ballots, members vote to "encourage", "discourage" or express "no opinion" on each contender.

Later rounds use colour-coded ballots to reveal whether any of the five permanent members (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States) intend to exercise their veto.

The first straw poll took place on 30 July, with further rounds expected throughout August and potentially into September and October until a single candidate secures broad support without a permanent member veto.

The Security Council will then formally recommend one candidate to the 193-member General Assembly, which is expected to confirm the appointment before the end of the year - ahead of the new secretary-general taking office on 1 January, 2027.

Two African candidates

Two African candidates are running this year: Macky Sall, the former president of Senegal, and Ugandan diplomat Olara Otunnu.

But Carlos Lopes, a law professor in South Africa and former executive secretary of the UN Economic Commission for Africa, believes the continent's chances of securing the prestigious post this year are low.

According to him, the first vote, in late July, only confirmed the weakness of Sall's candidacy.

"The official backing provided by President Bassirou Faye came late and failed to restore institutional coherence, if I may put it that way, because Senegal remains deeply divided over his legacy and his candidacy," Lopes told RFI this week.

Sall's candidacy was also poorly received by Senegalese citizens, given that he and his government were charged with corruption and embezzlement related to the management of Covid-19 funds and are accused of inciting electoral violence during the 2024 polls.

Otunnu of Uganda is already a respected figure in UN circles - as Uganda's permanent representative, he was a key architect of the introduction of what is now known as the "straw poll" (the indicative vote).

"This historic contribution is not enough, however, to offset his late entry into the race," said Lopes. "His political track record is rather difficult to decipher, marked by zig zags and a strained relationship with the current president. Consequently, his diplomatic prestige belongs more to history than to his current political reality."

Neither candidate has received the support of the African Union.

Senegal ex-president Sall 'could face charges' following public finances report

Regional rotation

Lopes believes the principle of regional rotation - an unwritten custom that alternates leadership posts among the UN's five geographic regional blocs to ensure global representation - also weakens any African bid this year, with this set-up favouring, at least informally, candidates from Latin America and the Caribbean this year.

"I believe Africa risks appearing to challenge a principle from which it has itself greatly benefited in the past," said Lopes. "The two [previous] African secretaries-general, Boutros Boutros-Ghali and Kofi Annan, were able to count on broad support from other regions of the Global South precisely because they respected this rotation logic."

Undermining this principle could also set a precedent that might ultimately work to Africa's disadvantage, he added.

"And I think that is precisely what is already undermining both candidacies from the outset."

First female secretary-general

Close 

Many experts also hope to see a woman secure the post of secretary-general for the first time, with three female candidates in the running.

Rebeca Grynspan is the current head of UN Trade and Development and former vice-president of Costa Rica. She came first in the initial straw poll with 10 "encourage" votes and is widely seen as the frontrunner.

Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana's UN ambassador and former foreign minister, finished second in the first poll with nine"'encourage" votes.

The third is Michelle Bachelet, the former Chilean president and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

"The two best-placed candidates following this first vote are Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett, I believe both have had truly remarkable campaigns. So, I think there is a real chance that one of them could ultimately secure the position," said Lopes.

This article was partially adapted from an interview by RFI's French service.

World.title: Kenya: Ruto, Oburu Lead Broad-Based Parliamentary Retreat in Naivasha Ahead of 2027 Election
World.content:
Naivasha — President William Ruto and Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) Chairman Oburu Oginga are leading a broad-based parliamentary retreat in Naivasha attended by more than 250 National Assembly members and 45 senators, a year ahead of the 2027 General Election.

The retreat brings together lawmakers from across the political divide as the country enters a crucial phase of preparations for the next General Election.

The gathering provides an opportunity for members of the broad-based government to review the administration's priorities, assess progress in implementing its agenda and strengthen cooperation between the Executive and Parliament.

The meeting comes exactly a year before Kenyans are expected to return to the ballot to elect the President, members of Parliament and county representatives.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

President Ruto is leading the retreat alongside Oburu, underscoring the political partnership that has emerged between the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) and ODM under the broad-based government arrangement.

The presence of more than 250 MPs and 45 senators makes the Naivasha meeting one of the largest gatherings of lawmakers under the current political arrangement.

The retreat is expected to provide a platform for lawmakers to deliberate on government priorities and the legislative agenda as the administration enters the final year before the 2027 elections.

The broad-based arrangement has brought together politicians who were previously on opposing sides of Kenya's political divide, with parliamentary cooperation becoming a key feature of the arrangement.

The Naivasha retreat comes as the government seeks to accelerate the implementation of its development and economic programmes ahead of the 2027 polls.

Lawmakers are expected to play a central role in supporting the passage of legislation and oversight measures required to implement government policies.

The engagement also offers the political leadership an opportunity to take stock of the government's performance and identify areas requiring greater attention during the remaining period of the current administration's first term.

Among the issues likely to dominate political discussions are economic growth, the cost of living, job creation, public service delivery, infrastructure development and the implementation of government programmes.

Close 

The retreat takes place as political activity intensifies ahead of the 2027 General Election.

With only one year remaining before the polls, political parties and alliances are increasingly positioning themselves for the contest, while lawmakers face growing pressure to demonstrate the impact of their legislative and development priorities.

The gathering could also offer an indication of the strength of the broad-based parliamentary alliance as the political landscape begins to take shape ahead of the election.

President Ruto has continued to consolidate support among lawmakers from different political parties, while the inclusion of senior ODM leaders in government has reshaped the traditional government-opposition dynamic in Parliament.

The broad-based government was formed following political engagements between Ruto and ODM leader Raila Odinga, creating a working arrangement between sections of the former opposition and the Kenya Kwanza administration.

The attendance of more than 295 lawmakers from both Houses highlights the significance of the parliamentary retreat at a time when political alliances are being tested ahead of the 2027 election.

For the administration, maintaining cohesion within Parliament will remain critical as it seeks to advance its legislative agenda and secure support for key government policies.

For lawmakers, the retreat comes at a crucial point in their five-year terms, with the 2027 election set to determine whether many will retain their seats.

World.title: Sudan: 'It Made Me Dream Again': the Students Refusing to Let War Stop Their Education
World.content:
Sarah Tekhlu was ready to give up on university. An Eritrean refugee, she had already been displaced once from Khartoum to Madani, then again to Port Sudan, as war tore through the country around her. Higher education, she had decided, was a luxury she could no longer afford to want.

"I was about to surrender to the idea that higher education was not necessary because I could not attend college," she says.

Then came a scholarship that changed her mind.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Since the war erupted between rival militaries in Sudan in April 2023, more than 14 million people have been forced to flee their homes, making it the world's largest displacement crisis.

'It made me believe in myself again'

Sarah is one of hundreds of refugee and internally displaced students in Sudan who have kept their degrees alive through the DAFI programme - scholarships backed by the UNHCR-Mastercard Foundation partnership and run with Windle Trust International.

© UNHCR/Assadullah Nasrullah Sarah Tekhlu is a refugee from Eritrea and works as a kindergarten teacher. The money covers tuition and living costs. But for Sarah, studying information management at Comboni College in the capital Khartoum, it offered something harder to put a price on.

"The biggest part is financial support. Also, it gives me psychological support. It made me believe in myself again. It made me dream again."

Azhari Ibrahim knows that feeling too. Displaced from North Darfur to Port Sudan, he was partway through a civil engineering degree at the University of Kordofan when the conflict threatened to derail it entirely.

"Maybe I would finish my university, but I would face so many challenges without the scholarship," he says.

For Azhari, the support went beyond fees. "It helped me in so many aspects, community support and psychological support, because I found someone nearby me."

Not alone

That sense of not being alone runs through the programme. Beyond tuition, students get mentoring, leadership training and the chance to connect with others walking the same path - young people trying to finish a degree while their country is at war.

© UNHCR/Assadullah Nasrullah Azhari Ibrahim fled from North Darfur to Port Sudan. Through peer workshops, students like Sarah and Azhari have become advocates in their own right, helping others navigate scholarship applications and university admissions.

Close 

"Every workshop I went to, I came out stronger, full of dreams and more dreams," Sarah says.

Azhari puts it more bluntly: "Students in Sudan are suffering. They need support at all levels - community support, economic support, and psychological support."

'Peace is the only solution'

Both students see education as something bigger than their own futures. "Education is important, especially for Sudanese. It will help them rebuild their community," Sarah says.

She now works as a kindergarten teacher alongside her studies and dreams of one day opening her own school. "I love working with kids. I hope one day I will have my own school."

For Azhari, finishing his degree is also about giving back, putting his engineering skills to work rebuilding the communities the war has damaged.

Both are clear about what Sudan needs most. "Peace is the only solution," Sarah says. "If there is no peace, we cannot build anything else."

Azhari's message to other young people trying to hold onto their education through war is simple: "Life will not stop. Don't try to stop your learning and don't try to stop your study. You have to engage, become strong, and patient to fulfil all your hopes and dreams."

The UNHCR-Mastercard Foundation partnership continues to support refugee and internally displaced students to pursue higher education, betting that a generation's future doesn't have to be defined by the conflict around them.

World.title: Africa: The World Has Changed. African Countries Must Rethink How They Grow Their Economies
World.content:
analysis

The prolonged disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has exposed how vulnerable Africa's economies are to geopolitical shocks. Fuel prices have remained elevated, squeezing economies that depend heavily on petroleum imports from the Middle East. These include Ethiopia, Kenya, Mozambique, South Africa, Tanzania and Uganda.

This vulnerability also puts at risk the continent's push to escape poverty through what economists call structural transformation: moving workers from low-productivity activities such as subsistence farming into more productive jobs in manufacturing and modern services.

The continent never fully participated in the export-manufacturing wave that transformed East Asia from the 1960s onward. And now Africa's industrialisation ambitions have become even more difficult to realise as geopolitical rivalry, fragmented supply chains and artificial intelligence reshape the global economy.

As an economist who has written about how weaponisation of global trade affects African economies, I believe structural transformation still matters. But it must be reinvented around four priorities:

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

larger markets

reliable electricity

Africa's comparative advantages

agriculture.

Why the old model worked

Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China and Vietnam all industrialised in broadly the same way. They expanded exports of labour-intensive manufactured goods such as garments, footwear, furniture and electronics. These industries created millions of jobs for workers with limited formal education while gradually building technological capabilities, productive firms and efficient logistics networks.

What made this possible was a relatively stable global trading system. Trade barriers generally fell, demand for manufactured goods expanded, and richer countries steadily moved out of low-wage industries as incomes increased. Governments could focus on becoming more competitive because the rules of international trade were comparatively predictable.

Africa never fully benefited from that opportunity. Manufacturing accounts for only about 10% of GDP in sub-Saharan Africa, compared with around 22% in East Asia and the Pacific. The continent's share of global manufacturing has fallen from roughly 3% in the 1970s to less than 2% today.

The continent struggled to establish internationally competitive manufacturing even when the global trading environment was relatively open. Among the factors holding it back were:

unreliable electricity

high transport and logistics costs

small and fragmented domestic markets

weak industrial capabilities

limited access to finance

unpredictable policy.

As a result, many economies remained dependent on commodity exports while importing most manufactured goods.

These longstanding constraints have not disappeared. Instead, Africa now faces a double challenge. It must overcome the structural barriers that prevented the traditional manufacturing-led development model from taking off in the past, and also adapt to a global economy that's changed dramatically. This challenge does not make structural transformation impossible. It simply means the old way of doing it won't work.

Four changes have rewritten the rules

The first change is that trade itself has become a geopolitical tool. Countries use export controls, financial sanctions and control over strategic technologies to pursue national security goals. The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz illustrates this.

The second is that manufacturing can't create jobs on the scale it once did. Automation has reduced demand for the low-skill factory jobs that once absorbed millions of workers.

This matters because by 2030 sub-Saharan Africa is expected to account for roughly half of all new entrants to the global labour force. That's around 15 million young people each year. Creating productive employment will require growth across manufacturing, modern services and higher-value agriculture rather than relying on factories alone.

Third, China has remained competitive in labour-intensive manufacturing. Rising wages led many economists to expect production of clothing, textiles and footwear to relocate to lower-income countries. Instead, China still dominates. This makes it much harder for African producers to enter sectors that earlier industrialisers used as entry points.

The fourth change is artificial intelligence. AI is becoming a general-purpose technology that can help economies move labour and capital into more productive activities. For example:

AI-powered tools can help farmers make better decisions about weather, pests, input use and market prices

businesses can use AI to reduce costs, improve quality and participate in regional and global value chains.

How governments should respond

The African continent still needs millions of better-paying jobs and much higher productivity to reduce poverty and raise living standards. What has changed is the route to achieving those goals.

First, pursue economic security collectively rather than nationally. Structural transformation requires firms to invest in new industries. But they are less likely to do so if export markets are uncertain or supply chains are easily disrupted. A larger integrated market can reduce those risks.

Acting together also gives African countries greater bargaining power as the US, China and Gulf states compete to invest in the continent's digital and physical infrastructure. Full implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area is more urgent than ever.

Second, invest in electricity. It is the foundation of both industrialisation and the digital economy. Manufacturing, digital services and AI-enabled industries cannot grow without reliable power. Yet electricity remains one of the biggest constraints. In sub-Saharan Africa 78% of businesses experience routine power outages. As a result they lose an average 8.4% of annual sales, compared with a global average of 5.2%. In Nigeria 86% of businesses own or share a generator. In Kenya it is 65%; in South Africa 63%.

Close 

This dependence on diesel generators increases reliance on imported fuel: a vulnerable spot.

Third, compete where Africa has genuine comparative advantages: industries linked to natural resources and growing domestic markets. Examples include:

processing critical minerals

agro-processing

construction materials

pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Finally, recognise that agriculture is central to structural transformation, not separate from it. Around half of sub-Saharan Africa's workforce is employed in farming. Higher farm productivity raises rural incomes, releases labour for productive activities and creates demand for manufacturing and services.

AI can accelerate this process by helping farmers.

Countries that successfully connect these new realities to the long-standing goal of shifting workers and resources into higher-productivity activities will be best positioned to achieve sustained and inclusive growth.

Jonathan Munemo, Professor of Economics, Salisbury University

World.title: Nigeria: Declare Your Assets, Serap Tells Tinubu, Atiku, Obi, Other Presidential Candidates
World.content:
Abuja — The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project, has called on the 19 presidential candidates announced by the Independent National Electoral Commission to publicly declare their assets and liabilities and reject vote-buying ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

SERAP also urged the candidates to disclose the assets and liabilities of their spouses and, where applicable, unmarried children below 18 years, as well as the legitimate sources of their significant wealth.

The organisation made the demands in an open letter dated August 8, 2026, and signed by its Deputy Director, Kolawole Oluwadare.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

SERAP urged the candidates to go beyond the minimum requirements of the law by voluntarily embracing higher standards of transparency, accountability and integrity as they seek Nigeria's highest elected office.

Among those listed by the organisation were President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress; former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress; Peter Obi of the National Democratic Congress; Senator Sandy Onor of the Peoples Democratic Party; Omoyele Sowore of the African Action Congress; former Cross River State Governor Donald Duke of the Peoples Redemption Party; and Okwori Ada Elizabeth Frederick of the National Democratic Party.

Others were Chukwu Anita Zugwai of the Young Progressive Party; Rufai Adekunle Omoaje of the Action Alliance; Adenuga Sunday of the Boot Party; Memeh Samuel of the Democratic Leadership Alliance; Nwanyanwu Daniel Danerechukwu of the Zenith Labour Party; and Okereke Sunday Chibuzor of the Labour Party.

On the list, too, were Okereke Iken Esther of the National Rescue Movement; Abbas-Bin Aliyu of the Action Democratic Party; Dikwa Suleiman Mohammed of the New Nigeria Peoples Party; Adebayo Adewole Ebenezer of the Social Democratic Party; Seyi Makinde of the Accord Movement; and Yusuf Kabiru of the Allied Peoples Party.

SERAP said presidential candidates seeking the powers attached to the office should be prepared to subject their personal financial affairs to reasonable public scrutiny before asking Nigerians for their votes.

"Candidates asking Nigerians to entrust them with enormous constitutional powers over public finances, natural resources, appointments and security institutions should be willing, before asking for their votes, to demonstrate that their personal financial affairs can withstand reasonable public scrutiny," the organisation said.

It argued that Nigerians should be able to choose their next president on the basis of policies, competence, integrity, character and vision rather than the financial strength of the candidates.

Close 

According to SERAP, voluntary pre-election asset disclosure would enable voters to identify potential conflicts of interest and scrutinise significant sources of wealth, while providing a baseline for monitoring changes in the assets of candidates who eventually assume office.

The organisation said the 2027 presidential election offered political leaders an opportunity to demonstrate that they regarded public office as a public trust.

World.title: Prince William was 'fuming' over request for Kate Middleton to spell her name differently: book
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Prince William was reportedly "fuming" after King Charles III and Queen Camilla suggested that Kate Middleton change the spelling of her first name when she joined the royal family, according to a new book.

"Charles and Camilla each had a royal monogram that consisted of interlocking C’s beneath a crown, and they expressed concern that a third royal cypher with a C was overkill," Christopher Andersen wrote in his biography "Kate! The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen." "Would Kate mind if she changed the spelling of her full name from ‘Catherine’ to ‘Katherine.’"

Andersen added, "Offended by yet another command from on high essentially aimed at placating Camilla, a fuming William replied on his wife’s behalf. The request was nothing less than ‘insulting,’ he told his father, not only to Kate but to her entire family."

KATE MIDDLETON IS 'INDISPENSABLE' TO ROYAL FAMILY AS SLIMMED-DOWN MONARCHY FACES MOUNTING PRESSURE: EXPERT

A Kensington Palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital they don't comment on books.

"The entire nature of Charles and Camilla's request — that Catherine was adding too many C's to the royal crests — shows just how much image and branding means to members of the royal family. The monarchy really is a giant game of one-upmanship," Andersen told Fox News Digital, adding that from the very beginning of their relationship "William has gone to war for Kate."

William’s top concern has always been for the Princess of Wales’ "safety," but he also came out "guns blazing" in her defense after topless photos of her sunbathing were published in France in 2012.

"He angrily ordered Palace lawyers to sue and even wanted to see those involved prosecuted criminally under French privacy laws," Andersen said. "When they started a family, it was William who made sure that Kate was not forced to take on too heavy a royal workload if it meant that she would have to spend too much time away from their children."

PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FINALLY FEEL FREE TO SHOW AFFECTION IN PUBLIC: EXPERTS

But, he said the king and Camilla "expected her to go along because she has always been a nice, cooperative team player … but didn't take into account the fact that she personally prefers to be known as Catherine and feels very strongly about the name her parents gave her."

While most of the world knows her by her nickname, Kate, her real name is Catherine.

The princess is "genuinely fond" of Charles and assumed that he got the "absurd" idea from someone else, Andersen explained, adding that she didn’t hold any ill will toward him.

"Besides, it wasn't long before they were having to deal with their simultaneous cancer diagnoses, which put everything else in stark perspective," he added.

KING CHARLES CONSIDERED QUEEN CAMILLA 'NON-NEGOTIABLE' AFTER PRINCESS DIANA, AUTHOR CLAIMS

And although Middleton comes off as "kind and compassionate," she still has a "will of steel," he said.

"Kate is very secure about who she is and how she wants to be perceived by the outside world," Andersen said. "Changing her formal given name for such a bizarre, almost comical reason was a bridge too far."

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard called the issue a "nonstarter" and a "lost cause," telling Fox News Digital that Charles and Camilla were thinking with a "business head" since she was known to the world as Kate anyway.

"Although a hopeless endeavour, I can see both sides of the coin," she admitted, explaining that William was not only offended for his wife but for his in-laws as well.

PRINCE WILLIAM REFUSES TO QUIT HOBBY THAT TERRIFIES KATE MIDDLETON: EXPERTS

But "the concerns were brushed aside. It wasn’t important enough to cause a fight. They had bigger fish to fry."

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner called it a possible "volatile moment" between Camilla and the princess as she joined the family, "but nowadays William was there to protect her. Since then, Kate has managed to stay one step behind when Charles and Camilla are around so as not to out stage them."

KING CHARLES SENDS 'DEFIANCE' MESSAGE TO PRINCE WILLIAM WITH BUCKINGHAM PALACE ROOM OFFER TO HARRY: EXPERT

He noted, however, that more recently the 44-year-old is "building a stronger brand in her own right as William tries to take on the reins of Kingmanship."

"If true it’s idiotic," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital of the story. "The idea is simply stupid. And why? Because her name began with C and theirs did!!"

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Andersen also felt the incident "speaks volumes about how conscious the royals are of all the bells and whistles — not just the gold coaches, the castles, and the crown jewels, but things as small as the letters in their crests and coats of arms. It may seem trivial to the rest of us, but to them things like this mean everything."

World.title: 2,200-year-old alcohol found sealed inside ancient tomb — and there's nearly a gallon of it
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Researchers in China recently uncovered a very unusual find: a large bottle containing an alcoholic drink buried for more than 2,200 years.

The ancient alcohol was found sealed in a bronze vessel in a Qin tomb at the Shanjiabao cemetery in China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. The findings were published in the June issue of the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.

The tomb dates to the Warring States period (475-221 B.C.), a turbulent era of rival kingdoms before China's first unification.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER FREEZE-DRIED POTATOES OLDER THAN THE US IN 'EXCELLENT' CONDITION

The preserved liquid was determined to be an ancient cereal-based alcoholic beverage, a fermented grain drink sometimes loosely described as "beer."

Unlike other recent discoveries in which archaeologists found only residue from ancient drinks, the bottle contained an impressive 3,740 milliliters, or 3.74 liters, of preserved liquid.

The researchers were surprised when they encountered the liquid, said Ruru Chen, a researcher at Northwest University's School of Cultural Heritage in Xi'an, China.

"What surprised us even more was the very large volume and the exceptional state of preservation," Chen told Fox News Digital.

SECRET CACHE OF 130-YEAR-OLD WINE UNCOVERED BENEATH MEDIEVAL CASTLE CHAPEL FLOOR

"Considering that this sample dates to the Warring States period, such a good level of preservation is extremely rare."

There was "no noticeable odor and a small amount of sediment at the bottom," she added, and the liquid "appeared clear and light blue-green."

It was found in a bronze bottle with a "garlic-shaped mouth," which Chen said was commonly used by the Qin people to hold alcoholic beverages.

"By combining evidence from organic chemistry, metabolomics, starch grain analysis, yeast remains and other microscopic analyses, we can directly identify the type of beverage once stored inside the vessel and even reconstruct how it was brewed," she said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"To our knowledge, this represents one of the largest volumes of alcoholic beverage residue ever recovered from a Warring States-period archaeological sample, making it an exceptionally rare discovery."

Based on starch grain analysis, researchers found the beverage was brewed primarily from broomcorn millet, with a smaller contribution from wheat and/or barley, Chen said.

"It would have been most similar to a non-distilled alcoholic beverage made from millet, or from a mixture of millet and wheat/barley."

Researchers identified high concentrations of lactic and oxalic acids, along with dozens of other organic compounds consistent with an ancient cereal-based alcoholic beverage.

"Therefore, it would have been most similar to a non-distilled alcoholic beverage made from millet, or from a mixture of millet and wheat/barley," she said.

CLICK HERE TO 

"It would not have resembled a distilled spirit."

Looking ahead, researchers are still hoping to solve some unanswered questions, including why the liquid survived so well for two millennia.

"The relatively dry local environment may have played an important role, but we also suspect that factors such as the bronze vessel itself, its sealing method and the burial conditions contributed to its preservation," Chen said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"These are questions we hope to investigate further in future research."

Researchers also hope that the discovery "will encourage greater interest in the study of ancient Chinese alcoholic beverages and traditional brewing techniques," Chen said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The research follows a similar recent discovery, when researchers in China uncovered evidence of ancient fermented beverages at a Bronze Age cemetery in northwestern China.

Researchers found microscopic residue inside pottery vessels, shedding light on how people brewed beer-like drinks from millet, rice, wheat and barley more than 3,000 years ago.

World.title: Apple Pay text scam threatens $8,250 loss in 35 minutes
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Paul C. in Washington, D.C., received an alarming text claiming Apple Pay had already charged him $8,250 and another $8,250 would go through in 35 minutes. That is the kind of message designed to make your stomach drop before you have time to think.

Paul did the smart thing. He stopped, avoided the callback number and sent the text to us. Let's break down every red flag and show you how to verify a charge without handing control to a scammer.

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com .

FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS

The Apple Pay scam text Paul received

The message claimed $8,250 had already been charged through Apple Pay and warned that a duplicate $8,250 transaction would "auto-approve" in 35 minutes. It told Paul to call an 855 number, quote "Case CA-3321" and "verbally kill the pending charge." We partially masked the callback number so no one calls it accidentally.

Every red flag hiding in this Apple Pay scam text

The message looks chaotic, but nearly every phrase has a purpose. The sender uses dramatic wording, fake authority and a tight deadline to push Paul toward one action: calling the number in the text.

1) The sender and callback numbers do not match

The message came from a number beginning with +44, the international calling code for the United Kingdom. Yet it claims to come from "Apple Pay Account Services" and tells Paul in Washington, D.C., to call a separate 855 toll-free number. A different callback number does not automatically prove fraud. However, an overseas sender directing a U.S. recipient to an unrelated support line should make you stop before calling.

2) The Apple Pay branding creates false trust

The text uses the Apple Pay name several times and signs off as "Apple Pay Account Services." It also arrived as a blue iMessage with the word "Encrypted" shown beneath it. Those details can make the message feel official. However, encryption only means the message was protected while traveling between devices. It does not confirm that Apple sent it. The signature also sounds generic. It does not name Paul's bank, identify the card involved or provide an official Apple support channel.

3) The huge charge and countdown are designed to trigger panic

The first line reads: "$8,250.00 APPLE PAY - 35-MINUTE DEADLINE". The message then claims $8,250 has already disappeared and warns that a duplicate $8,250 charge will be approved in 35 minutes. That raises the threatened loss to $16,500. The exact 35-mcxxcxxcxinute deadline feels calculated. It gives Paul enough time to call while discouraging him from checking Wallet, opening his bank's app or asking someone else for advice.

4) The wording sounds nothing like a real financial alert

The message says Paul's Apple Pay account has "hemorrhaged" money. It calls the situation a "catastrophic fraud event" and claims his contactless limit has been "crushed" to $0. It later tells him to "verbally kill the pending charge." Those words sound dramatic because they are meant to produce fear. A legitimate financial alert would normally use clear terms such as charged, declined, frozen or pending. It would not describe an account as hemorrhaging money or ask you to kill a charge.

5) The supposed merchants make little sense

The first transaction allegedly happened at: "an agricultural processing surplus in Stockton, CA". The second supposedly involved: "a payday lending chain in Modesto". Neither phrase identifies an actual merchant. They sound specific at first because they include industries and real California cities. However, they fall apart when you look closer. A legitimate transaction alert would usually show the merchant's name. It would not rely on vague descriptions such as "agricultural processing surplus."

6) The payment story contradicts itself

The sender claims Paul's contactless spending limit has been "crushed to $0." In the same message, it says the second $8,250 transaction is pending and "will auto-approve in 35 minutes." Those claims do not fit together. If the sender had already blocked contactless activity, why would another contactless charge automatically go through? The contradiction matters because it shows the message was written to create panic rather than explain a real account problem.

7) Every instruction leads back to the scammer

The message says: "Do not ignore this." It then orders Paul: "You must call." The sender provides a case number, tells him to "verbally kill" the charge and warns that the money will be "gone forever" if he fails to respond. It also threatens to blacklist his account and calls this his "only warning." That language gives Paul one supposed solution: call the number in the text. The message never tells him to open Wallet, check his bank's official app or call the number printed on his card. That is the biggest red flag of all. Every part of the message funnels him toward a stranger waiting on the other end of the phone.

AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS

How this Apple Pay callback scam likely works

The text serves as bait. The phone call allows the scammer to take control of the conversation. Once you call, the person may claim to see your account. They could ask for your name, card number or Apple Account email. Next, they may request a verification code and describe it as a way to cancel the charge.

A scammer could also ask you to install a remote-access app. That would let the person view your screen or guide you through financial transactions. Some callback scams eventually instruct people to transfer money into a "safe" account. Others claim they sent an oversized refund and demand that the extra money be returned.

The FTC warns that fake support agents may seek remote access, steal card information or convince people to move money. CyberGuy previously heard from another person whose Apple Pay scam text nearly led to a $15,000 loss. In that case, the caller used personal information and pressure to keep her on the phone while she drove to her bank.

How to check whether an Apple Pay charge is real

Do not call the number in the text. Instead, check through channels you already trust:

Open the Wallet app on your iPhone.

Ways to protect yourself from similar scam texts

These steps can help you check the warning safely without following the scammer's script.

1) Slow down when a message starts a countdown

A deadline can make a fake warning feel real. Give yourself time to check the account independently. A legitimate fraud department will still be there after you close the text and open the official app.

2) Verify the charge through a trusted channel

Do not call the number in the text or reply to the sender. Instead, open Wallet or your bank's official app and review recent transactions. You can also call the number printed on the back of your card. Never rely on contact information supplied in an unexpected message.

3) Never provide verification codes or remote access

A security code can approve a login, password reset or payment. Never read one to a caller, even when the person claims it will cancel a fraudulent charge. Also, do not install an app or share your screen because someone says they need access to fix the problem. 4) Use strong security software

Because this message impersonates Apple, take a screenshot and email it to reportphishing@apple.com.

Kurt's key takeaways

This Apple Pay scam piles on fear from the opening line. The $8,250 charge grabs your attention, while the 35-minute deadline tries to stop you from checking whether any of it is real. Even the strange phrases serve a purpose because they keep the message sounding urgent and severe. Paul made the right move by pausing instead of calling. When an unexpected fraud alert arrives, leave the message and check through Wallet, your bank's official app or the number printed on your card. World.title: Embattled Smithsonian director brought 'Marxist' activism, political agenda to roles through career: historian
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Smithsonian Institution Director Dr. Anthea Hartig has spent decades promoting what one historian described as an activist and Marxist-inspired approach to history, raising questions about whether the nation's premier museum system is being led by an activist rather than an objective historian.

Dr. Jody Edward Ginn argued that Hartig has worked to pivot traditional historical organizations toward activist missions, including during her time as president of the Organization of American Historians (OAH) and her leadership role at the California Historical Society.

"She's asserting herself as a historical scholar who should get the last word on these things," Ginn told Fox News Digital. "Well, there's more than one problem with that. And it starts with the fact that I don't think she's really ever been a historian, she has been an advocate, an activist."

Ginn said his research into Hartig's professional background yielded accounts from her former associates indicating that she has "long been known for" pushing such agendas.

HISTORIAN BLASTS SMITHSONIAN'S ACTIVISM SHIFT AFTER FIRST VISIT IN OVER A DECADE: 'COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PLACE'

One early example Ginn cited was Hartig's 1995 research article, "In a World He Has Created," published by the California Historical Society, where Hartig later served as an executive director for seven years beginning in 2011.

In the article, Hartig drew on the economic and social theories of Karl Marx to analyze the success of California's agricultural citrus industry, arguing that a wealthy "ruling class" had manipulated the Southern California landscape to reinforce and validate its own class power, including by physically concealing cheap labor.

By the second paragraph of the article, Hartig referenced photographs depicting the nearby estates and characterized them as "the standard paternalistic, elitist, racist, sexist promotional fare of the age."

Ginn argued that the article is significant because it "doesn't read as a historical examination" but instead as a "political treatise."

"The whole thing does not read as a scholarly historical examination," Ginn said. "It reads as advocating that for a particular point of view, a Marxist-informed point of view, and not an objective historical analysis."

WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ IN RESURFACED 2025 CLIP

In 2023, Hartig assumed a one-year presidency at the Organization of American Historians, an organization Ginn said is "well on the record for advocating for people's activism."

According to the organization’s website, "The OAH actively collaborates with advocacy partners to support history and advance our mission."

Hartig's 2024 presidential address, published in the Journal of American History, was titled "Where Have All the Women Gone? Let's Bring Them Back before It's Too Late."

In the address, Hartig asserted that despite decades of activism and historical research, women's "lives, accomplishments, bodies, and futures matter less."

Ginn also criticized Hartig's recent Capitol Hill testimony in July, in which she said the Smithsonian's work is governed by nonpartisanship and "does not take sides in America's political debates."

Ginn said he found the account dishonest, arguing that Hartig's research background and resurfaced video footage directly contradict her testimony.

The resurfaced video shows Hartig asserting that history should be used as a "tool of social justice."

"She's denying it. That's the most perplexing thing for me," Ginn said.

"That's kind of the first frustrating thing for me as a scholar," he added. "It's kind of hard to have an honest conversation about this, when they won't acknowledge the obvious."

World.title: A quiet rush for gold is sweeping the globe — here's why countries are stockpiling it
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As wars spread, trade tensions escalate and inflation remains stubbornly high, governments around the world are quietly buying more gold, a sign many are preparing for a future they believe will be more uncertain.

A new World Gold Council survey found that 89% of central banks expect global gold reserves to grow over the next year, while a record 45% plan to add to their own holdings. Central banks are the institutions that manage a country's money and financial reserves.

For everyday Americans worried about rising prices, growing government debt and what comes next for the economy, the trend is worth paying attention to.

A SINGLE TRUMP ANNOUNCEMENT SPARKS BILLIONS IN LOSSES ACROSS GOLD AND SILVER

Some experts say central banks buying more gold is a sign they expect today's economic and geopolitical uncertainty to stick around.

That's because gold has long been considered a safe place to put money during wars, market turmoil and periods of high inflation because it isn't tied to the economy or policies of any one country.

Why governments are buying gold

For decades, central banks have invested heavily in U.S. Treasurys — government debt backed by the U.S. and considered among the world's safest investments.

But Cavatoni said many countries are now adding gold because they want another layer of protection against inflation, global instability and economic turmoil.

WHAT TRUMP’S NEXT PICK TO LEAD THE FEDERAL RESERVE MEANS FOR YOUR WALLET

"They're looking at diversifying," Cavatoni said. "And gold fills that need because it provides liquidity, diversification and protection against inflation and geopolitical uncertainty."

The World Gold Council survey backs that up.

About 90% of central banks said gold's performance during times of crisis is one of the main reasons they hold it. Another 84% cited its role as a long-term store of value and inflation hedge, while 83% said it helps diversify their reserves.

Those reasons have fueled a global buying spree.

Who's buying?

While China has received much of the attention, it isn't alone. Central banks around the world have been steadily increasing their gold reserves.

According to Cavatoni, Poland, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, the Czech Republic, Chile, Jordan and Ghana have also been among this year's biggest buyers.

While the United States still owns more gold than any other country, much of today's buying is coming from developing economies looking to rely less on foreign currencies they don't control.

"The U.S. has no natural need to continue to accumulate more reserves in the form of gold," Cavatoni said.

The survey also found that nearly three-quarters, or about 74%, of central banks expect the U.S. dollar's share of global reserves to be lower five years from now, while they expect gold's share to increase.

What does this mean for everyday people?

The same concerns driving governments to buy gold are also attracting individual investors.

One trend that surprised Cavatoni is that even with gold trading near record highs, people aren't rushing to sell.

"It tells me a couple of key things," Cavatoni said. "People are less likely to let go of their gold."

For everyday investors, the trend doesn't necessarily mean they should rush out and buy gold. But it does offer a window into how some of the world's largest financial institutions are preparing for uncertainty, with central banks placing greater value on diversification and protection against economic and geopolitical risks.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

And individual investors appear to be showing a similar mindset.

Instead of cashing in, both investors and many central banks are holding on to or building their gold positions, a sign that they see gold less as a short-term investment and more as long-term financial insurance in an increasingly unpredictable world.

World.title: Descendant of slaves shames Smithsonian’s woke ‘indoctrination’ against the ‘greatest nation on earth’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Black bishop and author Earl Walker Jackson, a descendant of enslaved ancestors, is criticizing the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for what he said amounts to anti-American "indoctrination" against the "greatest nation on earth."

Although his great-grandparents were enslaved, Jackson believes that "if you were born an American, you hit the proverbial lottery because you have more opportunity and hope than any people living anywhere else on the planet."

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Jackson said the latest controversy over what the White House described as the Smithsonian’s woke "ideological capture" angered him because of what he views as smears against the U.S.

"It makes me angry when people do this to our country, but it's sad too because what it tells me is that the indoctrination machine is hard at work convincing people [of] this narrative," he said. "This is a wonderful country; it's the greatest nation on earth. And you've got people so indoctrinated into seeing our country sliced and diced into race and ethnicity and class and income and so forth that they fail to understand the blessing of the United States of America."

SMITHSONIAN'S TAXPAYER FUNDS FACE CHOPPING BLOCK AS GOP DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY FOR 'WOKE' HISTORY

The Smithsonian National Museum of American History (NMAH) has faced scrutiny over what the White House described as the museum’s promotion of woke ideology. In July, the White House Domestic Policy Council released its 162-page "Saving America's Story" report, concluding that the NMAH has undergone "ideological capture." The report included images of exhibits and placards and information about museum curators and leaders.

After the report was released, congressional hearings brought additional scrutiny to NMAH leadership. NMAH Director Anthea Hartig, who has led the museum since 2019, drew particular attention. A resurfaced video of a presentation by Hartig shows her calling "history as a practice" a "prime tool of social justice."

In a presentation to University of California, Los Angeles, students in February 2025, Hartig asserted that the "United States’ long and violent racial history continues to be present in our reckoning, if you will" and said that "redress in the form of reparation, of course, goes beyond acknowledgement of wrongdoing; it should leverage responsibility, it should think about the act of correction, as we pursue restorative justice and, for us [on the call], restorative justice through history."

In response, Jackson said, "She talks about how history should be a tool of social justice. No, history should be facts about what has happened in the past and leave others to draw their own conclusions about what those facts mean."

"But no, she wants to use history to try to get people to think a certain way and respond a certain way and, namely, to be somewhat angry and bitter and resentful of our country because of our past," he continued.

WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING

Though the White House report was released less than a month ago, Jackson said he has been warning for years about what he describes as woke ideology at the Smithsonian.

In 2015, he confronted the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery over the inclusion of Planned Parenthood founder Margaret Sanger in its exhibit on civil rights leaders. He took issue with Sanger’s inclusion because he said, "She was an elitist, she was a eugenicist, she was racist, she admired Adolf Hitler [and] she spoke for the Ku Klux Klan."

Jackson believes much of what he describes as ideological capture at the Smithsonian, as well as in the broader education system, entertainment industry, journalism and sports, stems from the influence of Howard Zinn’s book "A People's History of the United States."

Jackson said Howard Zinn "was a professed anarchist" who "wrote that book as a polemic against America."

He said he is "amazed at how few Americans understand that book has been more influential in teaching American history than any other book that the public schools or colleges have ever used," emphasizing, "And it's still being used."

As an example, Jackson pointed to materials currently promoted by the Zinn Education Project that draw a line between deportation operations today and Great Depression-era deportations, which the materials say derived from "a program of ‘racial expulsion,’ rooted in racism."

Fox News Digital reached out to Planned Parenthood, the Margaret Sanger Papers Project at New York University, the Zinn Education Project and the Zinn Trust for comment.

SPEAKER JOHNSON WARNS STUDENTS ARE 'INDOCTRINATED' TO SEE US THROUGH 'WRONG LENSES' AS NATION CELEBRATES 250TH

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"If you're learning that from the very beginning of your education, my goodness, by the time you're an adult and you've been through 20,000 hours of that, no wonder we've got people protesting outside of ICE facilities, and no wonder you've got people at the Smithsonian talking about America as if we're the worst place on earth to live," he said. "They frankly have been brainwashed and indoctrinated into it."

Jackson countered, "There is no place on earth that has been more affirming of human dignity, offered more opportunity for human flourishing. And frankly acknowledged in spite of the apparent differences that we have, that we are ultimately one nation under God."

"I think loving America is easy because, you’re right, I'm the great-grandson of slaves, I am a product of a broken home and foster care, and yet my life has just been wonderfully blessed," he concluded. "First, of course, by the grace of God, but also because I live in a country where anything is possible, where you're free, where you can dream, you can strive to fulfill your God-given gifts and talents and abilities."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Smithsonian Institution, National Portrait Gallery and NMAH for comment.
