World.title: Discovering Mexico: Puebla
World.content:
Listen to this article

Puebla is for you if you like: Colonial history, sweeping mountains, racing while holding tortillas

Mexico’s fourth-largest city, Puebla, has more going on beneath its colonial facades than most visitors realize. Its historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, holds 2,619 monuments — more than any other city in the Americas — plus the tallest cathedral bell towers in the country. The city’s well-preserved architecture has also made it a go-to filming location, standing in for 18th- and 19th-century Mexico and Spain in productions including “Frida” and “Man on Fire.”

All of this is before you get out into the wider state, where sweeping mountain ranges, active volcanoes and enormous cacti dot the landscape. The state is one of the last stops in southern Mexico before the jungle claims the country. We’ve collected some of our best pieces from the last few years, to help you experience one of Mexico’s most genuine — and stunning — regions.

Puebla’s capital — also, conveniently, called Puebla — is filled with the sort of magic that only Mexico’s oldest cities can really offer. Many of the nation’s most definining moments and people have filled these streets (and the tunnels underneath them).

Puebla’s identity is tied up in origin stories, although some more verifiable than others. Its early name, Puebla de los Ángeles, traces to a 1531 account of a bishop’s vision guiding Spanish settlers to the site. Its signature dish, mole poblano, is said to have been improvised by nuns at the Convent of Santa Rosa in 1680 when an archbishop arrived unannounced and the kitchen had little to offer but chilis, chocolate, nuts and stale bread. And on Nov. 18, 1910, the Serdán family home became the site of the first armed clash of the Mexican Revolution, two days before Francisco Madero formally launched the uprising; the bullet-scarred house is now a museum.

While its days of defining Mexico’s future are probably behind it, Puebla remains a fascinating destination for anyone who wants to understand how the modern country truly came to be.

While Oaxaca, Sonora and Yucatán often vie for the title of Mexico’s gastronomic heart, it’s really Puebla that deserves the credit for much of the nation’s great cuisine.

Puebla’s culinary reputation rests on three dishes with stories as rich as their flavors. Mole poblano, which rumour claims is a single flash of nun-driven inspiration, remains the most famous of Mexico’s 300-plus regional moles. Chiles en nogada, with its patriotic red, white and green color scheme, traces back to a 1821 feast honoring independence figure Agustín de Iturbide. Tacos árabes, born from Middle Eastern shawarma techniques brought by 1930s immigrants, is the progenitor of the iconic pastor.

The state is quite a bit more than just colonial architecture and great food, though. Just outside Tehuacán, Puebla’s second-largest city, sits a landscape that looks like it belongs on another planet.

The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Biosphere sprawls across 145,255 hectares of protected desert, home to more than 2,500 species of cacti — tall and candle-thin, round as beach balls, or shaped like something out of a sci-fi set. A day inside it turns into a full sensory tour of the region: 2,000-year-old salt flats still worked by hand at Zapotitlán Salinas, a lunch built around cactus flowers and hibiscus water (with insects on offer for the adventurous) and a pottery workshop in Los Reyes Metzontla where clay deposits — leftovers from an ancient sea — get shaped into earthy, hand-thrown crockery.

In a small Puebla town two hours north of the city, an entire industry is built on Christmas spirit. Chignahuapan produces an estimated 70 million hand-blown ornaments a year, and inside the country’s largest esfera factory, the process starts with nothing more than a glowing-hot glass tube and a steady breath. From there, silver coatings, hand-mixed paint and careful dabs of glitter transform each piece into something ready for the tree — some ornaments even take a year to master.

Step inside the traditional workshop where trompos, Nativity scenes and piñata-shaped baubles come to life, one painstaking layer at a time.

In the days before Day of the Dead, the Puebla town of Huaquechula holds a tradition unlike anywhere else: the trueque, an ancient barter market where locals swap goods — peanuts, sugar cane, homemade bread — for everything needed to build their altars. Families trade for marigolds and cockscomb flowers, while vendors carry stacks of pan de muerto in its many forms, from bone-topped loaves to body-shaped muertitos dusted in red sugar.

Beyond the market, the town runs on hospitality: cooks prepare meals for hundreds of festival participants around the clock, and visitors are waved into strangers’ homes to see their altars up close. Huaquechula offers a rare, local variation on Mexico’s most iconic holiday — equal parts market day, family reunion and open-door celebration of the dead.

Our glimpse into Puebla ends on a unique note. The annual Carrera de la Tortilla, a 5-km race through Tehuacán that retraces the daily walk local women make to market, tortillas and all. Most runners came from Santa María Coapan, the self-proclaimed “Tortilla Capital” of Mexico, who run decked out in traditional Mixtec dress.

Part sporting event, part tribute to the women who keep the tradition alive, it’s one of Puebla’s more charming annual customs.

Puebla, Where Magic Lives in Every Journey / Sub English

Watch this video on YouTube

How to get there

When it comes to arriving in Puebla, it really only makes sense to arrive from Mexico City.

By air

Puebla International Airport: 45 minutes from the city center, the airport offers connections to almost every major Mexican destination, plus Newark, Houston and Los Angeles.

Mexico City Benito Juarez (AICM): The big one. About 2 hours (traffic permitting) from central Puebal. Available from everywhere in Mexico, and almost every major global airport besides.

Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA): The eternally troubled AIFA is finally beginning to come into it’s own. 2.5 hours away, it offers similar domestic connectivity to AICM and flights in from Colombia, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic and Cuba.

By road

Mexico City: 135km (83 miles) somewhere between 90 minutes and 3 hours, depending on when you travel. National holidays often lead to enormous tailbacks, but tackling the drive early on a weekday often means you can get there in less than two hours.

World.title: Ohuira Bay communities weigh federal plan for Sinaloa ammonia plant
World.content:
TOPOLOBAMPO, Mexico — When federal officials finally unveiled a plan last week to address the 12-year conflict over a nearly completed ammonia plant beside Ohuira Bay, Indigenous Yoreme activist, rural sociologist and law student Melina Maldonado did not feel relieved.

She felt crushed.

After six days of roundtable discussions, she had begun to feel hopeful; it seemed they were really taking in new information and seeing a different side to the debate. The proposal led her to believe otherwise.

“They didn’t listen to our reasons for saying no,” Maldonado said. “They listened for a way to make it a yes.”

The federal proposal promises environmental safeguards, community monitoring and public investment around the German-backed GPO-Proman plant in northern Sinaloa state. But it leaves the project’s operation largely intact — and that has exposed the fundamental divide at the heart of the conflict: The government is offering ways to make the plant safer, while the communities closest to the bay are still adamant that it should not operate at all.

Those communities must now take the proposal into their own assemblies and, using their traditional Indigenous consensus-based governance model, decide whether to accept it. Until then, the blockade outside the gate to the plant — now in its 72nd day — remains in place.

A proposal, not an agreement

The plan emerged after six days of talks involving federal and state officials, representatives of GPO-Proman and members of the ¡Aquí No! (Not Here!) collective, which is led by Yoreme-Mayo communities surrounding Ohuira Bay and has become the principal force opposing the plant.

Federal officials presented the proposal as a path toward resolving a conflict that has become one of Mexico’s longest-running and most contentious environmental battles. But movement leaders emphasized that no agreement has been reached and that they do not have the authority to accept the plan on behalf of their communities.

The proposal must first be explained and discussed in assemblies in Ohuira, Paredones, Lázaro Cárdenas and Topolobampo. These communities surround the Santa María-Topolobampo-Ohuira lagoon system, a Ramsar wetland of international importance, and would bear the plant’s most direct impacts.

Community response to the proposal

“We have to hold our own internal assemblies,” said Claudia Susana Quintero, a Yoreme educator, resident of the village of Ohuira and one of the leaders of ¡Aquí No! “We have to explain it to the community, analyze it and decide how we are going to reach consensus.”

The representatives’ role is to take the proposal home and return with a decision reached collectively — not to accept it on their communities’ behalf.

The US $1.6 billion plant, designed to produce 2,200 metric tons (2,425 tons) of ammonia a day, is reportedly about 88% complete. Opposition began soon after the project was approved in 2014 and has centered on threats to fishing, the lagoon ecosystem, industrial safety and what Yoreme communities describe as a deeply flawed Indigenous consultation.

The current protest began in late May, when residents tried to block the movement of massive absorption towers from the port. Protesters later shifted their encampment to the plant entrance, where they have remained through extreme heat and intense storms.

A project the government considers strategic

President Claudia Sheinbaum has defended the plant as important to Mexico’s goal of achieving greater food sovereignty. Ammonia is a principal raw material in nitrogen fertilizers, and Sheinbaum has said Mexico currently imports nearly all the fertilizer it uses, apart from production by state-owned company Fertinal.

She has also emphasized that the plant is nearly finished, and that it underwent an environmental review and received majority support in the government-led Indigenous consultation — a process the four communities closest to Ohuira Bay continue to dispute.

The Economy Ministry says the GPO plant could reduce Mexico’s fertilizer imports by as much as 70% and keep approximately US $500 million now spent on imports within the Mexican economy.

For the federal government, the plant is part of a broader strategy to reduce dependence on imported agricultural inputs. Opponents say that national goal does not justify concentrating the risks in their communities.

What the government put on the table

The proposal leaves the ammonia plant in place, but would significantly alter how it operates. Among its most significant provisions, the plan calls for GPO-Proman to stop drawing water directly from Ohuira Bay and instead use water discharged through a nearby Federal Electricity Commission canal.

Opponents have long warned that the plant’s authorized system would pull large volumes of seawater from the lagoon and return warmer, saltier water, potentially disrupting fish and shrimp nurseries. Under the new plan, wastewater would instead be carried offshore rather than released back into the lagoon system.

The plan also proposes a new environmental baseline study, continuous water-quality monitoring and an oversight body made up of community members, scientists, government officials and company representatives. Additional measures would address sewage and agricultural runoff already entering the bay, as well as emergency preparedness and civil protection.

Other commitments focus on longstanding community needs, including housing, education, fishing infrastructure and assistance in certifying local shrimp and crab products so they can command higher prices.

Economic development plans in Topolobampo

Federal commissioner Mauricio Rodríguez Alonso, who has led the talks, stressed at a Tuesday news conference that the plan grew out of dialogue among the communities, GPO-Proman and government agencies. He said the company had agreed in principle to its commitments.

Ulises Pinzón, Topolobampo’s municipal representative, said the package could bring meaningful benefits. He was particularly encouraged by provisions giving communities a voice over future petrochemical development.

That is especially significant in Topolobampo, which the federal government has designated as an economic development hub where chemical and petrochemical industries are among the priority sectors. The plan would also keep proposed methanol and urea plants and a port terminal on hold unless the communities agree to them.

But Pinzón noted that many of the promises involve responsibilities the government should already be fulfilling, rather than concessions from GPO-Proman itself.

“On paper, honestly, I see an attractive proposal,” he said. “The question is how we can ensure that these commitments are actually fulfilled.”

That distinction — between a promising announcement and a binding, enforceable agreement — is now one of the central questions confronting the communities.

The risk that remains

For opponents of the plant, the most troubling unresolved issue is the danger of a catastrophic ammonia release. The government proposal does include new safeguards: an emergency-response center, joint industrial-risk monitoring, water curtains around pipelines and storage tanks, and a regional civil-protection plan — something Rodríguez acknowledged does not currently exist.

But movement leaders say emergency planning and mitigation cannot eliminate the underlying danger documented in the company’s own risk assessment.

According to that assessment, a five-minute leak could create a high-impact zone extending roughly 15 kilometers (9 miles) from the plant, encompassing Topolobampo and nearby Yoreme communities. A broader impact zone could extend as far as 45 kilometers (28 miles), reaching toward Los Mochis and other surrounding communities.

“That risk is still there, and it is still not clear to us,” Pinzón said. “The first people affected would be those of us who live in Topolobampo.”

Loss of life is not remediable

Company project documents show the plant is designed to store up to 75,000 metric tons (82,670 tons) of anhydrous ammonia near populated communities. Quintero said the proposal may reduce certain environmental impacts, but it cannot eliminate the consequences of a major industrial accident.

“You can remediate many things,” she said. “What you cannot remediate is the loss of life.”

For Maldonado, this is where the government’s proposal misses the point. Her own community, the Yoreme fishing village of Lázaro Cárdenas, looks across the bay at the plant every day.

The communities’ opposition has never been limited to the plant’s effects on water quality or fisheries, she said. It is rooted in the belief that a facility carrying such risks should not operate near people’s homes. She pointed to the company’s brightly colored risk map.

“This is the risk zone the company itself identified,” she said. “And now they are minimizing it or pushing it into the background.”

A decision made under threat

The communities will not consider the proposal in a political vacuum. Several of the movement’s most visible leaders have received threats related to their opposition to the plant and now live under government protection measures.

Four of ¡Aquí No!’s most visible leaders, including Maldonado, Quintero and Ohuira traditional governor Felipe Montaño, have been enrolled in Mexico’s federal protection mechanism for human rights defenders and journalists. Protection measures can include bulletproof vests and government-issued panic buttons intended to summon help in an emergency.

But Quintero said such equipment offers little comfort as the communities prepare to deliver an answer that government officials and project supporters may not want to hear.

“I know my community is going to say no,” she said. “But now the government is putting us in the line of fire against the rest of society that says yes.”

She worries that the plan could recast defenders as obstacles to jobs and economic development, increasing the pressure on people who have already spent years facing intimidation for speaking publicly.

“A bulletproof vest and a panic button are not going to help me much if someone decides to act tomorrow,” Quintero said.

The experience, she added, has gradually consumed the rest of their identities.

“We are no longer mothers, daughters or sisters,” she said. “We are nothing more than defenders.”

From shock to strategy

By Thursday evening, the mood inside the movement had begun to shift.

Enrique Ayala, a longtime activist staying at the blockade, said movement leaders spent six hours Thursday with scientists and lawyers analyzing the proposal and plotting their next steps.

“The government proposal is one-sided,” Ayala said. “They are pushing ahead with their project.”

But after years of being ignored, Ayala sees the government’s willingness to sit down with them as progress.

“We have to get up, keep going and make proposals of our own,” he said. “After 12 years when they paid us no attention, now we have them sitting at the table.”

And despite the government’s apparent intention to move the plant toward operation, Ayala said the movement has not abandoned its original goal.

“We still believe we can get the company to leave,” he said. “Sometimes you have to dream.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: From the archive: A guide to Mexican nicknames and how they’re given
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of giving nicknames in Mexico.

If you’ve spent much time among Mexicans, you’ve probably realized something. They love to give each other — and consistently use — nicknames.

I’m not just talking about diminutives of names, though these are also popular. Guillermo, for example, is Memo for short, the same way Bob is a diminutive of Robert.

How nicknames work in Mexico

There’s Alex for both Alejandro and Alejandra, Chio for Rocío, Lalo for Eduardo, Lola for Dolores and Chava for Salvador. There’s also short versions of double names, like Mafer for María Fernanda, Majo for María José and my favorite, Lucifer for Lucía Fernanda, a name most people do not give their kids. And of course, the classic “-ito” and “-ita” can go at the end of many names. So sometimes people call me Sarita, and my partner Juanito. Careful with using these, though, as they’re often infantilizing, and as you very likely know, some people do not like being infantilized.

So you get the idea: most names here have a shortened version. But Mexicans don’t stop there!

My nicknames

I’ll admit that this makes me very happy. As a kid, I never had a nickname, and I was jealous that I didn’t. Thinking back, it’s probably better; it wouldn’t have necessarily been a nice one, as I was both a crybaby and a showoff. Come to think of it, I might still be both of those things. Thankfully, I don’t currently have any nicknames related to either of those characteristics. Yet.

I do have some other fun ones though. “Sirena polar” — polar mermaid — might be the most creative, given to me by a friend of my ex-husband who was amazed that I insisted on swimming in ice-cold water after a hike. For reasons unknown to me, this same friend also often called me “cara de nutria”: otter face. Maybe because otters swim in cold water, too? Another friend, not quite as creative, simply calls me “mi gringa favorita.” I’d be more flattered if I weren’t one of the only gringos she knows.

The futility of protesting against your nickname

Many nicknames are purposefully funny, and sometimes shocking. And from what I can tell, people don’t seem to be insulted by them. Sometimes I wonder if they actually are bothered but know that trying to fight back against the Mexican urge to make fun of everything is futile.

So when you get a name like “El Frijol” because you’re very dark-skinned, you just go along with it, I guess?

In the particular case of another acquaintance, the guy was tall and good-looking. He was married, but seemed to have no shortage of women interested in him, or of self-esteem.

I always wanted to ask him if the nickname bothered him, but we were never close, so the opportunity was lost. But I did get to ask my ex-husband, who his friends had nicknamed “el bello camello” — the beautiful camel — supposedly because they thought he looked Arab.

The new generation of nicknames

Could this be one of those cultural things that’s dying out with more socially conscious and sensitive younger generations? I don’t think it is, as my daughter, age 11, has several nicknames herself. At school, her friends sometimes call her Plana, which means flat. It’s a synonym of her name, Lisa, which means “smooth” in Spanish and is often featured on hair conditioner bottles. And in her Scout troop, every kid has a nickname, each one the name of a bird. She’ll also respond to “Mona,” which is kind of nice. “Mona” is more of a Spanish-from-Spain word for “pretty,” but in this case, of course it’s about the Mona Lisa.

So perhaps the tradition will continue?

Don’t take yourself too seriously

After several years of watching the issue of how people address them being taken very, very seriously north of Mexico, I’ll admit that I find the ability to joke around with silly nicknames refreshing. Like all humor, though, it’s very culturally specific; there are plenty of unspoken rules regarding when it’s funny and good-humored and when it’s not.

It’s not that I want the freedom to be gratuitously mean, which is something very different. But I do think that it’s always worth it to not take ourselves so seriously all the time, something most of us can agree makes us generally unlikable.

So if you get a nickname here, try to go with it. Because people don’t get nicknames when they’re not being included in a group. Even if it’s not one you’d have chosen for yourself, it’s a signal that you are part of a community; people know you.

They might be making fun, but it’s affectionate fun. Try to take it that way.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: US suspends avocado certs, fracking studies continue and Peru rift ends
World.content:
Listen to this article

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s daily press conferences set much of the week’s agenda, moving from children’s social media use to a government transparency decree, a high-profile murder, fracking policy and a diplomatic breakthrough with Peru. Economic data told a mixed story too, with a strengthening peso set against a sharp drop in Pemex profit and a battered Sinaloa economy.

Security developments also kept pace, including the arrest of a former Guerrero governor on Ayotzinapa-related charges, a jump in U.S. rewards tied to CJNG’s new leadership, and a fresh U.S. suspension of avocado certifications in Michoacán. On the public health and safety front, a UNAM cheating scandal, a UNESCO deadline to protect the vaquita and a cyclosporiasis scare linked to Riviera Maya travel all drew attention.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Economy: Peso strengthens and avocado trade swings

Mexico’s currency extended a 10-day rally to reach its strongest level since February, helped by the Bank of Mexico holding its benchmark rate at 6.5% and a weaker US dollar following a soft American jobs report. The gains came even as Pemex reported a 70% annual drop in second-quarter net profit, which the state oil company attributed to higher financial costs, tax obligations and an unfavorable exchange rate. Economic disparities varied widely by region, with Sinaloa’s economy posting the worst quarterly contraction of any Mexican state, a result economists linked to the ongoing cartel conflict in the region.

Tourism data added to the mixed picture: Tourism GDP fell 0.8% quarter-over-quarter in the first three months of the year, according to INEGI, driven by a 5.9% quarterly drop in spending by foreign visitors, even as domestic tourism consumption rose 0.5%.

Mexico’s avocado trade also had a volatile week. New data showed exports to the U.S. jumped 35% in the first quarter compared to the previous year, according to Sader. Days later, however, the United States suspended avocado export certifications in Michoacán, citing an unspecified “threat against U.S. interests” — the third such suspension in just over four years. Michoacán’s governor deployed additional state security operatives and the Defense Ministry sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the region in response.

Energy: Government edges toward fracking while banning it in Mexico’s top basin

A government expert committee tasked with assessing “sustainable fracking” recommended prohibiting hydraulic fracturing in the Tampico-Misantla basin, Mexico’s largest-potential shale region, citing environmental, social and biodiversity concerns. Sheinbaum said her government would respect that recommendation, which she reaffirmed at Friday’s mañanera.

However, the committee recommended continued evaluation of two other northern basins. Reuters reported that pilot projects in Coahuila and Tamaulipas could begin as soon as next month if approved, as Mexico looks to reduce its reliance on natural gas imports from the United States.

Security: Pressure builds on cartels and past officials

U.S. authorities raised the reward for CJNG’s new leader, Juan Carlos Valencia González, to $25 million following the February death of cartel founder “El Mencho,” as part of more than $100 million in reward offers and new visa restrictions. Domestically, federal agents dismantled four illicit fuel processing centers in San Luis Potosí, Hidalgo and Morelos, seizing roughly 1 million liters of fuel. In Sinaloa, Sheinbaum acknowledged the murder of content creator César Gastélum, the ninth social media personality killed in the state since 2024. And in a case tied to one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved crimes, federal authorities arrested former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre on charges of concealing video evidence related to the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students; Sheinbaum said the arrest was not politically motivated.

Public health, environment and education

Sheinbaum laid the cornerstone for a new IMSS hospital in Oaxaca, part of a three-facility “Health City” complex the government frames as a step toward its planned Universal Health Service. And after the U.K. reported dozens of cyclosporiasis cases among travelers, Mexico stepped up health inspections at Riviera Maya hotels, while officials said the country has not been identified as the outbreak’s source.

Officials at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) confirmed that nearly 60,000 applicants must retake its entrance exam after widespread cheating undermined its first-ever online exam.

Separately, UNESCO gave Mexico until February to show concrete action to protect the critically endangered vaquita porpoise, of which only seven to 10 are believed to remain.

Diplomacy and governance

Sheinbaum signed a decree aimed at strengthening federal government transparency, which officials said would compel departments to disclose more information following the 2024 elimination of the INAI watchdog agency.

On the diplomatic front, Sheinbaum announced that Mexico and Peru would restore relations severed since November, after former Peruvian Prime Minister Bettsy Chávez was granted safe passage from asylum in Mexico’s Lima embassy.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test several threads left open this week: whether Mexican and U.S. officials can resolve the security concerns behind the avocado certification suspension, whether President Sheinbaum’s panel of experts finds acceptable conditions in northern Mexico to move fracking pilot projects forward, and how UNAM’s rescheduled in-person exams — set for mid-to-late August — play out after the cheating controversy. Mexico also faces UNESCO’s February deadline on vaquita protections and continued scrutiny of Sinaloa’s cartel-driven economic slowdown.

The insurer’s recurring profit hit R$888.6 million in Q2, with a 22.3% return on equity. Growth is solid, but credit risks linger.

Porto Seguro profit hit a record in the second quarter, with recurring net income of R$888.6 million (US$174 million). Return on equity reached 22.3%, a standout level for Brazilian financials. The result shows the insurer’s core operations are firing, even as credit pressures build in its banking arm.

Porto Seguro Profit Beats Expectations

Porto Seguro’s recurring net profit for Q2 2026 reached R$888.6 million (US$174 million), up 1.2% from a year earlier. That beat market forecasts, according to analysts at Genial Investimentos, who had modelled R$889 million.

Consolidated profit came in at R$879.4 million, nearly flat year over year. Revenue grew faster than profit.

Recurring revenue rose 11% to R$11.0 billion (US$2.15 billion), driven by higher premiums in auto, health, and life insurance. The insurer also saw solid gains in its property and casualty lines.

The 22.3% return on equity is the headline metric. It reflects disciplined underwriting and efficient capital use.

For comparison, many Brazilian banks struggle to reach a 15% return in a high-rate environment. Porto Seguro revised its 2026 guidance after the strong quarter, now expecting revenue growth of 9% to 12%, up from an earlier range.

What Porto Seguro does. Porto Seguro S.A., together with its subsidiaries, provides a range of insurance products and services in Brazil and Uruguay. It offers auto, residential, travel, cell phone, life, motorcycle, notebook and tablet, photo and video, smart and games, bike, real estate, green card, bail, and moving insurance products, as well as reinsurance, combined…

What Drove the Quarter

Auto insurance remains the core engine, with premium growth in the high single digits. The company has been gaining market share from competitors like Mapfre and Sancor Seguros, thanks to its digital claims app.

Health insurance was a surprise upside, with premiums jumping 15% year over year. New corporate contracts aided that growth, offsetting a weaker performance in credit insurance, where defaults ticked up.

Investment income also contributed, as Brazil’s Selic rate remains above 10%. That added about R$150 million (US$29.4 million) to pre-tax profit, per company materials.

Expense discipline improved, with the combined ratio improving to 87.5% from 89.1% a year ago. Lower claims frequency in auto and better cost controls drove the gain.

Credit Risk Lingers

Not everything is rosy. Porto Seguro’s banking arm, which offers payroll loans and credit cards, saw higher delinquency rates.

Analysts at Genial warn that this segment could drag on future results. The bank’s loan book grew 8% in the quarter, but provisions for bad debt rose 12%.

Management downplayed the risk, saying credit quality remains within historical norms. Still, the market is watching closely, and rising credit risk is not unique to Porto Seguro — Brazilian consumers are stretched by high interest rates and inflation.

That is why the insurer’s core insurance business matters more than its financial arm. The company is tightening underwriting standards for new credit and cutting exposure to high-risk borrowers, which should limit losses if the economy slows further.

Porto Seguro Profit and Why It Matters for Investors and Expats

If you hold Brazilian equities or bonds, Porto Seguro’s results offer a clear signal. The insurer’s profitability shows that consumer spending on protection remains resilient, even with a sluggish economy.

That is a good sign for the broader insurance sector. For expats living in Brazil, Porto Seguro is likely your auto or home insurer, and a strong, profitable company means stable premiums and better claims service.

The record profit suggests the firm will keep investing in digital tools for customers. Foreign investors often use Porto Seguro as a proxy for Brazilian domestic consumption, and the stock trades on the B3 exchange with a dividend yield of around 4%.

This result could support the share price soon. But note the credit risk — if you are considering buying the stock, watch the banking arm’s delinquency data, as a spike would dent earnings power despite the insurance strength.

Outlook for the Rest of 2026

Porto Seguro’s guidance implies a strong second half. Management sees net profit growth of 3% to 6% for the full year, assuming stable credit conditions.

That would put annual recurring profit near R$3.5 billion (US$685 million). The main risks are external, as a deeper recession in Brazil could push up claims and credit losses.

Regulatory changes in auto insurance pricing could also compress margins, though no such moves are imminent. Analysts at UOL Economia say the market already prices in a solid year, with the stock trading at about 8 times forward earnings.

If credit improves, there could be upside. For now, Porto Seguro looks well positioned, with its insurance business growing, its capital base strong, and its brand trusted.

The record profit is a reminder of why it is a market leader.

Both figures were released on 7 August 2026. What is Porto Seguro’s return on equity? Recurring return on equity reached 22.3% in the quarter. This is well above the average for Brazilian financial companies, which often hover around 15%. Why did Porto Seguro revise its 2026 guidance? Strong revenue growth, especially in auto and health insurance, led management to raise its revenue growth forecast to 9–12%. The company expects full-year profit growth of 3–6%. Is Porto Seguro’s banking arm a concern? Credit risk is rising, with higher delinquency in payroll loans and credit cards. But the insurance business is strong enough to offset this. Analysts advise monitoring credit provisions in coming quarters.

Brazil’s largest pharmacy chain posts strong revenue growth in the second quarter, though rising costs squeeze margins and slow profit gains.

Raia Drogasil posted another quarter of blockbuster sales growth, but investors are watching one thing: profits are not keeping pace. Brazil’s largest pharmacy chain lifted gross revenue 18.3% to R$12.778 billion (US$2.5 billion) in the second quarter of 2026. Adjusted net profit climbed just 7.4% to R$432.7 million (US$84.7 million).

Why Sales Growth Accelerated at Raia Drogasil

Revenue growth picked up speed, from 13.9% in 2025 to 18.3% this quarter. The push came from new store openings and a 55% jump in digital sales, as the company noted in its earnings release.

The chain added dozens of new drugstores across Brazil during the quarter. Management also leaned into its online sales push, which now makes up a growing slice of total revenue.

With over 3,000 stores nationwide, the company is expanding into smaller cities where demand for health products is rising. This geographic reach helps steady revenue even when the economy wobbles.

Why Profit Growth Lagged Behind

Profit growth slowed to single digits, even as revenue boomed. Analysts at Eu Quero Investir said higher operating costs and spending on logistics expansion are eating into what is left at the bottom line.

Rising wages and freight charges also added pressure. The company is investing heavily in new warehouses and delivery networks, which costs money today but should pay off later.

core earnings Holds Steady

Core operating earnings reached R$1.017 billion (US$199.1 million), up 17.9% year over year. The core operating earnings margin stayed flat at 8.0%, according to Reuters via InfoMoney.

That steady margin shows management is keeping costs in check despite inflationary pressures. But the slower net income growth suggests interest expenses and taxes are weighing more heavily.

Digital Push Drives Gains

Digital sales were the standout, jumping 55% in the quarter. This fits with Raia Drogasil’s strategy to build out its digital ecosystem, including the 4Bio platform.

The company’s adjusted net income includes 4Bio, its digital health arm. That segment is growing fast but requires heavy upfront investment, which drags on overall profitability.

Why This Matters for Latin America Investors

For anyone living in or invested in Brazil, this report signals where consumer spending is heading. Pharmacy retail is a defensive sector that reflects domestic demand, and an 18.3% revenue jump shows Brazilians are spending on health despite a still-tight economy.

But the profit lag is a caution flag. It suggests that expanding quickly in Brazil’s competitive retail landscape means accepting thinner margins, at least for now.

Analyst Views and Share Price

Despite the modest profit growth, investors cheered the results. Shares rose 5.4% on the news, as earnings per share beat expectations, according to Investing.com transcripts.

The market likely focused on the strong top line and stable core earnings margin as proof that Raia Drogasil’s expansion strategy is working. Over the longer run, higher volume should eventually turn into higher profits as digital efficiencies kick in.

Brazil’s Pão de Açúcar grocer posts R$252m Q2 loss as debt talks and stockouts weigh on sales.

GPA loss widens as a debt restructuring disrupts its stores. The company behind Pão de Açúcar reported a net loss of R$252 million (about US$49 million) for the second quarter of 2026, up from R$217 million a year earlier. That is a 16.2% worsening, and the GPA loss story shows why investors are nervous. Revenue fell to R$4.228 billion (US$828 million), down 6.1% from the same period last year. The stock has been shaky as markets weigh the recovery plan against a tough consumer environment.

What Is Driving the GPA Loss?

The company points to several reasons for the wider loss. The main one is the debt restructuring process, which temporarily caused stockouts and hurt store supply.

Ending the Aliados format also hurt, along with a shift in online sales and changes to which stores it operates.

A calendar effect added to these issues. Together, these items cut sales by 6.1%, the company said.

If you leave them out, the drop would have been just 0.8%, offering a bit of hope for investors. But the market isn’t cheering yet.

Profitability Holds Up, Barely

Despite the loss, core operating earnings rose 7.3% to R$450 million (US$88 million). The core operating earnings margin was 10.6%, up from a year earlier.

That suggests the core grocery business isn’t collapsing, even as restructuring costs pile up.

The real pain is elsewhere. The financial result was negative R$385 million (US$75 million), a 26.4% worsening from last year.

High debt and interest payments are eating into any gains from operations, a familiar story for Brazilian retailers in trouble.

The Restructuring Hangover

GPA entered a court-supervised debt renegotiation with creditors, called extracourt protection from creditors. The plan isn’t approved yet, and that uncertainty is hitting store shelves.

Suppliers have tightened credit, leading to what Brazilians call ’ruptura’ – empty spaces where products should be.

Fewer products mean fewer sales. It’s a vicious cycle: the restructuring hurts the business, which then struggles to generate cash to repay creditors.

The company says it’s temporary, but investors are watching the approval timeline closely.

Consumer Squeeze Adds Pressure

Beyond the restructuring, the bigger picture is tough. Household debt and late payments are rising in Brazil, and consumers are carefully choosing where to spend.

Competition for grocery shoppers is fierce, from discount chains to delivery apps.

GPA’s strategy is to cut some store formats and focus on its main brands. The Aliados model is gone, and online sales have been scaled back to what the company calls ’rebalanced’ levels.

The goal is to protect profit margins, but sales volumes are hurting.

How to Read the Numbers

One detail can be confusing: some headlines mention a R$204 million loss, others R$252 million. The lower number comes from ongoing operations only.

The higher one includes R$49 million (US$9.6 million) from discontinued operations – assets GPA is selling or closing.

For a fair view, look at the full consolidated number, as Valor reported. Also watch for one-off items.

The core operating earnings margin is cleaner than the bottom line, and at 10.6%, it shows the business is still operationally sound.

Why It Matters for You

If you live in Brazil or invest in Latin American retail, GPA is a good indicator. It shows how high debt and weak consumer spending can clash.

The company’s stockout problem is your problem too if you shop at Pão de Açúcar – you might have seen empty shelves.

For investors, the lesson is clear: turnaround stories in Brazil come with execution risk. Promises of ’temporary’ disruption can stretch.

Keep an eye on the court’s decision to approve the plan, which could set off the next big move in the stock.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did GPA’s loss widen in Q2 2026? GPA’s net loss grew 16.2% to R$252 million (US$49 million). The main reasons were the debt restructuring disrupting supply, stockouts, ending the Aliados format, and a calendar effect. The financial result also worsened, with a R$385 million negative swing. Is GPA’s core grocery business still profitable? Yes, operationally. Adjusted core earnings rose 7.3% to R$450 million (US$88 million), with a margin of 10.6%. The net loss comes mostly from high financial costs, not from selling groceries at a loss. What is the ’ruptura’ issue at GPA stores? Ruptura means stockouts – products missing from shelves. During the restructuring, suppliers tightened credit, so fewer items were delivered. This hurt sales and customer trust, though GPA says it’s temporary. When will GPA’s restructuring be finalised? The court-supervised debt plan is awaiting approval by a judge. The company expects it soon, but no exact date is set. Investors are watching for that approval as a key event.

Revenue surges 27.6% to US$4.18 billion, but net income falls to US$125 million as jet fuel prices bite. Cargo and passenger demand keep the carrier flying high.

LATAM Airlines posted second-quarter net income of US$125 million, a sharp drop from US$241.6 million a year earlier, even as revenue climbed 27.6% to US$4.183 billion and passenger numbers hit 21.1 million. The culprit is jet fuel, with prices nearly doubling year over year and eating into what would otherwise have been a stellar quarter for Latin America’s biggest carrier. For investors watching the region, this is the clearest signal yet that demand is booming but costs are the new battleground.

Revenue Growth Masks A Profit Squeeze: LATAM Airlines

Passenger revenue rose 27.9% to US$3.613 billion, driven by strong demand across South America and the growing Brazil network. Cargo added US$510 million, up 21.8%, as e-commerce and perishable exports keep freighters busy.

Total revenue of US$4.183 billion marks the company’s strongest top-line performance since its 2020 bankruptcy restructuring. The airline has rebuilt its finances and expanded operations since then, but new challenges have emerged.

Operating income tells a different story. Adjusted operating income fell 46.3% to US$227 million, down from US$423 million in the same quarter last year.

That decline highlights how quickly fuel prices can undermine growth. The operating margin now sits at 5.4%, roughly half of what it was in the year-ago quarter.

Fuel costs nearly doubled, according to Reuters, and that single line item erased most of the gains from higher ticket prices and fuller planes. Every extra dollar of revenue is being absorbed by the fuel bill, leaving less room for profit.

LATAM executives called the environment volatile, but note that jet fuel prices have started to ease in recent weeks. They remain cautious about the coming months.

What The Numbers Mean For Investors

The profit drop looks alarming at first glance, but the underlying business is healthy. Revenue per passenger is holding up, load factors remain above 80%, and the company is carrying more people than ever.

The fuel spike is cyclical, not permanent. Airlines have weathered similar cost pressures before, and demand remains robust across the region.

LATAM lifted its 2026 earnings outlook on August 4, citing easing fuel prices and sustained demand. That guidance upgrade came alongside the earnings release, sending shares up in early trading.

Management sees the worst of the cost pressure behind them. They pointed to forward fuel curves that suggest softer prices in the second half.

For investors holding LATAM shares, the key metric to watch is operating margin recovery. If fuel prices stay flat through the second half, even modest revenue growth should push margins back toward double digits.

If they fall further, the upside is significant.

Brazil Network Expansion Drives Growth

The carrier continues to expand its Brazil footprint, adding routes and frequency at São Paulo’s Guarulhos hub. Brazil is now the single largest revenue market for LATAM, surpassing Chile for the first time.

Domestic Brazilian traffic grew at double-digit rates in the quarter. That growth helped offset weakness in other markets and solidify the carrier’s regional leadership.

International routes from Brazil to North America and Europe are also performing well. The company has leaned into premium cabins and business travel, which carry higher margins.

That mix shift helped offset some of the fuel cost pressure. Premium demand has remained resilient, even as leisure travel shows signs of softening.

Cargo remains a quiet success story. The freight business generated US$510 million in revenue, with flower exports from Colombia and salmon from Chile leading the way.

LATAM’s cargo network now rivals its passenger operation in profitability terms. The company has invested heavily in dedicated freighter aircraft and ground handling.

Why This Matters For Latin America

LATAM is the region’s bellwether airline, so its numbers reflect the broader health of Latin American travel and trade. Strong passenger growth signals rising middle-class incomes and a rebound in business travel.

The cargo surge points to robust export activity across Chile, Colombia, and Brazil. Air freight remains critical for perishable goods and high-value electronics.

If you live in the region or invest here, even modest profit issues matter. Fuel cost spikes affect every airline in Latin America, from Avianca to Gol.

LATAM’s ability to pass costs to passengers while keeping planes full is a leading indicator for the sector. Watch the next two quarters for margin recovery as fuel prices stabilise.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did LATAM’s profit fall despite higher revenue? Jet fuel costs nearly doubled year over year. That single expense outweighed strong revenue growth from passengers and cargo. Operating income fell 46.3% to US$227 million as a result. How many passengers did LATAM carry in Q2 2026? LATAM carried 21.1 million passengers in the second quarter of 2026. Load factor reached 81.8%, meaning more than four in five seats were occupied across its network. Did LATAM raise its guidance for the rest of 2026? Yes. On August 4, LATAM lifted its full-year 2026 earnings outlook. Management cited easing fuel prices and sustained demand across South America and key international routes. How does Brazil contribute to LATAM’s performance? Brazil is now LATAM’s largest revenue market, surpassing Chile. Domestic traffic grew at double-digit rates, and the carrier is expanding routes from São Paulo’s Guarulhos hub to North America and Europe.

World.title: Mexico Remittances Top US$5.47 Billion in June, Extending Streak
World.content:
Mexico · Economy

Key Facts June total — US$5,471.8 million in remittances, up 4.2% from a year earlier.

— US$5,471.8 million in remittances, up 4.2% from a year earlier. Growth streak — Fifth consecutive month of year-on-year increases, per BBVA Research.

— Fifth consecutive month of year-on-year increases, per BBVA Research. Operations — 13.0 million sending transactions in June, up 0.3% year on year.

— 13.0 million sending transactions in June, up 0.3% year on year. Average size — Each remittance averaged US$422.0, a 3.9% rise from June 2025.

— Each remittance averaged US$422.0, a 3.9% rise from June 2025. First half — Remittances reached US$30,759.2 million, up 3.1% from H1 2025.

— Remittances reached US$30,759.2 million, up 3.1% from H1 2025. Data source — Banco de México published the figures on 3 August 2026.

Money sent home from abroad grew 4.2% year on year, marking five straight months of gains. For families and investors, the flow looks durable.

Mexico remittances topped US$5 billion again in June 2026, hitting US$5,471.8 million, up 4.2% from a year earlier. That marks five straight months of growth, according to BBVA Research. The flow of money from Mexicans abroad keeps defying predictions of a slowdown. Banco de México released the data on 3 August 2026, and the numbers show a resilient lifeline for millions of households. Even as some analysts expected a cooling, the steady rise points to deep-rooted economic ties.

Workers queue at a Mexico City bank to receive remittance payments in June 2026, a month when average transfers rose to US$422 each. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the June Data Shows: Mexico remittances

The June figure of US$5,471.8 million is the second-highest monthly total ever recorded, close to the record set in May 2025. Some Mexican media rounded the number to US$5,472 million; the underlying trend is unchanged.

This month also marked the fifth consecutive year-on-year gain, a streak that began in February 2026.

Remittances grew by 4.2% year on year, accelerating from the 3.5% pace seen in May. That momentum pushed the first half of 2026 to US$30,759.2 million, up 3.1% from the same period in 2025.

The steady climb has eased worries among economists who feared a sharper slowdown.

Banxico also counted 13.0 million sending operations in June, up just 0.3% year on year. The average remittance rose 3.9% to US$422.0, which means senders are wiring larger sums, not more frequently.

This shift toward bigger transfers is a notable change from earlier years.

For families in states like Michoacán and Oaxaca, this money often covers groceries, school fees, and home repairs. In urban centers like Guadalajara, it supports consumer spending and small businesses.

The extra cash also helps households build savings or pay down debts, adding a layer of financial security.

A fifth straight month of growth suggests the dollar earners in the US are not tightening their belts. That is good news for consumer spending in Mexico, which accounts for about two-thirds of economic activity.

It also signals that the labor market for Mexican workers remains strong despite broader uncertainties.

The steady rise also reflects the resilience of migrant workers who have held onto their jobs despite economic uncertainty. Their consistent support back home is a testament to the deep ties between communities on both sides of the border.

These flows are more than numbers; they are a lifeline for millions.

Why Growth Persists Despite the Headwinds

You might expect remittances to fall when the US economy wobbles. That has not happened so far in 2026.

Instead, the flow has grown steadily, surprising many forecasters who had predicted a decline.

BBVA Research notes that Mexican employment in the US remains strong, particularly in construction and services. These sectors hire many Mexican-born workers, and their wages have kept pace with inflation.

That stability gives workers the confidence to send more money home.

The average remittance of US$422.0 reflects that stability, since senders feel secure enough to wire larger amounts. The count of individual transfers barely moved, which shows that existing senders are doing more, not that new ones are joining.

This pattern points to a mature and dependable flow.

Another factor is the US dollar. When the peso weakens, each dollar buys more pesos back home.

This makes remittances more valuable to recipients, even if the dollar amount stays the same.

That dynamic encourages migrants to send money even if their wage growth is modest. Banxico’s data show the peso traded around 18.2 per dollar in June, slightly weaker than a year earlier.

A softer peso boosts the local purchasing power of each transfer.

For recipients in Mexico, that makes every remittance go further in local terms. It also gives them a little buffer against rising prices for food and other basics.

The combination of steady employment and currency effects helps explain the persistent growth.

The First Half: Steady, Not Spectacular

The six-month total of US$30,759.2 million may look less flashy than the monthly record, but it still marks solid progress. Growth of 3.1% is slower than the double-digit surges seen in 2021 and 2022, but it is consistent.

This steadiness is a sign of maturity in the remittance market.

It also beats most forecasts from late 2025, which predicted flat or negative numbers due to US immigration policy changes. Those predictions have so far not materialized, and the data shows resilience.

The trend, while moderate, provides a reliable foundation for household budgets.

Mexican media, including El Financiero and Mexico News Daily, credited Banxico’s August 3 release with easing fears of a remittance crash. The data shows no such crash.

Instead, it confirms that the flow remains robust and broadly in line with previous years.

Instead, it shows a maturing flow: more dollars per transaction, fewer new senders. That mix suggests the money is becoming more reliable, which is good for mortgage lenders and consumer credit companies.

For them, predictable remittance income reduces the risk of defaults.

What It Means for Your Money and Investments

If you have a bank account in Mexico or hold peso-denominated bonds, remittance growth matters. The money enters the economy through small towns and urban neighborhoods, often spent on groceries, school fees, and home improvements.

This steady inflow supports local businesses and financial institutions.

Retailers like Walmart de México and FEMSA see direct benefits. So do construction material suppliers, as families often use extra cash to build or renovate homes.

The spending ripples through the economy, creating jobs and income in various sectors.

For those of you watching the macro picture, remittances also support Mexico’s current account balance. They provide a steady inflow of foreign currency that offsets some trade deficits.

This helps keep the peso from depreciating too sharply against the dollar.

The central bank does not set interest rates based on remittances alone, but a stable flow reduces external vulnerability. That is one reason why the peso has held up against the dollar despite global turbulence.

For investors, that stability is a reassuring sign in uncertain times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What were Mexico’s remittances in June 2026? Mexico remittances reached US$5,471.8 million in June 2026, up 4.2% from US$5,251 million in June 2025. The figure represents a fifth consecutive month of year-on-year growth. How much did Mexico receive in remittances in the first half of 2026? The first half of 2026 brought US$30,759.2 million in remittances, a 3.1% increase from US$29,834 million in the same period of 2025. The growth was driven by higher average transfer sizes rather than a jump in transaction numbers. Why are remittances to Mexico still growing in 2026? Strong employment among Mexican workers in the US, especially in construction and services, keeps incomes stable. A slightly weaker peso relative to the dollar also boosts the value of each transfer in local terms, encouraging larger remittances. Where does the money from Mexico remittances typically end up? Most remittances go to households in states like Michoacán, Guerrero, and Oaxaca. They fund daily expenses, education, and home building. These flows also support local retailers and banks, contributing to consumer demand across the country.

Sources: Bank of Mexico; BBVA Research; Reuters

Local experts say Paraguay is now the world’s fourth-largest bitcoin producer, powered by dirt-cheap Itaipu hydro electricity. No independent ranking confirms it, but the numbers are turning heads.

Paraguay bitcoin is the story, and it is turning into a global sensation. Paraguay has quietly become a hotspot for bitcoin mining, powered by some of the cheapest electricity on Earth. Local experts say it now ranks as the world’s fourth-largest producer of the cryptocurrency, behind only Russia, the United States, and the United Arab Emirates. That claim comes from Joaquín Morínigo, a Paraguayan crypto specialist, as reported by La Tribuna on 7 August 2026. No independent audit yet confirms the ranking, but the underlying numbers are hard to ignore.

Cheap Hydro Power Draws the Miners: Paraguay bitcoin

Paraguay generates nearly all its electricity from renewable hydro sources. The Itaipú and Yacyretá dams produce far more power than the country can use, so surplus energy goes to miners at bargain rates.

Miners love that mix because bitcoin mining is energy-hungry, and cheap power is the single biggest cost.

Paraguay’s fully renewable grid also helps firms meet environmental scrutiny from investors and regulators.

The state utility, Ande, manages a special industrial group for intensive energy users. That group includes 41 companies with combined demand of 943.8 MW, about 13.5% of Paraguay’s Itaipú allocation, according to Bloomberg Línea Brasil on 6 August 2026.

For scale, one major mining complex uses electricity equivalent to the consumption of 20,000 middle-class homes. That is a facility-level example, not the national total, but it shows the sheer size of these operations.

The demand also highlights how much surplus power Paraguay has, as the Itaipú dam alone generates more than 14,000 MW in peak seasons.

Miners often set up near the dam to cut transmission losses. That proximity keeps their power bills low and their operations efficient.

HIVE Digital Leads the Foreign Push

Canada’s HIVE Digital is the most visible foreign player. In January 2025, it acquired Bitfarms’ Yguazú facility in Paraguay for US$56 million, closing the deal in the first quarter of that year, as reported by FinanceFeeds.

HIVE then expanded aggressively. By 31 March 2026, it had delivered 300 MW of new capacity in Paraguay across three phases: June 2025, early September 2025, and 10 November 2025, according to its FY2026 results covered by TradingView.

The company now has 440 MW of global power capacity, with most of it in Paraguay. That scale makes Paraguay central to HIVE’s strategy, not a side project.

HIVE’s moves have drawn attention from other miners. The combination of low power prices and a stable, dollar-linked economy makes Paraguay an attractive alternative to places like Kazakhstan or Texas.

The firm’s phased approach also lets it manage construction and grid integration smoothly. Each new phase adds capacity without overwhelming local infrastructure.

Government Support Grows

Paraguay’s government has warmed to crypto mining, seeing it as a source of export revenue. The sector generated more than US$250 million in 2025, Morínigo told La Tribuna.

That money flows into the economy through taxes, wages, and purchases of local goods. It also helps offset Paraguay’s energy surplus, which would otherwise go to waste.

The blockchain summit in Asunción this week, covered by Asunción Times, highlighted the government’s pro-crypto stance. Officials framed mining as a bridge to broader tech investment, including artificial intelligence data centres.

But there are concerns. Miners consume vast amounts of power, and some worry about strain on the grid during dry seasons.

Ande has tried to manage that risk by setting strict conditions for the special industrial group.

Officials also see mining as a way to attract foreign direct investment. That steady inflow of capital could help fund wider infrastructure projects.

Why This Matters for Investors

If you invest in Latin American energy, infrastructure, or tech, Paraguay’s bitcoin boom is a signal. It shows how surplus hydro power can be monetised, turning a national resource into a global export.

For expats and nomads in Paraguay, the mining boom brings jobs and investment. It also means more demand for housing, logistics, and services near the big mining sites.

The lack of an audited ranking should temper your excitement. Morínigo’s claim is plausible, but it is based on media reports, not verified data.

Watch for hard numbers on hashrate and output. If Paraguay truly produces this much bitcoin, someone will eventually publish audited figures.

Until then, treat the fourth-place claim as a strong indicator, not a fact.

The country’s stable currency and open economy add to its appeal for long-term capital. That stability is a rare commodity in the region.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Paraguay really the world’s fourth-largest bitcoin producer? Local expert Joaquín Morínigo says yes, per La Tribuna on 7 August 2026. He places Paraguay behind Russia, the US, and the UAE. But no independent, audited ranking has confirmed this claim, so treat it as an expert opinion, not a verified statistic. What makes Paraguay so attractive for bitcoin mining? Paraguay generates all its electricity from renewable hydro sources, mainly Itaipú and Yacyretá. That means abundant, low-cost power with a clean reputation. Miners can buy surplus energy at rates far below global averages, making their operations highly profitable. How much money does bitcoin mining bring to Paraguay? The sector generated more than US$250 million in 2025, according to Morínigo as reported by La Tribuna. That includes revenue from electricity sales, taxes, and associated economic activity. The government expects this figure to grow as more miners set up operations. Which companies are investing in Paraguay’s bitcoin mining? HIVE Digital is the most prominent, having acquired Bitfarms’ Yguazú facility for US$56 million in January 2025 and then expanding to 300 MW of capacity by November 2025. Other firms in the state utility’s special industrial group total 41 companies with 943.8 MW of combined demand.

Sources: Paraguayan crypto-sector estimates; ABC Color; Reuters

World.title: Uruguay Green Hydrogen: US$6B HIF Project Hangs in Balance
World.content:
Uruguay · Energy

Key Facts Six billion — US dollars at stake in HIF Global’s Paysandú project, cited by Álvaro Delgado in El Observador.

— US dollars at stake in HIF Global’s Paysandú project, cited by Álvaro Delgado in El Observador. Tariff tussle — HIF seeks US$40 per megawatt-hour; the state utility counters with US$45 per megawatt-hour under conditions.

— HIF seeks US$40 per megawatt-hour; the state utility counters with US$45 per megawatt-hour under conditions. Historic scale — Would be Uruguay’s largest private investment ever, per political and media reports.

— Would be Uruguay’s largest private investment ever, per political and media reports. Paraguay threat — Delgado warned on Friday the project could relocate if talks drag on.

— Delgado warned on Friday the project could relocate if talks drag on. No signature — The final investment contract remains unsigned, confirmed by Fernanda Cardona on 21 July.

— The final investment contract remains unsigned, confirmed by Fernanda Cardona on 21 July. Job creation — 1,400 construction roles and 300 permanent jobs reported by Búsqueda.

— 1,400 construction roles and 300 permanent jobs reported by Búsqueda. Export engine — First module could ship US$253 million annually; US$1 billion once all phases run.

Government warns the Paysandú investment could shift to Paraguay if electricity pricing disputes are not resolved. The final contract remains unsigned.

Uruguay green hydrogen is the story. Uruguay’s government has issued a stark warning: the HIF Global green hydrogen project, potentially the largest private investment in the nation’s history, could still fall through. The project remains unsigned, and a dispute over electricity pricing threatens to push the US$6 billion venture to Paraguay. If the deal collapses, you lose a landmark energy transition opportunity that promised 1,400 construction jobs and over US$1 billion in annual exports.

The Paysandú site would house US$2.881 billion in industrial plants and US$1.277 billion in renewable parks, creating 300 permanent jobs. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The Pricing Deadlock: Uruguay green hydrogen

The core issue is the electricity tariff. HIF Global wants to pay US$40 per megawatt-hour.

State utility the state utility insists on US$45 per megawatt-hour, with conditions attached, as reported by Búsqueda.

This difference is not trivial. Green hydrogen production is energy-intensive.

The tariff dictates whether the entire project closes economically for Uruguay, according to the Ministry of Industry, Energy and Mining.

What Uruguay Risks Losing

The numbers are staggering. HIF’s own plan, cited by Búsqueda, estimates US$5.385 billion in total investment.

This breaks down into US$2.881 billion for industrial plants and US$1.277 billion for wind and solar parks.

The remaining US$1.226 billion covers infrastructure, effluent treatment, and energy transport.

At full buildout, the Paysandú facility would produce 880,000 tons of synthetic fuels per year.

The export potential is equally significant. The first module alone could generate US$253 million in average annual exports.

Once all four phases are operational, that figure surpasses US$1 billion annually.

A Political Flashpoint

Former government official Álvaro Delgado made the warning public on Friday.

He accused his successor, Fernanda Cardona, of stonewalling the negotiation, according to El Observador and Telenoche.

Delgado explicitly stated the investment could move to Paraguay if Uruguay fails to close the deal.

Cardona responded on 21 July that no investment contract exists yet.

Búsqueda reported on Thursday that the ministry still believes the proposal does not close for Uruguay.

The government’s position is that current electricity-supply terms are not economically viable for the state.

Timeline and Next Steps

This is not a quick fix. The memorandum of understanding is still being finalised.

After that, HIF must secure financing and customer contracts before making a final investment decision.

That decision could come by late 2027 or even during 2028, according to Búsqueda.

The long timeline means there is room for negotiation, but also ample opportunity for the deal to unravel.

For investors, the critical question is political will.

If the two sides cannot bridge the US$5 per megawatt-hour gap, the project stalls.

If they can, Uruguay secures its energy future and a generational economic boost.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the HIF Global project in Uruguay? It is a green hydrogen and synthetic fuels mega-project planned for Paysandú. It aims to produce 880,000 tons of synthetic fuels annually using wind and solar power, with a total estimated investment of US$5.385 billion to US$6 billion, depending on the source. Why is the project at risk? The final investment contract has not been signed. The government believes the electricity tariff of US$40 per megawatt-hour sought by the company does not close economically for Uruguay, while state utility the state utility is pushing for US$45 per megawatt-hour with conditions. Could the investment really move to Paraguay? Former official Álvaro Delgado warned on Friday that this is a real risk if negotiations stall. The government is working to keep the project in Uruguay but has not confirmed any relocation plans. When will a final decision be made? After the memorandum of understanding is completed, HIF needs financing and customer contracts. Búsqueda reports the final investment decision could come by late 2027 or during 2028.

Sources: Uruguay’s government and state utility UTE; El País (Uruguay); Reuters

World.title: Haiti TPS Ends: 350,000 Face New Reality
World.content:
Haiti · Society

Key Facts Court ruling — Judge Ana Reyes lifted the last stay on August 5, 2026, allowing the TPS termination to stand.

— Judge Ana Reyes lifted the last stay on August 5, 2026, allowing the TPS termination to stand. Effective date — The US homeland security and immigration agencies treated Haiti TPS as terminated effective July 27, 2026.

— The US homeland security and immigration agencies treated Haiti TPS as terminated effective July 27, 2026. Population affected — About 330,000 to 350,000 Haitian nationals held TPS nationwide.

— About 330,000 to 350,000 Haitian nationals held TPS nationwide. South Florida impact — More than 158,000 Haitian TPS holders live in the region; 52,000 were in its workforce.

— More than 158,000 Haitian TPS holders live in the region; 52,000 were in its workforce. Work documents void — The immigration agency says employment authorization cards in categories A12 and C19 are no longer valid for jobs.

— The immigration agency says employment authorization cards in categories A12 and C19 are no longer valid for jobs. Legal status — Those without another immigration basis are now undocumented and face deportation risk.

— Those without another immigration basis are now undocumented and face deportation risk. Voluntary departure — The homeland security department is promoting a $2,600 payment for those who leave voluntarily.

A federal court cleared the way on August 5, and now Haitian TPS holders across the US — especially in South Florida — are navigating a changed legal landscape.

Haiti TPS is over, and roughly 350,000 people are feeling it. A federal court order on August 5 lifted the final block, and now Haitian TPS holders across the United States must decide what comes next. For many in South Florida, that means retreating from public life, losing jobs, or planning a departure.

A Miami community centre saw a drop in foot traffic in early August 2026, as Haitian TPS holders stayed home after the protection ended. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Changed on August 5: Haiti TPS

The termination of Haiti TPS was set in motion months ago. The US homeland security and immigration agencies treated it as effective July 27, 2026.

But a series of court challenges kept the policy in limbo until last week.

On August 5, Judge Ana Reyes issued a short order. She stated the prior stay was “no longer in effect,” clearing the way for the administration to end protections.

CNN and other outlets confirmed the ruling on the same day. That ended months of uncertainty for hundreds of thousands of families.

Who Is Affected

The numbers are stark. The Miami Herald counted 330,735 Haitian nationals with TPS approval as of March 31.

Other outlets and advocacy groups round that figure to about 350,000 nationwide. That is nearly the entire population of a mid-sized American city.

South Florida carries a heavy share of the burden. More than 158,000 Haitian TPS holders call the region home.

A Princeton researcher, Phillip Connor, told the Herald that about 52,000 were in the local workforce. Their departure or loss of work would ripple through the area’s economy.

Work and Daily Life

The end of TPS has immediate practical consequences. The immigration agency says employment authorization cards in categories A12 and C19, issued to Haitian beneficiaries, are no longer valid for work.

Employers must reverify affected workers. That means many people are being told they cannot step back on the job.

Without a valid document, many people cannot legally work. CBS Miami reported that Haitians without another pending or approved immigration basis are now considered undocumented.

They can be subject to immigration enforcement and deportation, and may lose driving privileges as well. That makes everyday tasks like grocery shopping or taking a child to school far harder.

The Mood in South Florida

The change is visible in the streets. The Miami Herald reported that “the streets are empty” as Haitians receded from public view in South Florida after TPS ended.

People are staying home, avoiding routine trips, and bracing for what comes next. Some churches and community centers have seen attendance drop sharply.

There is no solid public count of self-deportations yet. But the reporting describes a community pulling back, not just in fear of enforcement, but in uncertainty about the future.

Some families are exploring voluntary departure options. Others are waiting to see if any new legal avenue opens up.

What DHS Is Offering

One concrete option is voluntary departure. The homeland security department has promoted a $2,600 payment for migrants who choose to leave the country on their own.

The agency has said Haitians do not have to return to Haiti specifically, but they cannot remain in the US without another legal basis. That payment may help with travel costs, but it is a one-time sum.

That offer may appeal to some, but it carries a heavy decision. Leaving means uprooting families, abandoning jobs, and closing businesses that took years to build.

For many, the choice is between a difficult departure and an uncertain wait for enforcement. Both paths are painful.

Why This Matters to You

If you live in or invest in Latin America, this story is not distant. Miami’s Haitian community remits hundreds of millions of dollars to Haiti each year, and that flow will slow dramatically as people lose jobs or leave.

Those remittances sustain families, pay school fees, and support small businesses in one of the region’s most fragile economies. A sudden drop would ripple through Haiti’s markets and deepen its humanitarian crisis.

For expats and investors watching the region, this is a shift to track closely. The effects will be felt far beyond Florida’s coast.

What Happens Next

The legal path is not fully closed. Advocacy groups may pursue further challenges, but the Supreme Court’s earlier ruling has narrowed their options.

For now, the administration’s policy stands. The termination is in effect, and no court has blocked it.

Haitians with pending asylum claims, family petitions, or other immigration statuses may still have legal footing. But those without such protections face a hard deadline in effect.

Employers, landlords, and local agencies are now learning to navigate a new reality. The coming months will show how deeply this cuts.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Haiti TPS completely over? Yes. The US homeland security and immigration agencies treated the termination as effective July 27, 2026. A court order on August 5 lifted the last judicial stay, so the termination now stands. How many Haitians are affected? Reports cite about 330,000 to 350,000 Haitian TPS holders nationwide. South Florida is home to more than 158,000 of them. Can Haitian TPS holders still work? Not without another valid immigration basis. The immigration agency said employment authorization cards in categories A12 and C19 are no longer valid, so employers must reverify affected workers. What is the $2,600 offer? The homeland security department has promoted a payment of $2,600 for migrants who voluntarily leave the country. It is one option for those without another legal status, but not a requirement.

Connected Coverage

Sources: US Department of Homeland Security and USCIS; Miami Herald; Reuters
