World.title: BTL – From Beginning to End: Ashcroft Gets The Last Laugh?
World.content:
BTL – From Beginning to End: Ashcroft Gets The Last Laugh?

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Adam Flowers: From the very beginning in 1988, when the Esquivel-UDP first opened BTL to public shareholding, perennial Belizean boogeyman Lord Michael Ashcroft slowly sank his fangs into the company; and now nearly 40 years, several administrations, half a billion dollars and countless controversies later including this latest; he is taking one last bite of the BTL pie and having the last laugh.

After tooth and nail, BTL was finally nationalized in 2009; at an enormous gross nationalization-related outlay to Belize of roughly $564 Million. And even that figure does not necessarily represent the complete bill. Once years of accumulated interest, legal and arbitration expenses, tax concessions and other costs arising from the wider BTL saga are considered, contemporary estimates placed the overall cost closer to $700 Million. Opposition parliamentarians were already warning by 2017 that the final figure could approach $700 Million, though no single audited Government accounting has established $700 Million as an exact final nationalization cost. More than half the big B. The cost associated with liberation from Ashcroft’s near-total control of Belize’s telecommunications sector; only now to once again intertwine itself with Ashcroft-linked interests through the Speednet acquisition through 2030 for almost another $100 Million.

And are we surprised that the maturity of the amortization schedule coincides with the year in which the next general election cycle would culminate in 2030, if the current term runs its full course? It is an $80 Million acquisition with total scheduled payments of $91.46 Million, and for the Briceño shareholders, this represents an estimated total $20.59 Million based on amortization and interest terms for their 22.51% stake in Speednet, if the seller notes and interest are allocated proportionately to their shareholding.

Essentially, once principal amortization begins; BTL will need to pay Speednet shareholders about $5.5 Million every 3 months or almost $22 Million a year with a total interest of $11.46 Million. And the success of the deal hinges on many IFs: Like IF Smart is even worth $80 Million; IF Speednet’s annual free cash flow will meet the $22 million amortization requirement; or IF BTL will need to cover any shortfall; and IF BTL’s projections of cost savings and “synergies” will materialize.

Usually, if a deal seems too good to be true, it normally is. Speednet shareholders assert the company is viable for the foreseeable future but have agreed to unexpectedly favorable terms to BTL; to finance the $80 Million at 4.5% interest with the first year as interest only followed by 16 quarterly principal-and-interest amortization payments.

And as BTL completes the merger; certain jobs could become redundant, integration costs will increase; and in a one-company national mobile market regulated by a Public Utilities Commission (PUC) of Government appointees, who can guarantee that consumers will not eventually face higher service costs to meet payment demands?

It could be Lord Ashcroft’s parting gift to BTL for all the memories. BTL was incorporated in 1987 and by 1988, Ashcroft-alliance company Carlisle Holdings had already bought around 9% of shares. By 1992, Carlisle bought another 15% giving a 24% stake and in 1993, the outgoing George Price Administration gave Ashcroft/Carlisle “permitted person” status, effectively allowing Ashcroft to hold more than 25% of the company, despite the 25% cap that otherwise applied to ordinary private shareholders under the company’s original Articles of Association.

When the Manuel Esquivel UDP came to office later in 1993, it refused to honor the exemption and up to 1998, Ashcroft was blocked from exercising his permitted person status even though he continued buying shares, though they could not be registered against the 25% ownership cap. By the time the PUP under Said Musa came back to power, the stage was set. In 2001, Carlisle Holdings bought MCI’s roughly 25% block, bringing its total shareholding to 48.4%. Carlisle then bought about another 3% from other BTL shareholders, bringing its total to roughly 52%. The Musa administration allowed Carlisle to register all its shareholdings giving it majority control of BTL. Government even appointed Ashcroft Chairman of the Board.

The Telecommunications Act of 2002 provided for competition and new licenses and in 2002 Speednet is incorporated. By late 2003, Ashcroft agrees to sell his majority stake in BTL. Enter Jefferey Prosser. In 2004, Government buys Carlisle’s shares for US$57 Million, combines them with other shares and sells roughly 84% of BTL in a transaction worth approximately US$89.7 Million. However, by 2005, Prosser defaults on a US$57 Million payment and GOB takes back control of majority shares.

By the time Government finished disposing those shares, Ashcroft’s companies once again re-emerged as the controlling interest of BTL. By March 2005, SMART goes live. And as history records, in September 2005, Prime Minister Said Musa signs the infamous, secret Accommodation Agreement; guaranteeing BTL a minimum 15% annual rate of return, favorable tax treatment and import-duty concessions, restricted the granting of telecommunications licenses to any new competitors other than SMART and limited government interference. The Agreement did not merely give BTL favorable tax treatment. It also created a mechanism through which shortfalls under the guaranteed 15% rate of return could ultimately be set off against taxes otherwise payable to Government, including business tax, while also providing specific tax exemptions. By 2008, millions of dollars in taxes had already been offset under the arrangements. Years later, Barrow’s own Government placed an extraordinary value on getting rid of the Agreement: in 2016 Barrow put the savings attributable to its elimination at around $202 Million, and later described almost a quarter-billion dollars of the BTL award as being attributable to the Accommodation Agreement itself. Of incredible note, during this period of time, the Leader of the Opposition also acted as attorney for Ashcroft’s ECom in BTL litigation during the months leading to the signing of the Accommodation Agreement.

Between 2006-2007, the assets, rights, obligations and liabilities of Belize Telecommunications Limited were transferred to its successor, Belize Telemedia Limited and then the Dean Barrow administration comes to power in a red wave, owed significantly to public fallout over some of the very BTL deals made by the former PUP administrations. Barrow rejects the Accommodation Agreement and in August 2009 moves to nationalize BTL. But there is an extraordinary footnote to that morning. On August 24, 2009, the very day Barrow took the acquisition legislation to the House, lawyers acting for Telemedia and the Ashcroft interests formally communicated that they would accept Government’s repudiation of the Accommodation Agreement and treat it as terminated — effectively arguing that Government could get rid of the infamous Agreement without taking away the company. Barrow proceeded with the acquisition anyway, maintaining that Belize’s problems with Ashcroft’s control of Telemedia went far beyond the Accommodation Agreement. Government acquired approximately 94% of Telemedia’s shares and related interests. By around this same time, three Ashcroft-linked companies — Heaver Holdings, Callerbar and Riddermark Ventures — held around 77.38% of Speednet.

In 2011, the Court of Appeal strikes down the Government’s takeover of BTL. Within weeks, Barrow’s UDP passed new acquisition legislation and subsequently enshrined Belizean majority ownership and control of BTL in the Eighth Amendment to the Belize Constitution. The next few years are filled with legal battles and arbitration in which firms associated with members of the Barrow family act as counsel for the Government of Belize, with substantial legal fees being paid along the way; but ultimately Belize forked over roughly $564 Million in nationalization-related compensation and settlement payments tied to the Ashcroft alliance.

Now, to rid BTL of the Ashcroft-linked majority ownership in Speednet for good, BTL could pay another near $100 Million if the deal closes on the disclosed terms. It is a feather in the cap of Belize’s pied piper. And shockingly, despite opposition from the unions, civil society and the Chamber of Commerce, the wider public response to the new Speednet acquisition has been remarkably muted. It is as if we are resigned or sensitized to the Ashcroft feeding frenzy. Are we simply too cynical, or disinterested to care? Perhaps the lack of response to this issue is because the current voting generation, were in school during the early 2000s and only vaguely heard of the BTL-saga but never knew the intricacies, or because the upcoming generation have never heard of the boogeyman Lord Michael Ashcroft. But the time to have taken a stand against the Speednet acquisition may already have passed. The BTL board has already voted to proceed, though the PUC review and final transaction documents remain outstanding, and approval seems imminent at this point. If the deal closes on the disclosed terms, this money must be paid by the end of 2030.

But thank the good Lord for the laughs and the memories! But is it he who indeed has the last laugh?

There is, however, another uncomfortable reality that deserves consideration: Belize may simply be too small a market to sustainably support two completely duplicated national telecommunications networks indefinitely. Competition sounds good in theory and has undoubtedly benefited consumers, but if two companies continuously cannibalize an already tiny market until neither generates enough profit to properly invest in infrastructure, the consequences are different when one of those companies is BTL. If SMART crumbles, its private shareholders lose. If BTL crumbles, Government loses, Social Security loses and ultimately the Belizean public loses. From the narrow financial perspective of BTL and the Social Security Board, therefore, acquiring SMART and eliminating duplicated operating costs may actually make business sense. The larger national question is what Belize replaces that competition with. If BTL becomes the single domestic national mobile operator, then Belize must ensure genuine outside competition remains possible — whether through Starlink, other international providers or future entrants — while the PUC must enforce prices, service standards, consumer protections, privacy and open access. The real danger may therefore not be the merger itself, but allowing a Government-controlled monopoly to emerge without strong enough competition and regulatory safeguards around it.

World.title: Police went searching the bushes and found seven little bricks waiting
World.content:
Police went searching the bushes and found seven little bricks waiting

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in Orange Walk have cleared yet another hidden stash spot, this time pulling seven small bricks of suspected crack cocaine from a bushy area along Naranjal Street during a late-night search, with no one around to claim them.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Friday, August 7, 2026, at about 11:00 p.m., members of the Quick Response Team attached to the Orange Walk Police Formation conducted a search of a bushy area on Naranjal Street.

During the search, an officer found a small transparent plastic containing seven small bricks of a buff substance suspected to be crack cocaine.

No one was in the immediate area at the time of the discovery, and the suspected drugs were taken to the Orange Walk Police Station as found property.

At the station, the suspected crack cocaine was weighed on a working digital gram scale, amounting to 4.3 grams. The drugs were placed in a labelled envelope and deposited as found property.

No arrests have been made, and the matter remains under police attention.

World.title: 18 year old bolts from station yard and stays free for six weeks before police find her
World.content:
18 year old bolts from station yard and stays free for six weeks before police find her

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A young woman who bolted from the compound of the Orange Walk Police Station moments after being brought in, outrunning pursuing officers into the night, has been recaptured nearly six weeks later and formally charged with escape from lawful custody.

According to the Belize Police Department, the saga began on Sunday, June 28, 2026, at approximately 11:45 p.m., when officers on mobile patrol along Maskal Street spotted a group of women sitting inside a park on the street. Officers approached and asked each individual for her name, and in doing so, one officer recognized a young woman who was wanted in connection with a cybercrime matter.

She was informed she would be detained and taken to the Orange Walk Police Station pending charges, and was escorted to the police mobile without incident. The compliance lasted exactly as far as the station yard. Upon arrival, she was instructed to exit the mobile, which she did, and while an officer was opening the other door, she ran out of the police station compound toward Democracia Street. Police gave chase, but she made good her escape into the night.

The trail stayed cold through July. Then, on Friday, August 7, 2026, she was detained once more, this time with no door left ajar. At the station she was read and issued her suspect’s rights in custody acknowledgement form, signing voluntarily, and was placed into custody pending charges.

In the early hours of Saturday, August 8, at 5:05 a.m., police obtained a warrant in the first instance and formally arrested and charged Kailyn Jacobs, an 18-year-old unemployed woman of Liberty Avenue, with the crime of escape from lawful custody.

It should also be noted that the cybercrime matter for which she was originally wanted remains exactly that in the report, a matter for which she was sought, with any charge on that front still to be confirmed.

Escape from lawful custody stands as its own offence regardless of the underlying matter, and Saturday’s charge carries its plain arithmetic: the June dash bought six weeks, and its price is now an additional count before the court that the original detention never carried.

World.title: Orange Walk parking lot fight proves saying “excuse me” can apparently get very expensive
World.content:
Orange Walk parking lot fight proves saying “excuse me” can apparently get very expensive

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Friday morning scuffle in an Orange Walk business parking lot has ended with both women involved formally charged with harm, after a confrontation that began with a shove and a request for basic courtesy left each with injuries certified by a doctor.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 23-year-old woman of San Pablo Village reported that on Friday, August 7, 2026, she and her sister were standing in a business parking lot eating meat pies when two women passed by, one of whom she has known for about two years.

According to the report, one of the women pushed herself between the two sisters, prompting the complainant to tell her to say excuse next time. The woman then turned around, came at them, pushed the sister out of the way, grabbed the complainant by her hair, and scratched her below the left eye. The complainant fought back, scratching the woman on both hands and her face. The sister jumped in and tried to separate the two but could not, and the complainant called her father, who brought her to the Orange Walk Police Station. Police brought the other women to the station as well.

At the station, both injured women were issued medico-legal forms, and a doctor certified both of their injuries as harm. Statements were recorded from both, and both were detained pending charges.

On Friday, August 7, police obtained a warrant in the first instance and formally arrested and charged both Angelina Gonzalez, a 23-year-old of San Pablo Village, and Merari Ramirez, a 27-year-old supervisor of Chan Pine Ridge Village, with the crime of harm. Both were cautioned and chose to remain silent, and both were granted bail to appear before the Magistrate Court on Monday, August 10, 2026, at 9:00 a.m.

On Monday morning, both sides of Friday’s parking lot quarrel will stand before the same magistrate, and the shove that started it all will be measured at its full price.

World.title: Boss sent employee on a sales run, but the pickup and cash ended up in Mexico
World.content:
Boss sent employee on a sales run, but the pickup and cash ended up in Mexico

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An Orange Walk Town company is counting its losses after an employee sent out on a morning sales route failed to return with the company pickup or the cash he had collected, and immigration records confirm the man left Belize and entered Mexico that very day.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 50-year-old supervisor of a company operating in Orange Walk Town reported the matter on Thursday, August 6, 2026.

He told police that on Tuesday, August 4, at 8:00 a.m., an employee reported for duty at the company’s premises and was tasked to conduct sales within Orange Walk Town. The employee took the key and drove away in the company’s grey 2006 Nissan Frontier four-door pickup, valued at $20,000, approximately US$10,000, to commence his sales.

By about 6:30 p.m. that evening, the supervisor was informed by a colleague that the employee had not returned with either the company vehicle or the undisclosed amount of cash he had collected during the day. The supervisor further reported that company vehicles are for business use only, must be returned by 5:00 p.m. unless otherwise authorized, and are not permitted for personal use.

Police recorded a statement and circulated information to all border points, and the response settled the question of the man’s whereabouts: the northern border confirmed that the employee left Belize on August 4 and entered Mexico.

Several business places have been visited as part of the investigation, and a message for the man’s detention has been circulated to all police formations.

The border crossing places the case in increasingly familiar territory, joining a growing file of matters this season in which persons of interest have left the country as investigations opened, a pattern that tests the reach of Belizean officials and their cooperation with neighbouring states.

Anyone with information on the whereabouts of the company vehicle is asked to contact the Orange Walk police.

World.title: The weekend ends as it began: bright and hot
World.content:
The weekend ends as it began: bright and hot

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The weekend finishes the way it started, under sunshine. Mainly fair weather prevails across Belize this Sunday, with the familiar 95-degree inland heat, manageable seas, and one small twist: the northern districts may catch slightly more showers later today.

According to the National Meteorological Service, skies will be sunny with a few cloudy spells today and partly cloudy tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with slightly more possible over the northern districts later today, a change of assignment from the south, which has carried the shower duty most of the week.

Temperatures along the coast will reach a high of 89 degrees Fahrenheit (32 Celsius) and a low of 83 (28 Celsius). Inland areas will climb to 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 Celsius) before dropping to 74 (23 Celsius). In the hills, expect a high of 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) and a low of 68 (20 Celsius). The Sunday advice holds steady: water close, shade often, especially through the afternoon peak.

At sea, conditions run from a light chop to choppy, with easterly winds of 10 to 15 knots and waves of 2 to 5 feet, workable water for the weekend’s final boat runs with the usual care on smaller craft.

On the tropical front, the calm continues. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the region over the next 48 hours.

Looking ahead, Monday stays mainly fair with isolated showers or thunderstorms, before a few showers and thunderstorms may develop along the coast and some southern areas on Monday night, easing the country back into the working week.

Today’s high tides are at 6:11 AM and 8:32 PM, with a low tide at 2:10 PM and another low at 12:43 AM tomorrow. The sun rose at 5:34 AM and will set at 6:21 PM. The forecast was issued by forecaster Crystal Rosalez.

World.title: Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street
World.content:
Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Breaking Belize News has received reports of a serious traffic accident involving motorcycles on Mahogany Street in Belize City during the early hours of Sunday morning.

Preliminary information indicates that the accident occurred at around 2:00 a.m. and involved at least two motorcycles. Images from the scene show multiple persons on the roadway as bystanders and other individuals gathered nearby.

Initial reports indicate that at least one person may have died, while there are also unconfirmed reports suggesting that two persons were killed in the collision.

The identities of those involved and the circumstances leading to the accident have not yet been confirmed.

Breaking Belize News will provide additional information once an official report becomes available.

World.title: Bold Bruce
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Bruce Golding

NEW YORK, USA — Former Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding has earned the backing of many within the Diaspora community here for what is being described as his “bold, factual and truthful position” on the souring relationship between Jamaica and America, two staunch allies.

Speaking in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania last week, Golding expressed hopes that “the United States will soften the tone of its relationship with Jamaica and rekindle the strong, decades-old bond between both nations which Jamaicans cherish.

Saying that current demands by Washington are “at odds with the very essence of true friendship”, he pointed to the many challenges facing the island as established rules are being discarded and “new rules are being handed down, not after discussions and negotiations, but unilaterally by social media postings at 2:30 in the morning when most of us are asleep”.

The former Jamaican leader, who stepped away in 2011 and handed over the reins to now Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, was addressing the annual Team Jamaica Bickle Independence Gala on Emancipation Day, August 1, 2026.

The gala celebrated Jamaica’s 64th anniversary of Independence and raised funds in support of Jamaican and other Caribbean athletes’ participation in the yearly Penn Relays in the US, a must-stop on the annual sports calendar for speedy Jamaican high school students.

Golding appeared to be voicing sentiments many Jamaicans in his US audience feel but could not express themselves. Some murmured among themselves that he must not fear losing his US visa.

Called to ask his view Sunday, Golding said he did not wish to trivialise the matter and he had said enough on the subject.

But reacting to the former prime minister’s assessment of the bilateral relations, Stafford Grant, founder and president of the US-based Jamaica Ex-Service Men and Women Foundation, said after the speech:

“Golding didn’t just give a speech, he gave Jamaica a masterclass in geopolitical survival. His address laid bare the brutal reality of being a small island nation caught in the cross hairs of superpower diplomacy.

“The former prime minister’s speech should serve as a profound wake-up call for every Jamaican. His vocal defence is more critical than ever, and I trust Jamaicans will understand that international diplomacy is shifting from collaborative negotiations to unilateral madness,” Grant declared.

Raymond Rhoden, a Florida-based retired adjunct professor, described Golding’s stance as “bold, principled, factual and diplomatic”, adding that he believes Jamaica needs to stand up and take a principled position on the current situation.

Irwine Clare Sr, co-founder of Team Jamaica Bickle, said the issues raised by the former head of government were “pungent, timely, and well articulated on behalf of the voiceless and those who have avoided the conversation due to fear of reprisal or just being downright spineless”.

“This speech must also be placed in context, because clearly he [Golding] recognises the agonising situation that Caribbean leaders find themselves in, especially against the backdrop that they do not speak from a united perspective,” said Clare Sr.

In his address, which was punctuated by applause, Golding spoke of the discontinuation of the Cuban medical mission programme, America’s fierce opposition to China’s investments in Jamaica, and the highly controversial third-country nationals arrangements between the US and a number of Caribbean countries, as examples of actions that run counter to harmonious relations.

“True friends don’t abuse your friendship; they don’t make unreasonable demands of you. They should be there to help you. Holding a gun at your head and insisting that you must be reasonable and do things their way is not friendship,” Golding suggested.

“The United States has put us under severe stress, and that’s not what friends are for,” he said, pointing to the damage the Jamaican economy could suffer should Jamaica stand up and try to fight back.

“There are many at home and abroad who are outraged at what is taking place, who are incensed at what is being meted out to us, who are angry that we have not pushed back, that we haven’t stood up like President Lula da Silva of Brazil who declared that, ‘Brazil’s destiny is for Brazilians alone to determine — without foreign interference or otherwise.’ “

Noting that Brazil is large and provides a US$57-billion market for American exports, Golding warned that little Jamaica is not in that league, struggling to find markets for its own goods.

“With the US market accounting for half our total exports, if our exports to the US market were slapped with a 50 per cent tariff our manufacturing sector would fall apart and thousands of persons would lose their jobs,” said Golding.

Agreeing with Golding, Dr Rupert Francis, who heads the Jamaica Diaspora Task Force on Crime Intervention and Prevention, argued that “we need to get back to the more amiable friendship we had with the United States for many years”.

University lecturer Dr Allan Cunningham said Golding’s speech focused on what he describes as the “hypocrisy of the rules-based order”, noting that “the speech acts as a call for regional realism — that without a unified foreign policy Caribbean states remain vulnerable to US cowboy diplomacy”.

Pics

Irwine Clare Jr

World.title: Public funds not enough for climate resilience — Samuda
World.content:
Matthew Samuda, minister of water, environment and climate change, delivers the keynote address at National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited’s inaugural Corporate Insights Breakfast. Addressing business leaders, Samuda underscored the importance of public-private collaboration in strengthening Jamaica’s climate resilience and preparing businesses, communities and the wider economy for the growing risks associated with climate change..

MINISTER of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda is arguing that Jamaica cannot rely on public funds alone to build the infrastructure and systems needed to withstand the growing effects of climate change.

Samuda said greater participation will be required from private investors, financial institutions, and international partners as the country seeks to strengthen critical infrastructure and improve its ability to recover from climate-related disruptions.

“Public funds are simply not enough to address the challenges posed by climate change. We need financing from all available sources — including public, private, domestic and international partners — if we are to successfully transition to climate resilience,” Samuda said.

He was speaking at the inaugural NCB Corporate Breakfast Series, hosted by National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited (NCBJ), which brought together policymakers, business leaders and financial sector representatives to discuss climate resilience, infrastructure, and investment.

Samuda said strengthening Jamaica’s resilience will require cooperation across the public and private sectors as the country responds to the increasing threat posed by extreme weather and other climate-related events.

The issue has taken on greater significance as disruptions to electricity, water, telecommunications, transportation and other critical services can have wide-ranging effects on households, communities and businesses.

NCBJ Interim Chief Executive Officer Sheree Martin said the changing environment also requires organisations to rethink how they prepare for and respond to disruptions.

“Strategy sharpens in conversation, not in isolation, and capital works best when it is guided by an honest read on where a business is heading,” Martin said.

She said access to financing, strong partnerships, and informed decision-making will become increasingly important as organisations adjust to economic and structural changes.

“As businesses adapt to changing realities, access to informed perspectives, strong partnerships, and the right financial solutions become increasingly important,” Martin said.

Hugh Graham, director of Paramount Industries, said businesses also have a responsibility to prepare for disruptions and protect their operations and employees.

“For businesses, resilience is about being able to keep operating, protect jobs, and continue serving customers when disruption occurs,” Graham said.

“That requires investment and preparation at the company level, but it also requires strong infrastructure, sound policy,and access to financing.” Graham said closer coordination among Government, financial institutions, and businesses could improve Jamaica’s ability to withstand shocks and recover more quickly. “The more Government, financial institutions, and businesses can plan together, the better positioned we will be to withstand shocks and recover more quickly,” he said. NCB said the breakfast series is intended to bring together policymakers, business leaders, and other stakeholders to discuss issues affecting Jamaica’s economic development and long-term sustainability.

World.title: High marks for Redeemed: A Father’s Love at première
World.content:
Executive Producer Rev Dr Otis Manning (left) and gospel recording artiste Kevin Downswell at the première of Redeemed: A Father’s Love held at Carib 5 on Monday. Garfield Robinson

Carib 5 cinema in Kingston was the epicentre of laughter, gasps, cheers, and spontaneous outbursts on Monday night as audiences reacted to the twists, turns, and emotional moments of Redeemed: A Father’s Love at its official Jamaican première.

The faith-based crime drama, which blends suspense, family, faith, and redemption, drew a diverse audience for the red carpet affair, with members of the cast and supporting individuals stepping out in snazzy pieces for the occasion.

The première also attracted strong support from several church communities, reflecting the film’s faith-based foundation. Among those in attendance were gospel entertainers Kevin Downswell and Petra Kaye, who joined members of the cast, production team, and other guests for the screening.

For Executive Producer Reverend Dr Otis Manning, the warm reception from the audience was among the most rewarding aspects of bringing the project to the big screen.

“I’m grateful. I’m thankful. Everything turned out well. The most exciting thing is that people are loving it. I’ve loved it, but, it’s more exciting to watch people loving what you’ve done,” Manning told the Jamaica Observer at the première.

Redeemed: A Father’s Love follows the devastating aftermath of a childhood kidnapping, as long-buried secrets begin to surface and dangerous truths threaten to unravel the lives of those involved. Through its exploration of betrayal, identity, forgiveness, and unconditional love, the film challenges audiences to confront difficult questions about truth, family, and redemption.

Leading the cast is acclaimed American actor Malik Yoba, whose commanding performance anchors the emotionally charged narrative. He is joined by an accomplished ensemble including Co-producer Jacinth Headlam, veteran actor Cornelius Grant, social media personality Julie Mango, gospel dancehall singjay Prince Saj, Justin Awn, and entertainer Safaree Samuels, whose recent public declaration of faith has drawn renewed attention to his appearance in the film.

Although faith is at the heart of the production, Manning and the film-makers are clear that Redeemed: A Father’s Love is not intended solely for Christian audiences. The film’s themes of broken families, lost identity, forgiveness, unconditional love and the hope of restoration are presented as universal experiences that can resonate across cultures, geographical boundaries, and religious backgrounds.

For Manning, the film’s ability to affect people on a personal level is perhaps its greatest achievement.

“The best part of the film was listening to testimonies. A veteran in the business, Chris Browne told me that he’d shot movies for 40 years and there is nothing he would’ve changed,” he said.

Manning also recalled an experience involving one of the film’s actors, who came to a personal realisation while working on the production.

“I was also doing an interview with one of the actors, on set, and he said while we were filming the movie taught him that there were some stuff he had in his heart that he had to forgive. It was on the movie set, while doing the role, that he realised, ‘I messed up.’ That was awesome; to know that my movie is really helping people. I am hoping that it will have the same effect on other viewers,” he said.

Manning shared that

Redeemed: A Father’s Love marks his foray into film-making. He said the idea of making a movie had been on his mind for some time, but he waited until he felt ready to pursue it.

“I knew I wanted to do a movie, but I wasn’t ready for it. When I was ready, I met somebody who was an actress and I left it hanging for a year. When I called her, she explained that she’s done films before. She came down and she literally walked me through. So, big up to Jacinth Headlam. She literally taught me what to do, and how to. She and I did the screening for the actors and everything. Sometimes I had to pull up my socks very hard, but I’m grateful that she really gave me the balance,” Manning said.

Attendees were left in awe following Monday’s viewing.

“I absolutely loved it. It had everything that I look for in a great film; the suspense, the drama, the humour and, most importantly, a powerful message. I found myself laughing one minute and sitting on the edge of my seat the next. It was really well done, and I think a lot of people will be able to relate to the story,” one viewer told the Observer.

Manning added that the film was produced out of pocket through the support of the church community, but believes greater investment is needed to propel Jamaica’s film industry forward.

He is calling for increased support from both the Government and the private sector, arguing that local film-makers need more resources and opportunities to develop and produce quality content.

World.title: ATL Automotive driven to succeed — now in 21 Caribbean territories
World.content:
The ATL Automotive Prestige Centre at Ferry, St Catherine

One doesn’t have to be a motor vehicle enthusiast to feel the pride and joy of Jamaicans who have witnessed the relentless speed of the evolution of ATL Automotive into a Caribbean hub, covering 21 countries and territories stretching from Bermuda in the north to Panama in Central America.

From its one iconic Honda brand, the Caribbean hub has expanded outwards from the Jamaican capital, Kingston, to become the regional distribution, dealer development and support division of ATL Automotive Group, the region’s largest and most diverse of its kind.

The hub acts as the central link between international automotive manufacturers and dealer partners across the Caribbean and surrounding markets. It provides the infrastructure, expertise and hands-on support required to successfully introduce, operate and grow global automotive brands across what is a complex region.

With a portfolio boasting an impressive array of the hottest deals on wheels, like BMW, MINI, BYD, Foton, MG, Omoda & Jaecoo, and Jetour, brand representation varies by market, with each franchise placed according to the opportunities, customer requirements and strength of the local dealer partner.

And although ATL Automotive began with one brand, operating from one dealership in Kingston, the ambition was always bigger — an automotive network with the scale, expertise and infrastructure required to give customers across the region greater choice, stronger support and better representation from global manufacturers.

Mission accomplished.

Across the 21 countries and territories, ATL Automotive now works through approximately 35 dealer operations, having grown itself into a position to deliver a level of automotive choice and regional support unmatched in the Caribbean. It’s a story Jamaica has seen before. “During the 1990s, Sandals demonstrated that a Jamaican company could successfully expand across the Caribbean by respecting the individuality of each destination while building the strength of a regional brand,” says Executive Chairman Adam Stewart.

In the 1980s, Sandals Resorts grew from a single Jamaican property into the country’s most successful home-grown international superbrand. It achieved that growth by recognising the wider potential of the Caribbean, building scale across multiple markets and combining strong regional knowledge with international standards.

A car enthusiast of some renown himself, Stewart notes that the approach taken in the automotive industry is a replication of the resort brand that pulls the world to the Caribbean. “We don’t try to make the Caribbean fit one model; we build solutions that recognise the uniqueness of every market while harnessing the collective strength of the region,” he recounts.

“By bringing markets together, ATL is able to create stronger purchasing power, more competitive pricing, improved warranty support, greater access to technical expertise, more consistent retail standards and stronger representation from manufacturers,” Stewart is now showing off.

He drives home a key point: ATL gives Caribbean customers access to more brands, more vehicle types and more mobility solutions than individual markets could easily secure on their own.

“The goal is not simply to sell more vehicles or collect more brands. It is to build a connected regional platform that gives manufacturers a credible route into the Caribbean, gives dealers access to world-class support and gives customers more choice, better service and greater confidence,” explains CEO Patrick Wilson.

Wilson suggests that for their manufacturing partners, the value is clear. Instead of managing relationships across dozens of individual dealerships, they have one trusted regional partner with the experience, capability and governance to deliver consistently high standards across multiple markets.

“Our leadership team brings decades of automotive and commercial experience, allowing manufacturers to focus on strategy while we manage the complexity of execution across the Caribbean,” says Wilson.

The road from ATL Automotive to Caribbean hub has been eventful. ATL Automotive was awarded the regional master dealership for BMW and MINI in November 2015 — a big deal for a small country — getting the operation on the road in Jamaica in April 2016, with capacity to provide regional support to eight Caribbean markets.

Next came BYD and the subsequent introduction of further passenger, commercial and new-energy vehicle brands. Today, the hub represents seven international automotive brands across the 21 countries and territories, reflecting significant growth in both geographic reach and the breadth of its automotive portfolio.

The ATL Automotive Caribbean Hub currently operates across Antigua and Barbuda; Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao; The Bahamas; Barbados; Belize; Bermuda; the British Virgin Islands; the Cayman Islands; Grenada; Guyana; Haiti; Panama; St Lucia; St Martin; St Vincent and the Grenadines; Suriname; Trinidad and Tobago; the Turks and Caicos Islands; and Jamaica.

Not every brand, Wilson notes, is represented in every market. The hub works with manufacturers and local dealer partners to determine the most appropriate brand and product opportunities for each territory.

“For example, Jetour is represented regionally but is not currently represented by ATL in Jamaica, while MG is among the brands represented in Haiti,” he says, adding that ATL Automotive also represents Honda, Kia, Audi, Volkswagen, and Porsche in Jamaica but they are not currently managed regionally through the Caribbean hub.

The centralised structure of the hub enables international manufacturers to work through one experienced regional organisation while maintaining strong, locally operated dealer businesses in each territory.

A central part of the role is the development of people through a dedicated training centre in Kingston, providing hands-on training for dealer personnel from across the region. Training includes sales, product knowledge, after sales operations, technical diagnosis, service procedures, warranty management and high-voltage systems for electric and hybrid vehicles.

The Kingston-based training operation helps ensure that dealer teams across the network are equipped to meet the technical, operational and customer-service standards required by each manufacturer.

For the hub, a thing of pride is its specialist “Flying Doctor” service for dealer partners facing technical matters that cannot be resolved locally. Senior technical specialists can be deployed to regional markets to support diagnosis, repair and complex technical cases.

This service gives dealers access to advanced technical expertise without requiring each individual market to independently maintain every level of specialist capability.

Under a dedicated regional marketing operation out of Jamaica, the team works alongside manufacturers and dealer partners to plan and execute campaigns suited to individual markets while maintaining the global standards and identity of each brand.

Support can include regional campaign development, digital marketing, social media, public relations, product launches, lead generation, creative execution, and dealer-level marketing activity.

Most dealer operations within the hub network are independently owned local businesses, all working closely to benefit from the brand access, training, technical expertise, operational standards and marketing support needed to build strong and sustainable businesses.

Wilson pointed to the two regional joint ventures — Guyana — CAM Motors — an automotive operation supporting ATL-represented brands in Guyana; and Trinidad and Tobago — Spectra Motors and LAFAST Motors — supporting ATL-represented brands in Trinidad and Tobago.

“Our customers remain our most important concern and the hub helps to ensure that vehicles are backed by trained teams, recognised retail standards, manufacturer-supported warranty processes and consistent after-sales care,” Wilson emphasises.

Executive Chairman Stewart explains the vision:

“Many people look at the Caribbean and see one region. We see distinct markets, each with its own culture, economy, currency, regulations and way of doing business. That understanding has been built over decades, and it’s what makes the ATL Automotive Caribbean hub so powerful.

“By connecting these economies under one umbrella, we’re creating greater scale, stronger partnerships, better support for our dealer network and new opportunities for global automotive brands. It’s a model that benefits everyone — our manufacturers, our dealer partners, our Jamaican-based regional team and, ultimately, the customers we all serve.

“It’s proof that world-class regional businesses can be built from Jamaica, creating value not only for our company but for the wider Caribbean economy.”

In sum, according to Wilson, the hub works alongside its dealer partners, supporting where they need it most, sharing best practice and providing additional resources that help them grow while always respecting that they know their local market best.

“We do the hard work behind the scenes, ensuring every brand is represented to the highest standard in every market,” says Wilson, unable to hide his passion for the job.

World.title: Who should get the Reggae Icon Award?
World.content:
Bob Marley, the Third World’s biggest reggae megastar

At last Thursday’s Independence Grand Gala, Busy Signal and Wayne Wonder joined Sizzla Kalonji, Capleton, Beres Hammond, Leroy Sibbles, Derrick Morgan, Rita Marley, Morgan Heritage, Third World, Ken Boothe, Toots Hibbert, Dawn Penn, Melody Makers, Byron Lee and the Dragonnaires, Shaggy, Grub Cooper, and Sanchez, as recipients of the culture ministry’s Reggae Icon Award.



In this article shared with the Jamaica Observer, Dr Leo Gilling, criminologist, Diaspora strategist, journalist, philanthropist and policy analyst, questions what exactly does the award measure and why a slew of apparently deserving artistes were leapfrogged by some of the current recipients.

Following is part one of a lightly edited version of the article:

Let me begin with what this article is not.

This is not an argument that Sanchez, Wayne Wonder, Busy Signal, Sizzla Kalonji, Capleton, Beres Hammond, Leroy Sibbles, Derrick Morgan, Rita Marley, Morgan Heritage, or Third World et al are undeserving of national recognition.

They are accomplished artistes who have made significant contributions to Jamaican music. My question is different.

If Jamaica has established qualifications for determining who should receive the Reggae Icon Award, do those qualifications adequately explain who is selected — and, just as importantly, who is selected first? That distinction matters.

An award does more than recognise achievement. A national award helps establish a standard. It tells younger artistes, the music industry, Jamaicans and the wider world: This is what we mean when we call someone a Jamaican music icon.

If Jamaica creates a national award intended to represent the highest standard of musical excellence, then the first recipients should help define that standard. The pioneers should establish the benchmark.

Subsequent generations should have something meaningful toward which to aspire. If you create a benchmark, you should begin with the benchmark.

The five qualifications

The qualifications publicly associated with selection for the Reggae Icon Award can be summarised in five broad areas:

1. Pioneering Foundation & Evolution

The artiste should have played a foundational role in originating, developing, or evolving Jamaican genres such as ska, rocksteady, reggae, dancehall, or dub.

2. Authenticity & Conscious Message

The artiste’s work should demonstrate cultural grounding, positive or uplifting messages, social consciousness, spirituality, national pride, or advocacy for social justice.

3. Global Ambassadorship

The artiste should demonstrate sustained international impact and help expand the global footprint of Jamaican music.

4. Longevity & Artistic Consistency

The artiste should demonstrate decades of artistic excellence, influential recordings and resonance across generations.

5. Community & Nation-Building Impact

Consideration is also given to mentorship, charitable activity, youth development and other contributions to Jamaican communities.

At first glance, these appear to be reasonable qualifications. But something interesting happens when we actually apply them.

For purposes of analysis, I assigned each qualification a maximum of 10 points, producing a possible total of 50.

These are not Government of Jamaica scores. They are my analytical application of the qualifications and are intended to encourage discussion about how the criteria operate when applied consistently.

Artiste Pioneer / Evolution Cultural / Conscious Global Longevity Community Total /50

Rita Marley – 9 10 10 9 10 48

Leroy Sibbles – 10 9 9 10 8 46

Beres Hammond – 8 9 10 10 9 46

Derrick Morgan – 10 8 9 10 8 45

Sizzla Kalonji – 8 10 9 9 9 45

Capleton – 8 10 9 9 8 44

Peetah Morgan / Morgan Heritage – 8 9 10 9 8 44

AJ Brown / Third World – 7 9 10 9 7 42

Busy Signal – 8 8 8 8 7 39

Sanchez – 4 7 8 10 7 36

Wayne Wonder – 6 6 9 9 6 36

Reasonable people will disagree with individual scores. That is expected. But the numbers themselves are not the central argument. They simply force us to examine what the qualifications actually mean.

When viewed against those qualifications, the pattern of selections can appear erratic and inconsistent, particularly when artistes with demonstrably stronger claims to pioneering influence, historical importance and global impact remain outside the list.

And perhaps nowhere is the difficulty clearer than with the word “pioneering”. What exactly is a pioneer?

A pioneer is not simply someone who became successful, popular, or enduring. A pioneer changes the architecture of the music; introduces something; transforms something; opens a previously closed door, or creates an approach upon which subsequent generations build.

That distinction matters because if “pioneering” is one of the measures of icon status, it cannot simply become another word for longevity or popularity.

Derrick Morgan has a genuine pioneering claim because his career reaches into the formative development of ska, rocksteady and reggae.

Leroy Sibbles has one because his work as vocalist, musician and arranger intersects directly with the development of Jamaica’s early reggae sound.

But consider Sanchez.

Sanchez is unquestionably one of Jamaica’s great vocalists. His voice is distinctive. His longevity is extraordinary. Generations of Jamaicans know his recordings. But a substantial part of his career has involved interpreting songs written and previously recorded by others.

That is an artistic accomplishment. It can even be an extraordinary artistic accomplishment. But it is not necessarily pioneering. If pioneering means originating, developing, or substantially evolving Jamaican music, longevity cannot simply be substituted for innovation.

The same question arises, although differently, with Wayne Wonder.

Wayne Wonder became an important participant in modern dancehall and reggae crossover and achieved significant international success. But was he a pioneer of that evolution, or an exceptionally successful participant within it? Those are not the same things.

This distinction is important because otherwise every successful artiste eventually becomes a “pioneer”. That empties the word of meaning.

A great singer can be an icon without being a pioneer. A great songwriter can be an icon without being an international superstar. An artiste can revolutionise Jamaican music without operating a charitable foundation. And an artiste can achieve enormous international commercial success without having created a new musical form. These are different kinds of achievement. A credible national recognition system should be capable of distinguishing among them.

The historical question

Now consider something else.

The Reggae Icon Award was introduced in 2019. Reggae was not. Neither was Jamaican popular music. By the time this award was created, Jamaica already possessed more than half a century of extraordinary musical history. There was therefore already a historical backlog of giants.

Artistes had helped create ska. Others had shaped rocksteady.

Others had helped create reggae. Some revolutionised the Jamaican deejay tradition. Others developed dub. Others helped establish dancehall.

Some carried these musical forms around the world. Others influenced musical genres far beyond Jamaica. So when Jamaica established a new national award bearing the word “Icon”, there was an important question to answer from the beginning: Who establishes the benchmark?

If the qualifications emphasise pioneering, longevity, international impact, cultural authenticity and national contribution, one would reasonably expect the earliest recipients to include the artistes whose careers most completely embody those qualities.

This is why the sequence matters. It is not enough to ask whether an individual recipient qualifies. We must also ask: Who else qualifies more strongly? And: Why did one qualifying artiste receive recognition before another?

Those questions do not diminish anyone who has already received the award. They test the integrity of the selection architecture.

The fairest way to examine this is simple. Take exactly the same qualifications. Do not change them. Do not create special rules for anyone. Apply them to Jamaican-born artistes who have not received the award.

What happens when Bob Marley, Toots Hibbert, Jimmy Cliff, Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, Burning Spear, Marcia Griffiths, Dennis Brown, U-Roy, Gregory Isaacs, Shabba Ranks, Ini Kamoze, Eek-A-Mouse, and others are placed beside the existing recipients?

If the qualifications are sound, they should help us understand the hierarchy. If they cannot, perhaps the problem is not the artistes. Perhaps the problem is the criteria.

That is where Part II begins.

Tomorrow: Jamaica’s Reggae Icon Award – when the same test is applied to the giants

World.title: Two spectacular weeks of agricultural immersion at Tuskegee for Jamaican high school students
World.content:
Cornwall College students (from left) D’Andre Granston, Jeremiah Bent and Samijana Gardner who participated in the Tuskegee summer programme.

TWELVE students and three teachers from a collection of Jamaican high schools were blown away by their recent immersion in agriculture, as part of the Tuskegee University Agri-Trek Summer Programme in Alabama, United States.

The schools included Cornwall College, Maldon High, Knockalva High, Herbert Morrison Technical High, Montego Bay High and Cambridge High, all from St James.

They spent two weeks receiving hands-on learning across agriculture and education, during which they were given a chance to experience the rich history and culture of Tuskegee University and the surrounding Tuskegee area.

The students were effusive in their reflections on the experience which, they all concluded, had positioned them for greater things that would provide them with valuable educational, cultural, and personal development opportunities, bound to redound to the benefit of Jamaica.

In their joint report on the trip, Cornwall’s Jeremiah Bent, Samijani Gardener and D’Andre Granston, and Maldon High’s Deontae Forrester, and Dave Brown described the Tuskegee University Agri-Trek Summer Programme as “an unforgettable experience”, meeting with the 140 participants, Jamaica being the only other country outside the United States.

Through mentors in different fields the students participated in research activities, laboratory exercises, discussions, and poster presentations that helped develop teamwork, communication, and critical thinking skills.

“We learned how technology can be used to collect, analyse, and display geographical information. Others explored biotechnology and learned how scientists can extract DNA from one plant and transfer it to another.

“Students involved in veterinary science learned practical skills such as measuring goat weight, determining body condition scores, and conducting FAMACHA scoring to assess animal health,” read the joint report.

FAMACHA is a method used to assess anaemia risk in livestock by examining the colour of an animal’s eyelid against a five-point scale.

One of the most rewarding aspects of the programme was interacting with students from the various states across the USA, they noted, adding that they proudly shared aspects of Jamaican culture and taught the Americans some Jamaican expressions.

They visited a canine detector facility where they learned how specially trained dogs assist in protecting agriculture by detecting prohibited agricultural products.

The report continued: “We also toured the Atlanta International Airport Plant Inspection Station where we learned about inspections, invasive pests, plant diseases, and regulations that protect the agricultural sector from harmful organisms entering the country.

“One of Jamaica’s main sources of income is within the agricultural field. The inspections and regulations that we have learned can help to better protect our agricultural integrity from invasive pests and diseases from foreign countries.

“Another memorable experience was the trolley tour of Tuskegee University’s historic 5,000-acre campus. We visited museums and learned about the rich history of the university; its founders; and its contribution to agriculture, education, and scientific advancement.”

Maldon High’s science teacher Glenviel Wynn said walking the Tuskegee campus was inspiring as the university’s legacy as a centre for African American education, innovation, and leadership under Booker T Washington is still very present.

“The Tuskegee area itself reflected that same spirit — a strong sense of community, agricultural heritage, and commitment to service. That history reminded me that agriculture and education are not just about production, but about empowering people.

“One of the most impactful parts of the visit was observing Tuskegee’s approach to pedagogy. Lessons were not confined to lectures. Instructors used experiential learning — students learned by doing, troubleshooting, and reflecting.

“This showed me that effective agricultural education must connect theory to practice. I plan to apply this by structuring future lessons with more field-based activities, group problem-solving, and reflection sessions so learners can take ownership of the process.

“The exposure to vertical hydroponic farming showed me how space and water can be used more efficiently. Seeing crops growing in controlled environments without soil made climate-smart agriculture tangible.

“This is especially relevant given the increasing unpredictability of weather here in Jamaica… I now see vertical farming as a viable way to produce vegetables year round, reduce water use, and involve youth in agriculture,” said Wynn.

The experience took them to Auburn University’s aquaculture unit where their small-scale fish production and water-quality management helped students to understand the link between fish, water, and plant systems through integrated approaches.

Wynn said it gave him ideas for diversified, resource-efficient enterprises and improving the system at Maldon High School.

Even at a small scale, aquaculture can improve household nutrition, place less stress on natural aquatic systems, and provide additional income, he noted.

The students were thankful to the Maldon and Cornwall alumni, the Sweet Water Foundation, and the Tuskegee University “for the knowledge, mentorship, hospitality, and the chance to connect with such a powerful legacy”.

World.title: Lionel Messi bids farewell to father who guided his glittering career
World.content:
ROSARIO, Argentina (AFP) — Argentina football icon Lionel Messi bid farewell Sunday to his father Jorge, the global star’s emotional anchor and agent since childhood who passed away following a battle with cancer aged 68.

The eight-time Ballon d’Or winner touched down on a private flight from Miami late on Saturday with his wife Antonela Roccuzzo and their children.

A private ceremony with close family and a few Argentina teammates took place at a cemetery in the town of Perez, adjacent to Rosario, later Sunday.

The gates of the town’s El Prado cemetery displayed handwritten messages from fans — “Stay strong, Leo, we love you” and “Stay strong, Messi family” — alongside a large floral wreath.

Messi’s teammates rallied around their captain following the announcement that Jorge Messi had passed away late Friday at a clinic in Rosario.

“It will surely do him good for us to be there,” Boca Juniors midfielder Leandro Paredes told journalists after his team’s match on Saturday.

“I need to speak with a few of my teammates to see if we go now or sometime tomorrow.”

According to media reports midfielder Rodrigo de Paul — a close friend of Messi and his Inter Miami teammate — travelled to Argentina.

After scoring a goal in a 2-1 defeat to Monterrey in Miami on Saturday, De Paul paid tribute by taking off his shirt to reveal Messi’s number 10 jersey.

There was a handful of fans outside the cemetery, including 15-year-old Lucas Blanco, who hung a sign reading “Stay strong, Messi” on the gate.

“He has brought so much joy to this country, now it’s our turn to give a little back and offer him some comfort,” he said.

“We drove 700 kilometres to be here. We wanted to stand by Leo during this time,” said Carlos and Ana, a couple who travelled from Tres Arroyos, a town south of Buenos Aires.

The cause of death was not disclosed, but local media reported that Jorge Messi had been suffering from cancer.

His unusual absence from the World Cup in June had already attracted attention.

Messi’s family asked the media for “humanity” during the tournament amid persistent rumours over Jorge’s health.

After bursting into tears after scoring against Algeria, 39-year-old Messi had admitted to dealing with “a situation outside of sports”.

“I went through a few difficult, complicated days,” he later acknowledged. “But I am grateful to the entire delegation and my teammates, because they stood by me, as always.”

Immediately after the World Cup final defeat against Spain, Messi returned to spend a few days with his family in Rosario.

– Humble beginnings –

A guiding figure throughout his son’s career, Jorge Messi was his first coach who left everything behind to accompany his son to Spain.

A metalworker in Rosario, 340 km north of Buenos Aires, Jorge managed youth teams at the small local club Grandoli.

He was the one who introduced Argentina’s future captain to the game aged four on vacant lots where local kids played.

His life changed course in 2000 when Barcelona invited the young prodigy, then aged 13, to Catalonia to continue treatment for a growth hormone deficiency while playing for the club’s youth teams.

Jorge left behind his job in Argentina, his wife, and his three other children to settle in Spain with Lionel.

“When we arrived in Barcelona, I used to lock myself in my room to cry alone, and my father did the same — either without me seeing him or thinking I didn’t see him. We pretended we were both fine, but we were struggling,” Messi later said.

His father was later the agent who negotiated contracts on his behalf, from Barcelona to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami.

Messages of sympathy have poured in since Saturday from the football world, including from the clubs Messi played for and the Spanish Football Federation.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) ordered a minute’s silence before matches and that black armbands be worn at games across all age groups for the week.

World.title: Bravery born of pain
World.content:
HIGGINS...I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society

FUELLED by her own childhood experiences with sexual assault and incidents of incest that she’d witnessed, Susan Higgins helped track down Troy Ellis, the man accused of the rape and murder of eight-year-old Talia Thompson in Discovery Bay, St Ann, in 2023.

Just shy of three years later, her actions have earned her national recognition. Higgins is among four Jamaicans slated to receive the Badge of Honour for Gallantry at this year’s national honours and awards ceremony scheduled for October.

Ellis, while receiving treatment at hospital under police guard following Talia’s death in September 2023, reportedly escaped. But Higgins later encountered him on the road and played a key role in getting him back into police custody.

For the 50-year-old, the national recognition is deeply personal.

“I feel happy and blessed to know that I can be a help to the helpless and a voice of the voiceless,” she told the

Jamaica Observer.

“When I opened the paper [last Thursday] and I saw Susan Higgins, mi dear! It was 140 people and fi mi name in there, me seh! No man, me feel good,” she added, erupting in laughter.

Talia was allegedly raped and murdered on September 23, 2023. Ellis, who was reportedly known to the family, was subsequently taken to hospital after allegedly injuring himself.

When Higgins heard that he had escaped from police custody, she said she immediately felt a sense of urgency to do something.

She said she was on her way home and her daughter was with her. When they got to the vicinity of the Firearm Licensing Authority office in Discovery Bay, she noticed a man attempting to conceal his face when the motor vehicle headlights illuminated him.

She said she immediately became suspicious and asked the driver to turn the vehicle around.

When they approached the man, Higgins said she began questioning him about his injury, deliberately remaining calm and acting as though she was simply curious about why he was on the road so late. She recalled Ellis telling her that he had recently been discharged from hospital.

Higgins said she continued to speak with him through the window of the vehicle while it drove slowly beside him, at the same time her daughter was conducting a quick online search. The search, she said, confirmed that the man she was speaking to matched the description of the escapee.

“I told him to pull up his shirt to let me see his wound. I was just playing slick because I wanted to see if he had a gun on him. When I saw that he didn’t have a gun, I asked him where he was going, and he said ‘Portland Road’,” she recalled.

“I said, ‘Do you need a ride?’ And he said, ‘Yes,’ not knowing it was the police me a carry him to. I said, ‘All right, when you reach your destination you tell me.’ During the ride, he was talking so intelligently to me. He didn’t show any sign of [being of] unsound mind, so I talked to him and talked to him until he said, ‘Me a come off here so.’ When he said that, me dumb, deaf, and blind, and stopped talking. I took him straight to Discovery Bay police,” said Higgins.

When they arrived, Higgins said the station’s door was closed, so she instructed her daughter to knock.

A cop came outside and Higgins said the driver immediately announced that they had found the man wanted in connection with Talia’s death. At that point, Higgins said Ellis became aware that he had been identified and attempted to resist.

She said she struggled to restrain him before eventually getting him into the police station, after which his identity was confirmed and he was returned to police custody.

For Higgins, the decision to intervene was not about recognition or praise, it was about doing what she would hope someone else would do if her child was in danger.

“Too many times children are being murdered, raped, left abandoned. As a woman, I didn’t get the love and the care of a parent. I actually grew up in the wild because my parents gave me away to a family, and [a man] attempted to rape me. It made me so aggressive, and I said if anybody ever do this to any pickney, if me catch them, me a go unalive them, but I did my best that night to not do what I wanted to because my little daughter was there and I couldn’t bear to do it,” she told the Sunday Observer.

“So many kids get raped and murdered, and so many of these cases go unanswered. I said, I am going to stand up and be a voice for the voiceless and a help for the helpless,” said Higgins.

“I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society,” she said. “I didn’t know the parents or the grandparents of that child, but I feel elated that I can help a mother to get some form of justice,” said Higgins.

“As I go along, I will always try to help somebody. My living will not be in vain,” she declared.

World.title: EU conservative chief demands migrant return hubs in Africa
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her right-wing government are among the harshest critics, with Rome introducing border controls for travelers from Spain on Friday and sparking retaliation from Madrid.

Weber echoed proposals made last week by EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner, arguing that countries outside the bloc could be offered closer trade ties, economic collaboration and legal migration opportunities in exchange for accepting the installation of return hubs.

“Migrants who have no right to remain must leave Europe — no ifs, ands or buts!” he wrote, adding that returns must no longer depend on the political will of individual member countries.

Weber also rejected internal border controls within Europe as a long-term solution. “They may be necessary in exceptional situations. But they do not address the root cause of the problem … There can therefore be only one answer: strong, joint European protection of the external border.”

In early June, the European Parliament and European Council announced new EU rules on migrant returns, including removals to countries outside the bloc in return hubs.

Weber also argued that the Ceuta crisis, which left around 100 dead, was the result of unilateral national action and said that the Spanish government’s “political signals” have had “an immediate impact on migration routes.”

World.title: What will Burnham do on AI?
World.content:
Artificial intelligence could transform the economy, the workplace, and even the way we think — but is Britain ready for it? And is Andy Burnham?

In the second of Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy’s summer box set conversations, they sit down with POLITICO UK tech editor Isobel Asher Hamilton to look at the choices facing the new prime minister this autumn.

Should Britain be building the next OpenAI, or focusing on using AI to revive manufacturing? Can the UK compete with the US and China? And where will the government land on the biggest political battles ahead, from copyright and data centres to the future of work?
