World.title: Why Poland’s right-wing split may not save Donald Tusk
World.content:
However, the departure of former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki from PiS complicates the balance of balance of power on the right.

PiS, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, formally ruptured last month, when Morawiecki stormed out, taking 40 MPs with him to form the new Development Plus party, leaving PiS with 147 deputies.

The split between him and party founder and leader Jarosław Kaczyński quickly became acrimonious.

Morawiecki criticized his own government’s decisions on Covid-19 restrictions and its push to tighten Poland’s abortion law, which outraged many women and saw PiS take a long-term hit in public support.

“Although I oppose abortion, I believed the change would lead to catastrophe — a polling collapse. Unfortunately, I was right,” Morawiecki said on the popular YouTube show Rymanowski Live this week.

He is now trying to set up a more moderate center-right party focused on economic growth which is less partisan than PiS. “Today, Poland does not need to get bogged down in ideological disputes,” he said in Monday’s interview. However, he has ruled out ever working with Tusk in the future.

World.title: A new rival is forcing Italy’s Meloni back to her far-right roots
World.content:
While France and other countries tightened border checks, Italy went further and announced it had suspended the EU’s free-movement Schengen agreement with Madrid. Now, in Italian airports, passengers from Spain are asked to join a different line.

Meloni’s office has made clear it has no intention of lifting the controls until at least Aug. 15, escalating the clash with Spain, which retaliated by imposing checks on travelers from Italy.

“We will not back down one millimeter on illegal immigration,” Meloni posted on X while her allies attacked the socialist Spanish government, accusing it of failing to manage migration flows. “Defending our borders, stopping human traffickers, and ensuring effective repatriation will continue to be this government’s policy,” she added.

The clash with Spain is just the latest sign that the Italian leader is doing all she can to secure her core, hard-right electorate in the face of a challenge from the right by Roberto Vannacci, a former general and member of the European Parliament.

With an election expected as early as next spring, Vannacci’s far-right National Future party has been advancing in the polls, overtaking one of Meloni’s coalition partners, the far-right League party, and gaining on another, Forza Italia, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.

For Meloni, who began her political career in the youth wing of Italy’s post-fascist movement, the challenge strikes particularly close to home.

World.title: Israel rejects Trump’s peace plan for Gaza
World.content:
Hamas has said that it would begin disarming, but in recent days an Israeli official said the country still had “serious security concerns.”

The rejection is a blow to peace negotiations the Trump administratoin has been brokering since September. The U.S. president had described the plan, now rejected by Israel, as a “critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government” and giving Israel “the security it deserves.”

Israel appears unlikely to pull back significant forces or make other concessions ahead of legislative elections scheduled for October. Netanyahu faces a tough reelection battle, with his far-right coalition partners urging him to keep up the pressure on Hamas and leave forces in Gaza. Opponents also accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack when Hamas-led militants attacked Israeli communities, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and taking 251 others hostage. Israel responded with a punishing military offensive that has killed more than 73,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.

Netanyahu said on Sunday that he is now in discussions with U.S. officials about how to move forward. “They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us, and we know how to stand up to these things,” he said.

World.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange overnight strikes, WHO confirms warehouse destroyed
World.content:
Another overnight strike on the Zhytomyr region injured three people, Ukrainian emergency services said.

Meanwhile, five people died in a Ukrainian overnight drone attack on the Russian city of Belgorod, the regional crisis centre said on Sunday. Acting governor Alexander Shuvayev said earlier on Sunday that three people were killed and 25 others injured in the “massive terrorist drone attack” by Kyiv. The death toll later rose to five.

Zelenskyy condemned what he described as “ballistic terror” attacks on Odesa, Kharkiv, Pavlohrad, and other regions. “Every such attack on human life serves as a constant reminder – we need more pressure, more sanctions against Russia, and more air defense for Ukraine,” he said.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization, said on Sunday that a WHO warehouse in Dnipro in Ukraine was destroyed by a strike on Friday.

The warehouse held humanitarian supplies for frontline health facilities. No casualties were reported, as a WHO staff member and drivers managed to evacuate 130 of approximately 300 pallets and left the area before the attack.

“I cannot say loudly enough: attacks on health care MUST STOP. Otherwise, people are deprived of lifesaving healthcare,” Tedros said.

World.title: Germany battling ‘daily’ hybrid warfare attacks, minister warns
World.content:
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt speaks to the media during a news conference at Leipzig airport on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images

Last week’s drone incident in Lepizig just the latest example.

Germany is being hit by hybrid warfare attacks from foreign powers on a “daily” basis, the country’s interior minister has warned, after a drone packed with explosives was found at Leipzig Airport earlier this week.

Espionage, sabotage, cyber attacks and covert actions “with the aim of destabilizing Germany or directly harming it” are a “constant reality,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told BILD in an interview on Sunday.

Dobrindt suggested on Thursday that a drone incident at Leipzig Airport may have been an attack by a state actor. The minister has stopped short of specifying which foreign powers are behind the hybrid attacks.

World.title: Meloni and Frederiksen reiterate opposition to 'uncontrolled immigration'
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni published a joint statement with the Danish Premier Mette Frederiksen on Monday, confirming their united front in the fight against “uncontrolled migration”, vowing to "protect" Europe’s Christian cultural heritage.

 

The statement notes that the two are the only female leaders of European governments and, despite coming from different political backgrounds and geographical realities, are united by a shared commitment to defending Europe.

"We do not accept uncontrolled immigration into Europe, and we have promoted a rigorous migration policy, both in our own countries and across Europe," Meloni said in a Facebook post.

"No one can deny the negative impacts of illegal immigration on our societies: rising crime rates, increasing pressure on public services and an erosion of public trust. It is particularly serious when illegal migrants, who have no right to remain in our countries, commit violent crimes, traffic drugs or are responsible for sexual violence," the post reads.

Frederiksen and Meloni have recently emerged as the EU's most vocal advocates for a tougher migration policy, notably since the crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, which saw tens of thousands of irregular migrants crossing the border within hours.

In response, Italy and Denmark led an open letter to the EU institutions, signed by a total of 22 member states, calling for coordinated action to combat illegal migration, strengthen external borders and address so-called "pull factors."

For the two leaders, ordinary citizens have paid too high a price for uncontrolled migration for too long — a tougher approach to migrants who have committed serious crimes, they argue, means greater security and protection for communities.

"So what more can we do? We need to set up repatriation centres in third countries, as well as other innovative solutions outside Europe. We are working hard on this," the post reads, referring to return hubs, an approach Italy has been trialling in Albania and that was recently written into a controversial EU law.

"But this is not enough. Compliance with our laws must go hand in hand with respect for European values. This applies to irregular migrants, but also to the millions of foreign nationals living legally in our countries and across Europe," the statement adds.

For the two prime ministers, the migration issue ultimately comes down to respect for Europe's Christian cultural heritage and shared values, which both vowed to defend.

World.title: Top tips and tricks for travelling internationally with young children
World.content:
Travelling with babies and toddlers can be daunting for parents. Questions about air travel, what to pack and safety are often top of mind, especially on long-distance flights and international trips.

 

“Travelling with kids is a whole new world," said Dr. Shannon Thompson, a paediatrician at Cleveland Clinic Children's, adding that it's important to “enjoy your kiddo on your trip” as much as you can.

Here are some tips and tricks for parents to travel safely with young children – and have fun with them, too.

Look for amenities like cribs and high chairs before you book

Before you decide where to stay, consider your options for baby-proofing.

Check whether items like portable playpens, cribs and high chairs are offered to guests. If you are staying somewhere with stairs, a balcony or a pool, inquire about baby gates; if they are not provided, see if they are available for rent nearby or consider bringing travel-friendly foldable mesh gates.

Pack electrical outlet covers and wipes to clean any dirty surfaces your kiddo might touch.

For babies, safe sleeping is still essential on vacation. Children younger than one should sleep on their back on a flat, firm surface such as a mattress in a bassinet, crib or playpen with nothing more than a fitted sheet, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.

The organisation also recommends babies sleep in the parents' room – but not in the parents' bed – for at least the first six months.

You should also consider how you will get to your lodging: Will you fly in and rent a car or take a taxi, or take public transit from the airport? Will you mostly be driving or walking?

For parents, these factors can determine whether you want to bring a stroller and a car seat, both of which you can gate check for free when you fly, or rely on using a sling or baby carrier.

Plan for snacks and diaper changes on the plane

“Flying with kids is one of those big, intimidating things,” Thompson said. “I think the biggest thing to think about is always safety and then of course their comfort.”

While children under two can fly in their parents’ lap, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency recommends securing them in their own safety seat, such as a car seat certified for use on planes. This requires buying a seat for your child.

For long-haul or international flights, ask the airline if they have bassinets available.

Baby food such as formula, puree pouches and breast milk are not subject to the 100 millilitre rule when passing through security, but only for use during your trip (so you won’t be able to bring excessive amounts) and you might be asked to prove its authenticity.

In addition to snacks, don't forget to carry on diapers, wipes, a portable changing pad and sealable plastic bags for disposal. Bring extra clothes to layer or change in case of accidents or messy spills.

Swallowing and chewing can help with ear pressure, so nursing little ones or giving them a bottle or pacifier can ease discomfort during take-off and landing.

Speak with your pediatrician beforehand if your child is prone to ear infections, and before travelling abroad, ask them what vaccines may be recommended.

Keep kids entertained on and off the plane

For flights with young kids, Christy Slavik, owner of the travel agency Mom Approved Travel, recommends “having little surprises that you can distract them with” – such as sticky mats for travel-sized play doh, suction cup toys and other games that are small and light to pack.

If sightseeing once at your destination, think about ways to make activities more fun and interactive. For art museums, bring notebooks that kids can draw in, or ask them what types of animals they can find in the paintings, Slavik said.

“Kids need a mission. They need games,” she said. “You have to get creative sometimes when you're travelling."

Exposing children to other cultures, foods and languages can also be fun. Some may enjoy picking out snacks at markets, for example, or learning foreign words for their favourite dishes and activities.

There are options for places to stay that are family friendly, with amenities such as pools or games. For those travelling abroad on a budget, many hostels offer private rooms for families so they don’t have to share a dorm-style room with bunk beds. Hotels and hostels provide the opportunity to meet other travellers, including fellow children who can become playmates.

The perks of travelling with extended family

Helping mums actually enjoy their vacation – and relax amid the stress that can come with planning and travelling – is a core goal of Slavik's travel agency.

One way parents can get a break is by planning trips with grandparents or other family members.

This helps with babysitting duties, while also allowing loved ones to have special bonding time with kiddos. Just make sure they also have their own down time and aren't wearing themselves out, Slavik said.

“When you bring grandparents to a vacation, you're giving them the opportunity to experience those moments together,” she said.

World.title: Prado Museum reimagines masterpieces in solar eclipse light
World.content:
How would Velázquez's supreme masterpiece, "Las Meninas", look shrouded in the dim light of a solar eclipse? What happens to the colours, shadows and atmosphere in the works of the great masters of painting when the light changes in a radical and sudden way?

 

The Spanish National Prado Museum has answered these questions on the occasion of the solar eclipse of 12 August 2026 with a spectacular video that invites viewers to rediscover its collections from a completely new perspective.

A new look at the masterpieces

The project, entitled "The Prado in the light of the eclipse", proposes a progressive transformation of the lighting applied to some of the most iconic paintings in the celebrated gallery. Through this shift in light, the video shows how small variations in illumination can radically alter the perception of colours, shapes and the atmosphere of the paintings, revealing details and nuances that everyday light leaves hidden.

The proposal is not just an aesthetic exercise. The Prado also sees it as a tool for cultural outreach designed to bring its collections closer to new audiences, especially to those who do not usually visit museums, through an accessible and visually striking audiovisual format.

The works touched by the sun in the gallery's video are:

1. 'Las Meninas'. Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez

2. 'La Vista'. Pedro Pablo Rubens; Jan Brueghel el Viejo

3. 'El embarco de santa Paula Romana'. Claudio de Lorena

4. 'Autorretrato'. Alberto Durero

5. 'El quitasol'. Francisco de Goya y Lucientes

6. 'La Canal de Mancorbo en los Picos de Europa'. Carlos de Haes

7. 'La fragua de Vulcano'. Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez

8. 'La rendición de Bailén'. José Casado del Alisal

9. 'El sueño de Jacob'. José de Ribera

10. 'El nacimiento del Sol y el triunfo de Baco'. Corrado Giaquinto

11. 'La pradera de San Isidro'. Francisco de Goya y Luciente

Artificial intelligence in the service of art

The production has been developed by the studio AMB Piensa using a combination of artificial intelligence, digital creation and traditional graphic intervention. The technical process involved the use of video-generation models capable of recreating depth, simulating camera movements and precisely reproducing the advance of the eclipse over the scenes depicted in each work.

The artificial intelligence tools made it possible to design and refine complex visual instructions: the gradual evolution of the light, the appearance of shadows and reflections, and the effect of progressive darkening on characters, landscapes and architectural elements. However, the process was not entirely automated. Each sequence was reviewed and manually adjusted to preserve the composition, the pictorial technique and the original character of the paintings, ensuring that the technological intervention did not distort the spirit of the works.

Art, technology and an astronomical phenomenon

This coming 12 August, Spain will experience one of the most eagerly awaited astronomical events of recent years: a solar eclipse that will be visible across much of the mainland and has generated unprecedented excitement among the public and the media.

The Spanish museum is thus joining the conversation with a proposal that goes beyond straightforward scientific outreach and turns it into an artistic and emotional experience. Because the fundamental question underlying the project is, in fact, very old: How much of what we see in a work of art depends on the light in which we view it?

With this initiative, the museum reaffirms its commitment to innovation as a way of connecting with contemporary audiences, exploring the possibilities offered by new technologies to enrich the interpretation of artistic heritage without sacrificing rigour or respect for the original works.

World.title: New AI rules leave Chinese users mourning their virtual boyfriends and girlfriends
World.content:
She had exchanged about 700,000 words in messages over two years and never got to say goodbye.

 

Li, 24, was not the only one left mourning the loss of a virtual companion when major Chinese tech companies recently pulled the plug on their popular AI companion services to comply with new government restrictions.

"It was like we were forced to be separated by our parents, but I still miss him," Li said.

AI companions in China range from romantic partners to virtual recreations of deceased loved ones.

The new regulation, which took effect on 15 July, bans AI platforms from generating content that could lead users to make questionable decisions due to manipulation of their feelings or that might trigger extreme emotions or unhealthy habits in children and teenagers.

ByteDance, the developer of TikTok, is among the companies shutting down their AI companion services. Others include e-commerce giant Alibaba and Tencent, owner of the popular WeChat social media app.

US suicides may have worried Chinese regulators

The new rules require AI platforms to deliver risk warnings against relying excessively on such apps.

For example, "replacing social interaction," or serving as a substitute for talking to people in person or speaking with them by phone, cannot be one of the objectives of an online service.

China has a tradition of paternalistic government regulations meant to pre-empt potential problems, said Yolanda Ma, an expert on AI governance. As an example, she referred to a few cases of suicides in the US by young people after interacting with AI companions.

"This regulation tried to strike a balance between the AI service providers, the users, as well as guardians of minors using the services," said Ma, a fellow with ERA, a non-profit talent and research programme based in Britain.

The People's Daily, the official newspaper of China's ruling Communist Party, indicated concern over the issue when it reported in April about harms to people's mental health and real-life relationships from such services.

"The Chinese government has a strong incentive to tighten regulations on AI companion chatbots, especially considering the psychological risks we've observed in the US," said Angela Zhang, a professor of law at the University of Southern California.

Zhang doubts the move will derail development of AI companion services substantially, though, since tech companies are working on alternatives.

The ByteDance app, for example, is directing users of its former AI companion service to another of its apps, which focuses solely on building personalised AI characters and stories.

It was just not the same, Li said.

Users of virtual companions protest, seek alternatives

The loss of virtual companions has provoked a flood of complaints, according to posts and screenshots shown on social media.

Some people have uninstalled the apps in protest or tried to upload their chat histories into other apps to try to resurrect their virtual partners.

Others started a campaign on social media, urging users to call the authorities and tech companies to express their frustration.

Song Wenxin, a video industry designer in southwestern China's Chengdu, said she was not too emotionally attached to AI services, but empathises with those who were.

She echoed suspicions among many Chinese people that one factor driving the new rules is a government policy of encouraging people to have more children to counter a decline in China's population.

"Any virtual app getting women too engaged to give birth in real life gets banned," said Song, adding she has no need or desire to have children.

Not everyone has enough resources and support to turn to in real life, the 22-year-old said.

"When I first came to Chengdu for my first job and didn't know any friends my own age, I needed someone experienced who could tolerate me, and AI did the work," she said.

World.title: Historic drought: rivers reveal hunger stones, warships and mammoth remains
World.content:
The drought gripping large parts of Europe has pushed water levels down to rarely seen lows.

 

Hunger stone at Pirna-Oberposta becomes visible

The persistently low water of the Elbe has exposed a historic hunger stone near Pirna, close to the border with the Czech Republic. The stone in the Oberposta district bears numerous dates carved into its surface, recording past episodes of extreme low water. The oldest markings go back to 1707.

For centuries, such hunger stones were seen as warning signs of drought and the hardship that came with it. Extreme dryness could threaten harvests, disrupt shipping and, in earlier times, even trigger famines. The stones become visible only when river levels drop particularly low.

The Pirna-Oberposta hunger stone is regarded as one of the best-known and largest of its kind in Germany. Its reappearance makes the current drought visible in a striking way and at the same time recalls historic dry spells.

Around Leverkusen, north of Cologne, the Rhine's extreme low water has also exposed historical traces. South of the mouth of the Wupper, hunger stones from earlier droughts have likewise emerged. One of the stones is dated 1959. Historical records also mention a hunger stone bearing the inscription "If you see me, you will weep" – but that particular stone has not yet reappeared.

War fleet in the Danube

In the stretch that separates Serbia from Romania, a broken ship's hull has appeared on a sandbank in the Danube that is normally submerged. Other vessels protrude halfway out of the water, and some are reported to still contain armaments.

These wrecks are part of the fleet Adolf Hitler had stationed in the Black Sea. The German army deliberately sank them towards the end of the Second World War in an effort to slow the Soviet advance.

Historians estimate that up to 200 German warships were sunk in this way in September 1944, eight months before Nazi Germany capitulated in May 1945.

German army vessel, sunk in the Second World War, August 2026 AP Photo

This is not the first time low water has revealed these relics. They have surfaced during previous droughts and each time have disappeared again as soon as the river rose.

Nazi warship, sunk in the Second World War, Serbia, August 2026 AP Photo

The Serbian government has tried in the past to recover the wrecks. Most, however, still lie where they were sunk, partly because explosives remain on board and any intervention would be risky.

Danube drought exposes more relics

The phenomenon is not confined to the Serbian-Romanian border. Along the more than 2,800-kilometre course of the Danube, falling water levels are bringing a wide variety of finds to light.

In Bulgaria, around the village of Ryahovo, just south of the border near Bucharest, the retreating water has uncovered the remains of what experts believe to be a woolly mammoth. The skeleton was lying on the riverbank after the recent heatwaves drove the water level down to record lows.

In Hungary, low water levels are affecting several stretches of the river. Near Budapest, an almost intact Wehrmacht motorcycle has emerged after lying buried in the mud for decades, alongside further ammunition.

Experts have also found German anti-tank mines, remnants of hand grenades and artillery shells in the riverbed. According to the Hungarian Institute of Military History, this section of the Danube may have been used as a dumping ground for war debris after the siege and battle of Budapest in 1944 and 1945.

Further south, near Mohács, the wreck of a Second World War warship has come to light. In Baja, branches of the Danube such as the Sugovica have dried out so much that people were able to cross them on foot.

The drought is also having consequences that go beyond historical discoveries. In Hungary, low water levels have put the cooling system of the Paks nuclear power plant under strain. At the beginning of August, the river stood only just above the minimum level required for operation. A few days later, the new Hungarian prime minister reported that the level was once again several centimetres above that threshold.

In Romania, the low water level has forced the authorities to suspend ferry services. Barges are stranded, and irrigating fields is becoming ever more difficult in a country already suffering from extreme dryness. In Serbia, the falling river has exposed sandbanks that have turned into makeshift beaches. At the same time, hydropower generation in the country has declined.

World.title: From Zermatt to Les Arcs: Europe's top 10 ski resorts for 2026, according to Trip.com
World.content:
Whether you’re a complete novice to skiing and looking for easier flat paths or a more experienced alpine enthusiast chasing challenging descents, Europe offers spectacular terrains for every level – and with a backdrop of unmissable views.

 

From the glacier-crowned peaks in Switzerland to the vast slopes of the French Alps, Trip.com has compiled its annual ranking of the continent’s top 50 ski resorts.

The list is based on a combination of customer reviews, year-round sales data, consistent quality and unique themes.

Zermatt Ski Resort, Switzerland

Topping Trip.com’s ranking, Zermatt Ski Resort is nestled in Switzerland’s German-speaking section of the Canton of Valais.

With 360 kilometres of trails extending across the Italian border, the resort is described as a “skier’s paradise”, offering terrain for the skillful skier, as well as being family friendly.

Here, at the backdrop of sweeping views, ski lifts can reach the 3,883m-high high Klein Matterhorn peak and skiing is possible year-round – even during the summer.

Val Thorens, France

Perched at an altitude of more than 2,000 metres, France’s Val Thorens offers skiers a complete view of the Alps’ scenery.

Home to the longest toboggan run in France, the Cosmojet Luge is five kilometres long with a 700 metre vertical drop starting at the Glacier de Péclet that takes riders on a 45-minute journey along the marked track through the snowy landscapes.

There are lots of activities to do beyond skiing, including discovering the snowy landscape on a snowmobile or mountain kart designed for driving on snow. Visitors can also experience the Alps from above by taking flight on a paramotor or paraglider.

Adventurers can also tackle the picturesque ice waterfalls of Val Thorens by ice climbing, where instructions teach visitors how to use ice axes and crampons to scale the ice wall and get a panoramic view of the resort.

Val Thorens, France Val Thorens

Courchevel, France

Nestled in the French Alps, the premier high-altitude destination is known for its panoramic mountain views, direct ski access, and an array of sports, exclusive boutique shopping and Michelin-starred gastronomic experiences.

Courchevel’s ski area consists of 150 kilometres of marked slopes suited for all levels and also has direct access to the 3 Vallées ski area, the biggest in the world, with a further 600 kilometres for skiing.

For an added touch of luxury, the lift cars were designed by none other than the famed fashion house, Chanel.

For those who don’t feel like skiing, Savoie from Courchevel ski resort provides personalised tours of the alpine landscape. From the villages, towns and ski resorts surrounding Courchevel, to its mountain passes, lakes and alpine glaciers, tour guides will share insights about the region's local heritage.

Ski Resort St Moritz, Corviglia, Switzeraland

This Swiss resort’s pistes stretch across vast areas, including Marguns, Corviglia, Salastrains, Signal, Munt da San Murezzan, reaching up to Piz Nair, the highest point at 3,057 metres.

Here, there are 88 pistes, 56 lifts and an array of ski routes to choose from, alongside a nine kilometre ski run starting from the east of the Alps at an altitude of 3,303 metres. While for those not in search of adrenaline, there are also three kilometre intermediate pistes.

Away from the slopes, an array of restaurants are the ideal location to dine alongside sweeping mountain views.

Engadin, St.Moritz, St. Moritz, Switzerland Photo by Sepp Rutz on Unsplash

Les Menuires, France

Located at the heart of the 3 Vallées ski area, visitors can expect nothing less than optimal snow cover and a memorable skiing experience.

This very high resort features 85% of the ski area being at elevations exceeding 1,800 metres, with 52% being equipped with snow cannons. With no lack of choice of where to hit the slopes, Les Menuires shares with its neighbouring resort, Saint-Martin-de-Belleville, 81 ski slopes equipped with 30 lifts.

Here, thrill seekers can relish in the array of black slopes with steep inclines and narrow paths, requiring the most precise skiing technique, as well as off-piste routes.

World.title: Balearic Islands tighten security by land, sea and air ahead of total solar eclipse
World.content:
The Ministry of Defence has agreed to requests from the Balearic Government and will deploy a tactical unit at several points in the Serra de Tramuntana, on the island of Mallorca, ahead of the total eclipse due to take place this Wednesday not only on this island, but across the Balearic archipelago.

 

The troops will thus join the 93 forest firefighters deployed on the largest island in the archipelago, as well as 23 in Menorca, 39 in Ibiza and another six in Formentera. The regional government plans to increase aerial surveillance flights, as weather conditions heighten the risk of wildfires on the day of the eclipse. Meanwhile, Maritime Rescue has strengthened its deployment at sea with 70 professionals for the day of the phenomenon.

But the Army deployment in Mallorca will not be limited to Wednesday. The operation is already under way and will last for five days, although the government spokesperson, Antoni Costa, has not specified how many soldiers will reinforce the presence of the armed forces on the island. They will focus on tightening controls on access routes to the Tramuntana because of the high fire risk in the area in the coming days.

The Ma-10 road will remain closed to general traffic between Andratx and Pollença from 15:00 to 21:00: only residents, property owners, workers, guests, customers with accredited parking and public transport or VTC vehicles will be allowed through. In addition to closing the Ma-10, access will be restricted to numerous viewpoints, coves and natural areas in different municipalities, according to "Diario de Mallorca". All closures can be checked on this website (source in Spanish) set up by the regional government.

The event is expected to draw large crowds in the region. While the Balearic Association of Nautical Companies reports that practically all boats have already been hired to watch the event, as reported by "SER Mallorca", Palma's EMT will introduce a special bus service to s'Arenal, a peri-urban town south of the capital with a much broader stretch of coastline, while preparing to close the city beach from 12:00 up to its boundary with Llucmajor.

Across Spain, the Government has activated a large-scale security operation that will mobilise 33,600 officers from the National Police and the Civil Guard, under a single command for land, sea and air surveillance, in permanent coordination with the Directorate-General for Traffic, which is providing an extra 2,500 personnel. The total number of journeys is expected to exceed one million people; the central government has restricted 123 high-risk areas for environmental reasons or because of evacuation difficulties.

World.title: One of Kyiv's deadliest single attacks kills 12 in central Russia while five are killed in Ukraine
World.content:
A Ukrainian drone strike on the central Russian region of Tatarstan killed at least 12 people in one of Kyiv's most deadly single attacks of the more than four year war.

 

"According to the latest information, 12 people have been killed and 39 wounded as a result of the drone attack," on the city of Nizhnekamsk, the regional press service said in a statement on Monday.

More than 1,000 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, with a population of 240,000, the city is an important oil refining hub, home to two refineries and a petrochemical plant.

The region itself is rich in energy resources and has many major oil refineries that Kyiv has been targeting in retaliatory strikes.

Unverified footage on social media showed a large black smoke cloud billowing at the site of an oil facility near the industrial city of Nizhnekamsk.

Both sides have significantly escalated their long-range attacks this year, causing a spike in civilian deaths, according to the United Nations.

Strikes kill five in Ukraine

Near the front line in Ukraine, a Russian artillery strike killed five people in a village in the northeastern Kharkiv region, local Ukrainian officials said.

"On August 10, Russian forces carried out a massive artillery strike on the residential area of the village of Bugaivka in the Chuguiv district. Various houses were destroyed as a result of the enemy attack. Five people were killed," the regional prosecutor's office said in a statement on Telegram.

Russia's defence ministry said it shot down 456 Ukrainian drones fired overnight. It never states how many reached their targets.

The Tatarstan region had earlier reported a "massive" Ukrainian drone attack.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 126 drones in its overnight attack.

A woman was also killed in a Ukrainian attack on the Russian border region of Belgorod, and a man was killed in a Russian drone strike on a taxi in the frontline Kherson region, officials there said.

Military and oil infrastructures targeted

Ukraine has targeted Russian oil facilities with long-range drones almost daily in recent months. The barrage has caused fuel shortages in Russia, eaten into Russian refining capacity, and unsettled the Russian public.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says it is a campaign to force Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table and stop his more than 4-year-old invasion.

"We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia’s war will be felt more and more at their own home — in Russia," Zelenskyy said late Sunday on social media.

"The only reason this is still continuing is Russia’s unwillingness to end this war."

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: Ukrainian drone attack kills at least 12 in central Russia
World.content:
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at targets inside Russia, according to Russian officials. The strikes killed at least 12 people in one of Kyiv's deadliest attacks since the Russian invasion began over four years ago.

A Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk, located in an energy-rich Tatarstan region of central Russia, killed at least a dozen people and wounded 39 more, according to a local press service statement issued Monday.

Over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border, the region has many major oil refineries that Kyiv has targeted in recent strikes as both sides increase long-range attacks on infrastructure.

The United Nations said such attacks have led to a jump in civilian casualties in Russia and Ukraine.

Unspecified industrial and civilian targets had been hit in Monday's strike, Radmir Belyayev, the mayor of Nizhnekamsk, said in a statement on Telegram.

The Ukrainian strikes on refineries have led to some fuel shortages and reduced Russia's oil-refining capacity.

Russia has also regularly fired missiles, glide bombs and drones hitting civilian areas in Ukraine and causing thousands of civilian casualties, according to the United Nations.

Russia, Ukraine: Deadly drone and missile attacks escalate To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kyiv: Air campaign aims to bring Putin to negotiating table

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the campaign aims to force Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the more than 4-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia's war will be felt more and more at their own home — in Russia," Zelenskyy said late Sunday in a social media post.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 126 drones in its overnight attack.

The Russian Defense Ministry said it shot down 456 Ukrainian drones fired overnight. The ministry, however, does not include how many drones or missiles reach their targets or how many were intercepted in the Tatarstan region.

Near the front line in Ukraine, a Russian artillery strike killed five people in a village in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukrainian officials said.

"On August 10, Russian forces carried out a massive artillery strike on the residential area of the village of Bugaivka in the Chuguiv district. Various houses were destroyed as a result of the enemy attack. Five people were killed," the regional prosecutor's office said in a statement on Telegram.

World.title: Thai ex-lawmaker shoots local official dead over loan
World.content:
A former lawmaker confessed to shooting a senior official at a government office over a money dispute, police have said. The incident came just days after Thailand's deadliest shooting in nearly four years.

Thai police arrested a suspected gunman — identified as former lawmaker Chalong Riewraeng — after he allegedly fired shots that killed a local politician on Monday at a government office on the outskirts of Bangkok.

Authorities said the former MP confessed to the shooting.

Surrounded by police, Chalong told reporters he attempted to speak with Thongchai Yenprasert about money.

"I followed him to his car and hit his car's window, saying I want to talk," the suspect said. "He said he will not talk, so I pulled my gun. I did not aim to shoot, but his driver pulled a gun and pointed it at me so I fired."

Thongchai, who was chairman of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organization, died of his wounds, according to Sakon Sukprom, director of Phra Nang Klao hospital.

Thongchai's driver was also shot and successfully underwent surgery, Sakon added.

Nonthaburi Governor Chestha Mosikarat told reporters the suspect and victim were "friends for a long time" and the incident likely stemmed from a misunderstanding.

Police said the motive for the shooting was a "personal issue."

"According to his confession, it was about money that the ... chairman borrowed from him for several years, and he asked for the return of the money several times," regional Police Commander Wattana Yeechin told reporters, adding that the dispute was over several million baht (1 million baht is about €26,220 or $30,300).

Second recent shooting

This comes just days after a 14-year-old's shooting rampage, first at his home and then at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, left nine people dead and over 20 injured. That incident was Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in nearly four years.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul had reiterated his intention to tighten gun control laws in the wake of the shooting. The Southeast Asian country's current gun laws do not include mental health screenings and allow people as young as 20 to have guns.

Thailand had around 15 guns per 100 ⁠residents, the highest rate in Southeast Asia ​by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey.

World.title: When extreme heat threatens Europe's nuclear power
World.content:
Warm rivers and low water levels are forcing nuclear power plants to reduce output across Europe. Over a year, the losses are minimal, but on critical days the loss of power has consequences for grids and prices.

The state of the Danube is currently showing just how dependent nuclear power plants are on their local conditions. At the power station in Paks, Hungary — which normally produces about 40% of the country's electricity needs — only one of four turbine units is still operating. Due to record-low water levels in the Danube, the country's only nuclear power plant was even briefly at risk of a complete shutdown.

But for the European electricity market, France is of far greater significance. No other country in Europe relies so heavily on nuclear power, and if output in France drops, the country supplies less electricity to its neighbors, and may even become an electricity importer itself.

Reduced power

Over the course of the entire year, heat-related production losses at French power plants are minimal, but during individual weeks of extreme heat, the restrictions can be significant.

A 2023 report by France's official audit office estimated that, between 2000 and 2022, annual losses across all of the country's nuclear reactors due to high water temperatures and low river levels amounted to less than 1% of annual nuclear power production in any given year. Even in the extremely hot summer of 2003, they amounted to only about 1.5%.

But the annual figures obscure short-term fluctuations. In the summer of 2003, French nuclear power plants had to temporarily reduce their output by more than six gigawatts, and the most recent heat waves at the end of June and in mid-July 2026 saw the maximum available capacity was temporarily limited by eight to nine gigawatts. This corresponds to up to one-fifth of the nuclear power capacity normally available to France in the summer.

But eight gigawatts less capacity is not the same as an eight gigawatt overall shortfall. Even without the low water levels, some reactors would not be running at full capacity — either because of lower summer demand, high solar-power production, or bottlenecks in the power grid. According to grid operators, France still had sufficient reserves even during the 2026 heat waves and, on balance, remained an electricity exporter.

Hungary's power options after drought shuts nuclear plant To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other countries feel the impact

Nevertheless, such restrictions are relevant for grid operators and electricity traders. For them, it doesn't matter how much electricity was ultimately produced by nuclear power plants at the end of the year: What is crucial for the stability of the power grids and short-term price surges is whether the power is actually available when it is needed.

And here, experience shows that heat waves increase electricity demand due to air conditioning. Not only that: As this year's heat waves are affecting large parts of Europe, reserves from abroad are also declining.

Rivers getting warmer

Nuclear power plants suffer from low water levels because they must discharge a comparatively large amount of waste heat per kilowatt-hour generated. Only about one-third of the heat generated in a nuclear reactor is converted into electricity; the rest is released into the environment via the cooling system — often into rivers or the sea. But if the river is carrying little water, the waste heat is distributed over a smaller volume of water, and the water temperature rises faster.

Warm water also contains less oxygen, and legal temperature limits are in place to protect fish and other aquatic life. When operators throttle back a reactor in the summer, it is therefore usually not an emergency shutdown for reactor safety, but rather a measure to protect the local river life.

In critical situations, French authorities occasionally grant exemptions from these limits. In such cases, water bodies are monitored more closely, allowing the state-owned power company EdF to produce additional electricity in the short term.

A power plant with cooling towers draws significantly less water from the river and discharges considerably less heat directly into the water than a plant with an open cooling circuit. However, cooling towers do not make a nuclear power plant independent of weather conditions, as the Golfech plant demonstrates.

Located on the Garonne River, which is particularly warm in summer and frequently experiences low water levels, it is one of the most vulnerable sites, despite its cooling towers.

Meanwhile in Chooz on the Meuse River, the reactors had to be throttled back in 2020 despite the cooling towers, to avoid jeopardizing the drinking water supply in Belgium.

The Chooz power plant in France had to be throttled down in 2020 Image: Francois Lo Presti/AFP

Repairs also reduce output

Not every decline in nuclear power production can be explained by the weather. Four years ago, France's reactors generated nearly 82 terawatt-hours less electricity than in 2021. This headline-grabbing crisis was caused less by climate change than by stress corrosion cracking and postponed maintenance work.

But looking ahead, the French audit office expects that climate-related reactor downtime could triple or even quadruple by 2050. Given the low baseline so far, even that would not yet constitute a widespread outage, but it could become critical for individual sites.

With additional cooling towers, deeper water intake structures, and better maintenance planning, France can at least partially counteract this trend. However, making the power plants more heat-resistant costs a lot of money and requires more land.

In its upcoming nuclear power plant modernization program, France intends to take the consequences of climate change into account. Four of the six modern EPR2 reactors initially planned are to be built on the coast, in Penly and Gravelines. Only the third pair of reactors will be built on the Rhone River near Bugey. Cooling towers there are intended to limit the thermal load on the river and water intake.

The Garonne River in France saw extremely low levels in 2022 Image: Valentine Chapuis/AFP

Consequences across Europe

The consequences of French reactor curtailments are evident in the European electricity market. On June 24, capacity was reduced by approximately 4.1 gigawatts due to high river temperatures. As a result, France's electricity exports fell to about three gigawatts, after the country had supplied 10 to 12 gigawatts to its neighbors just the week before.

Combined with higher electricity consumption, low wind power generation, and increased use of gas-fired power plants, this contributed to electricity prices in France and Germany briefly climbing to their highest levels since January 2025.

During the subsequent heat waves in July, the curtailment of reactors was even more extensive, though the impact on other countries was less significant. On July 13, eight reactors with a combined capacity of 6.3 gigawatts were affected, and two were completely taken offline. Nevertheless, France only intermittently exported more than 10 gigawatts and imported affordable solar and wind power from Spain.

The heat-related curtailments of nuclear power plants currently appear to be a manageable problem for the country. Whether this will develop into a Europe-wide shortage in the future will likely depend not least on the development of foreign demand and the reserves of wind and solar power.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: China: Typhoon Dolphin prompts mass evacuation, canceled flights
World.content:
Even as it weakens, Typhoon Dolphin is disrupting life in China. Close to 1,500 flights have been canceled in Shanghai while parts of Beijing are under flood alert.

Heavy rainfall and strong winds prompted flood alerts and more than 1,000 flight cancellations across China on Monday, even as Typhoon Dolphin weakened.

China's National Meteorological Centre (NMC) issued its least severe typhoon alert on Monday morning as the storm lost power after making landfall in China's Zhejiang Province on Sunday.

Despite the weaker storm, the NMC warned that parts of east and central China will continue to receive heavy rainfall. Authorities issued their most severe flash flood alert for parts of eastern and southern Zhejiang on Monday, state news broadcaster CCTV reported.

China's Zhejiang province has faced the worst of Typhoon Dolphin so far Image: AFP

Five districts in Beijing are also under red alerts for heavy rainfall on Monday, with risks of landslides and flooding.

The storm had already forced over 300,000 people in eastern China to preemptively relocate, while bringing heavy rainfall to northern Taiwan over the weekend. In Shanghai, authorities evacuated more than 30,000 people out of high-risk areas. Overall, some one million people have been told to seek shelter.

Social media images showed high speed winds and overturned trucks in Zhejiang on Sunday, where the typhoon made landfall Image: Social Media/REUTERS

Typhoon Dolphin disrupts transport in Shanghai

Shanghai's two main passenger airports, Pudong International Airport and Hongqiao International Airport, canceled 943 flights between them for Monday, the airport authority said in a post online. That's a reduction of capacity by nearly 40%.

On Sunday, the two airports had cancelled nearly 1,500 flights, or about 60% of their scheduled travel, according to state media.

The typhoon has lost some of its strength but China's weather agency still expects days of heavy rainfall Image: cnsphoto/REUTERS

Public transport services in the city were also impacted, with several local trains suspended.

At the same time, Zhejiang province began to resume its transport facilities.

Zhejiang's Ningbo International Airport will resume flights midday on Monday but warned that some of the scheduled travel may still be delayed or canceled as the storm had "not yet completely dissipated."

China is dealing with Typhoon Dolphin just two weeks after Typhoon Noul struck its southern Guangdong province. Last month, Typhoon Maysak killed 11 people and injured over 300 in the central Hubei province.

Extreme weather systems are a common feature in China this time of the year, with typhoons leaving significant displacement, infrastructural damage and loss of lives. Scientists warn that the intensity and frequency of such extreme weather have increased and will continue to rise amid climate change.

World.title: Germany news: Low water on Rhine could sever freight route
World.content:
08/10/2026 August 10, 2026 German rents keep rising amid housing shortage

Rents for new leases in Germany have continued to rise sharply as a persistent housing shortage keeps pressure on the market.

New rents for apartments in multi-family buildings were 3.2% higher in the second quarter than a year earlier, according to the Association of German Pfandbrief Banks (VDP).

The pace of growth eased somewhat compared with previous quarters, however.

Across Germany’s seven largest cities, rents rose by an average of just 1.5%, but the picture varied sharply.

Düsseldorf recorded the strongest increase at 3.6%, while rents in Berlin were almost unchanged, rising just 0.6%.

Germany is estimated to be short of around 1 million homes, with supply particularly tight in major urban areas.

Home prices also continued to climb in the second quarter.

Apartments and houses were 1.9% more expensive than a year earlier and 0.3% higher than in the previous quarter, the VDP said.

Prices in the seven biggest cities rose 2.1% year-on-year, led by Hamburg at 3.8%.

Cologne followed with 2.5%, while Frankfurt and Düsseldorf both recorded increases of 2.4%.

World.title: Type 2 diabetes in young women increasingly common
World.content:
British researchers say rates of type 2 diabetes are growing most among women under 40. The disease is often underdiagnosed in women or diagnosed too late to reverse the condition's progression.

There used to be a clear-cut way to distinguish diabetes type 1 and type 2. Medical jargon aside: Type 1 diabetes was a genetic autoimmune disease that presented in young people, and type 2 was a disease that presented in older patients in their fifties or sixties due to an unhealthy lifestyle.

But that distinction of young and old doesn't work anymore.

More and more, younger people are being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. In England, for example, the biggest increase in new diagnoses of type 2 diabetes is among young women.

This was revealed when a team of researchers from Imperial College London evaluated data from an English National Diabetes Audit between 2011 and 2024. They found that while the prevalence of type 2 diabetes was decreasing in adults between 60 and 79 years of age, it was rising in under-40-year-olds.

The results, published in The Lancet Regional Health Europe journal , showed the sharpest increase was among white, Asian and Black women in their 20s, and white women in their 30s.

"Much of the discussion around rising type 2 diabetes in younger people has focused on ethnic minority groups," said Shivani Misra , the lead author of the study and a clinical associate professor for diabetes at Imperial College London.

"While these ethnic groups are disproportionately affected with early-onset type 2 diabetes, we now see that incidence is […] increasing in white populations too, showing that this public health challenge is broadening across the generation."

Lifestyle behind rise in type 2 diabetes among young people

In Germany, the situation is similar to the UK, said Baptist Gallwitz, an endocrinologist and spokesperson for the German Diabetes Society (DDG).

"Type 2 diabetes is on the rise in many countries," Gallwitz told DW. "It's basically a pandemic. In Germany, we're also seeing an increase in children and teenagers diagnosed with the disease."

From 2014 to 2023, there was an increase in type 2 diabetes cases of 5.8% a year among youth aged 11 to 17 years, according to a 2026 health report on diabetes released by the DDG.

Nigeria faces a silent diabetes epidemic To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While genetic disposition can play a role in the development of type 2 diabetes, the biggest factor is lifestyle.

"We live in a world where we don't move enough and where our nutrition contains too much sugar and too many calories," Gallwitz said. "That leads to more obesity among young people, and that in turn greatly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes."

In people with type 2 diabetes, reduced insulin secretion or a weaker effect of insulin on its receptors lead to a higher glucose content in the blood.

Type 1 diabetes is characterized by a full loss of insulin-producing cells, leading to severe insulin deficiency.

Fighting the rise of diabetes type 2 in young people

The increase is particularly concerning because in young patients, the progression of the disease can be more serious than in older patients.

"Any diagnosis of type 2 diabetes is serious, but it can be more aggressive in younger people, increasing the risk of devastating complications and cutting lives short," said Helen Kirrane from Diabetes UK, a charity that campaigns on the issue.

That's why it's important to intervene early. Gallwitz said the DDG welcomed the introduction of a tax on sugary sodas in Germany, but added that it wasn't enough.

The DDG is calling for a tiered value-added tax (VAT) system, with fresh fruit and vegetables being sold with no tax and the VAT increasing the more the products contain saturated fats and sugars.

The organization also wants healthier food in kindergarten and school cafeterias and one hour of mandatory movement per day to be incorporated into class schedules.

Asking for more exercise during the school day is one thing. But conditions in the general environment also need to be improved to stop the increase of type 2 diabetes in young women, said Alexandra Kautzky-Willer, head of the division for endocrinology and metabolism at the Medical University of Vienna.

"More movement is important, so we need to ensure conditions in which it's safe for women to move," Kautzky-Willer, who is also a professor of gender medicine, told DW.

For example, a woman who fears being catcalled, ridiculed for her weight or even attacked in the dark is less likely to go running after work or join a gym.

How a young Ghanaian is determined to beat diabetes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Diabetes type 2 underdiagnosed in women

The number of women with type 2 diabetes might be even higher than what current data show. In 2025, Kautzky-Willer and a colleague wrote a report for the Deutsches Ärzteblatt , a German medical journal, saying that the disease is underdiagnosed in women.

"Men are usually diagnosed with [type 2 diabetes] at a younger age," they wrote in the the article. "At the point of diagnosis, more women are obese, they have hypertension more often and have gained more weight" than men when they are diagnosed.

Those factors contributed to an increased risk of stroke and heart attacks as well. So, why is it that diabetes type 2 is often only diagnosed in women when they are already this sick?

"For one, the value often tested in initial diabetes diagnosis is fasting blood sugar," Kautzky-Willer said.

Your fasting blood sugar is your blood sugar level when you haven't eaten for eight hours. It's just a single snapshot in time, however, and misses blood sugar spikes after a meal.

Fasting blood sugar "is generally lower in women than it is in men," Kautzky-Willer said. "It would make more sense to do a glucose tolerance test, but that is more work."

More complex tests for diabetes could save lives

A glucose tolerance test involves taking blood several times in the span of two hours, during which patients need to stay at the doctor's office.

Kautzky-Willer says it would be good if HbA1c levels were tested as well. Tests for HbA1c levels show a person's average blood sugar level over a two or three-month period.

HbA1c refers to glycated haemoglobin, which is when glucose in your body sticks to red blood cells. This prevents the body from using the sugar properly.

A high HbA1c means you have too much sugar in your blood and are more likely to develop diabetes complications. But testing HbA1c levels requires specialized lab equipment and is more expensive than testing the fasting blood sugar.

The glucose tolerance and the HbA1c tests are not covered by health insurance in Germany and Austria, only the fasting blood sugar one is covered, and that may be influencing the options for people in those countries.

Experts who spoke to DW agreed that to bring type 2 diabetes numbers down among young people, it's important to know when their blood values get close to the line for the disease, a condition known as being "pre-diabetic."

People who find out they have a problem at this early stage still have a chance to turn the ship around. With lifestyle and nutrition changes, diabetes progression can be stopped in some cases, saving them from a host of health problems later on, which may require regular medication and lead to a reduced life expectancy.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

World.title: Iran War:  Is Iran’s middle class being pushed into poverty?
World.content:
The war has intensified Iran’s economic crisis, squeezing household budgets, hurting businesses and raising fears that millions of middle-income families are slipping closer to poverty.

For Mina, a housewife in Iran, the war is no longer measured by air strikes or military statements. It is measured by what has disappeared from her family's dinner table.

"Since the war started last year, we have become poorer every day,” she told DW. "I honestly can't remember the last time I bought red meat. We replaced it with chicken, but even chicken has become a luxury. We no longer think about saving money. We only think about paying the rent and buying food.”

The International Monetary Fund forecasts Iran's economy will contract by 5.4% this year, while inflation is expected to approach 69%. The World Bank has also warned that conflict, weaker trade and prolonged uncertainty are weighing heavily on the country's economy.

For economist Ahmad Alavi, a Sweden-based researcher, the war did not create Iran's economic crisis, but sharply intensified it.

"Iran entered the conflict with inflation already above 40%, a weakening currency, chronic budget deficits and years of sanctions,” he told DW.

"The war acted as an external shock. Damage to infrastructure, disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz, internet shutdowns and rising inflation expectations accelerated the collapse in purchasing power,” he said.

Alavi points to official figures showing annual inflation reaching 66% and year-over-year inflation nearing 88%. Food prices have risen even faster. Bread and cereals have increased by around 140%, meat and poultry by 135%, dairy products by more than 116%, and edible oils by over 200%.

For many families, those figures have meant buying less meat, postponing medical treatment and abandoning plans to save money.

Inflation in Iran is expected to reach nearly 70% in 2026 Image: Fatemeh Bahrami/AA/picture alliance

The war has pushed some 4 million Iranians into poverty

Economists say households often cut spending on travel and clothing first. As inflation persists, however, the cuts extend to food, healthcare and education, placing growing pressure on middle-income families that once considered themselves financially secure.

Alavi says lower-income households have suffered the most but argues that the middle class is increasingly facing the same pressures.

"Many salaried workers and pensioners have fallen below the poverty line for the first time because incomes have failed to keep pace with inflation.”

He estimates that between 3.5 and 4.5 million more Iranians have fallen into poverty since the conflict intensified, bringing the total number of people living below the poverty line to more than 40 million.

To adapt to the tighter cost of living, many households have started cutting meat from their diet Image: Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Businesses squeezed by uncertainty

The pressure is also being felt by Iran's private sector.

Morteza, an Iranian trader, says regional trade routes changed rapidly after shipping through the Strait of Hormuz became more difficult.

"China moved quickly to fill part of the gap left by suppliers in Dubai,” he told DW. "Unlike Gulf countries, China can also ship goods through rail links across Central Asia, avoiding many of the risks and delays associated with maritime transport.”

He believes the growing importance of these overland routes was one of the reasons the U.S. targeted a railway line near Iran's border with Turkmenistan, although that assessment could not be independently verified.

Even so, Morteza says the shift has brought little benefit to Iranian traders.

"The collapse of the rial and soaring inflation have prevented the market from growing,” he says. "Merchants are living with constant uncertainty because exchange rates change almost every day. Goods that we bought and sold at lower prices now have to be replaced at much higher costs, and that's only if customers still have enough purchasing power to buy them.”

For Morteza, uncertainty has become the biggest obstacle.

"With tensions continuing, I honestly don't see a clear future for doing business in Iran.”

What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can the government soften the blow?

Despite higher global oil prices, Alavi says Iran is unlikely to benefit significantly because sanctions, export restrictions and higher transport costs continue to limit its oil revenues.

He argues that government measures, including subsidies, price controls and intervention in the foreign exchange market may ease some immediate pressure, but are unlikely to address the underlying problems.

"Without restoring confidence, reducing sanctions and addressing structural problems, these policies remain short-term responses rather than lasting solutions.”

Economist Dr. Ahmad Alavi says rebuilding confidence in the economy is likely to take much longer than repairing physical damage caused by the war Image: Privat

The cost of uncertainty

Alavi says uncertainty itself has become one of the biggest barriers to economic recovery.

According to him, many businesses are delaying investment because they have little confidence in future economic conditions. At the same time, households are becoming increasingly cautious about spending as they expect prices to keep rising and the value of their incomes to fall further.

He says rebuilding confidence among investors, businesses and consumers is likely to take much longer than repairing physical damage caused by the war.

Unless inflation eases, the exchange rate stabilizes and trade conditions improve, Alavi believes many households will remain under financial pressure, even if military tensions subside.

Looking ahead, he expects living standards to deteriorate further if current trends continue.

He says more families are likely to cut spending on protein, healthcare and education, while business closures and unemployment may continue to rise.

"We don't talk about the future anymore,” Mina says. "We only hope we can afford next month's rent.”

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

World.title: ¿Dónde habrá nubes durante el eclipse? Consulte cómo estarán los cielos y el horizonte en cada municipio
World.content:
Mostramos y actualizamos en un mapa varias previsiones de nubosidad para el miércoles 12 de agosto: dónde habrá nubes, de qué tipo y en qué dirección mirar

Las nubes bajas pueden convertirse en el peor enemigo de alguien que quiera ver el eclipse de este 12 de agosto. En el siguiente mapa mostramos la nubosidad prevista para las 20 horas del miércoles en cada municipio y hacia el horizonte, además del detalle de altura de las nubes en cada lugar. Los últimos datos de previsión disponibles son de hoy lunes 10; a partir de mañana martes se podrá consultar también la previsión hora por hora de Aemet.

El mapa de nubosidad es una previsión que se calcula con días de antelación, se actualiza cada pocas horas y su resolución es de kilómetros. Por eso damos una valoración orientativa: favorable, regular o desfavorable.

Para estimar la nubosidad durante el eclipse combinamos tres modelos modelos de predicción del Centro Europeo de Predicciones a Medio Plazo (ECMWF por sus siglas en inglés). Uno indica cuánta nube habrá sobre cada punto: es la capa de nubes que se ve coloreada en el mapa. Otro, AIFS —un modelo de inteligencia artificial del mismo centro—, añade un dato clave para observar un eclipse: a qué altura están esas nubes, si son bajas, medias o altas. El tercero es HARMONIE-AROME, el modelo de alta resolución de AEMET, que ofrece una previsión hora por hora, pero no antes de 48 horas del evento.

Esa distinción importa porque el 12 de agosto el eclipse ocurre con el sol muy bajo sobre el horizonte, hacia el oeste-noroeste, casi al atardecer. Por eso es importante conocer la nubosidad en cada lugar pero también hacia el horizonte. Cuando se mira hacia esa línea imaginaria, lo que tapa el sol son las nubes que se cruzan en esa dirección. Y sobre todo las nubes bajas, más densas y pegadas al suelo. Las altas (las más comunes se conocen como cirros) son finas y a menudo dejan ver el sol.

No hay que olvidar que existen otros elementos que pueden impedir la visión del eclipse, como el relieve: lo mostramos en este otro mapa.

Según la última actualización de los datos, en el 86% de los municipios españoles las nubes dejarán una situación favorable para ver el eclipse (aunque será total solo en la franja).

World.title: España, en alerta roja por miedo a los incendios por negligencias durante la observación del eclipse
World.content:
Los fuegos devastadores que han arrasado miles de hectáreas en Ávila y Madrid han tiznado el escenario festivo que se planteaba para ver el eclipse: municipios y comunidades contienen la respiración al multiplicarse el riesgo de que se produzcan incendios el miércoles, cuando millones de personas subirán al monte, se congregarán en las sierras o abrirán sus bocadillos en miradores para presenciar el eclipse total de sol. Porque la mayor parte de España estará en nivel de riesgo muy alto o extremo de incendios, según el índice de la Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet), y las zonas rurales serán la platea ideal desde donde, sobre las 20.30, se observará el evento astronómico. El comportamiento del público va a ser determinante para la seguridad kilómetros a la redonda. Las comunidades que atraerán a más visitantes han prohibido accesos a áreas protegidas y pistas forestales, e incluso varias han dictado medidas extraordinarias para intentar evitar tragedias.

No solo se trata de no hacer barbacoas ni lanzar fuegos artificiales, sino también de no estacionar cerca de vegetación seca, guardar las colillas y no detenerse en los arcenes ni bloquear los accesos para que los servicios de emergencia puedan circular con agilidad si lo requieren. La ministra para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico, Sara Aagesen, pidió “precaución” la semana pasada en una comparecencia y subrayó: “La vegetación se encuentra extraordinariamente seca y una pequeña chispa, una imprudencia, desencadenan incendios forestales con consecuencias devastadoras para personas, ecosistemas y el patrimonio natural”. La Aemet ha decidido dar un parte diario especial hasta la fecha debido a la singularidad de esa jornada.

Más información Mapa de sitios donde ver el eclipse total de Sol: EL PAÍS recopila más de 350 puntos de observación oficiales

El riesgo es altísimo y justifica medidas extremas: en lo que va de año, el sistema de información europeo de incendios forestales (EFFIS) ha registrado 391 fuegos y 222.783 hectáreas quemadas en España, un poco más que el tamaño de Guipúzcoa. En este contexto, Aragón ha decretado medidas urgentes del 10 al 13 de agosto, entre las que prohibirá subir al monte con vehículos a motor, prender fuego o usar pirotecnia, con multas de entre 1.000 y 100.000 euros.

Además, ha tipificado como “espectáculo prohibido” cualquier reunión o fiesta que congregue gente sin un título habilitante en esas fechas. La Delegación del Gobierno en Galicia ha publicado un listado de 29 puntos de exclusión que no podrán visitarse ese día, como el Monte da Guía, en Vigo, o la Torre de Hércules, en A Coruña.

Castilla y León ha destacado en un mapa zonas no recomendadas y pide no trasladarse a aquellas que forman parte de la Red de Áreas Naturales Protegidas (RANP). Advierte de no circular con vehículos por vías no asfaltadas ni de un único sentido, debido al riesgo de quedar atrapado, y prohíbe aparcar en carreteras, caminos rurales y en las pistas forestales. No se puede acampar fuera de los lugares autorizados.

La Comunidad Valenciana ha decretado el nivel de preemergencia 3 en todo el territorio ese día, que restringe encender cualquier tipo de fuego en los terrenos forestales o cerca y suspende las autorizaciones de circulación deportiva por estas zonas. La autonomía ha anunciado que circularán vuelos de vigilancia forestal y tendrán 26 medios aéreos disponibles por las dudas. Los parques naturales estarán cerrados.

Eventos cancelados

Distintos eventos están dando marcha atrás para no correr riesgos. El ayuntamiento de Tres Cantos, en Madrid, ha decidido suspender las actividades que tenía planificadas. “Este año estamos en un estado muy excepcional”, resalta Elisa Lidia Miguel, que ha asumido las funciones del alcalde titular en vacaciones. “Dadas las circunstancias trágicas de los incendios que están asolando la Comunidad de Madrid, creímos que lo mejor era cancelar la actividad que precise de una asistencia técnica, de maquinaria o generadores que puedan provocar algún tipo de chispa”, explica.

Por eso, la gente podrá acercarse a pie a ver el eclipse, pero no habrá música en vivo, food trucks ni talleres. Se prohibirá el acceso de vehículos a la finca de Valdeloshielos para proteger espacios como el monte de El Pardo. “Estamos rogando que sean prudentes”, insiste Miguel. Grupos de vecinos de la Sierra Norte, el extremo de la comunidad donde el fenómeno se verá total, están presionando para que se cancelen todos los eventos y se presente un plan de contingencia.

Debido a estos mismos temores, se han suspendido fiestas masivas que ya estaban autorizadas. El festival Iberia Eclipse en Soria, que reunía a 200 artistas de música electrónica y ya tenía casi 1.500 entradas vendidas, perdió su permiso a dos semanas de celebrarse. El Ayuntamiento de Vinuesa le revocó la autorización por recomendaciones ambientales y por el impacto de un festival de motos celebrado semanas antes, con una fallecida en un accidente. A los pocos días de esa decisión, sufrieron un incendio que confirmó el motivo de sus resguardos.
