Michelin-starred cuisine is also coming to Sziget

One of the festival’s most notable gastronomic additions this year will be found in the VIP area. Costes, one of Hungary’s best-known fine-dining names and associated with Michelin-starred cuisine, will be among the restaurants serving festival-goers.

The VIP food line-up will also include Buja Disznó(k), Digó and 101 Bistro, while TOKIO will bring a more refined take on modern Asian cuisine. It is an unusual combination: one moment you can be watching a major international act, and the next you can be eating food associated with some of Budapest’s leading restaurants.

Sustainability is also on the menu

Sziget is also placing greater emphasis on sustainability across its food operations. The festival will continue its composting programme, which was recognised with an international innovation award in 2019. This year, the system will be extended across all of the festival’s food courts.

Organic waste, as well as the biodegradable plates and cutlery used at the festival, will be collected separately and composted.

The organisers are also requiring participating food vendors to make at least three sustainability commitments. These can include offering vegetarian or vegan main courses, avoiding red meat, using organic ingredients, sourcing products from Hungarian producers or using sustainably sourced palm oil.

A new Green Hospitality Programme will also launch this year, with higher sustainability standards for participating vendors. The first businesses to receive the new certification include Hot by Sophie’s Delight, Vegan Island by Napfényes, Crunchy, Zing Burger & CO, Pasta Vibes and Mambo Pasta Bistro.

A farmers’ market is coming too

For those looking for something fresher after several days of burgers, pizza and lángos, Sziget will also feature its first Farmers’ Market. Local producers will offer fresh vegetables, fruit and other products, giving festival-goers another option beyond traditional festival food.

An Aldi store will also return to the festival, with a full shop built on site. One unusual feature is that visitors will be able to buy fresh meat for grilling and have it prepared for them at the festival. There will also be options for people with dietary restrictions, including gluten-free and/or lactose-free dishes, as well as vegan food.

Sziget food is no longer just about burgers and lángos

Festival food has changed considerably in recent years. What was once largely a choice between a burger, pizza or lángos has evolved into a much broader gastronomic experience.

At Sziget this year, visitors can start the day with brunch and coffee, grab Asian street food in the afternoon, enjoy a Neapolitan pizza before a headline show, or even opt for fine-dining-inspired dishes in the VIP area.

And for those who simply want to eat well without spending a fortune, the HUF 3,500 budget-food option offers a much-needed cheaper alternative. The full list of participating food vendors and further details are available on the official Sziget website.

World.title: Drugging fears emerge after multiple women fall ill during DJ show in Hungary
World.content:
Concerns have emerged over alleged drink spiking at the site of Budapest’s Sziget Festival after several festivalgoers reported that women suddenly became seriously unwell during Hungarian DJ and presenter Balázs Sebestyén’s Saturday night show.

One young man said his sister collapsed and became unresponsive after having a drink at one of the festival’s food and drink outlets. According to reports shared on social media, as many as 18 young women were treated at one medical point with similar symptoms.

The reports have not been independently confirmed as cases of drink spiking, and Hungarian police have reportedly not received an official complaint about such incidents at the festival.

Young woman reportedly collapsed after a drink

Norbert Galambos, who attended the event with his sister and a group of friends, described what happened in a widely shared Facebook post.

According to his account, his sister suddenly collapsed after drinking at a festival bar and stopped responding. When the family sought medical assistance, he said paramedics initially asked how much alcohol she had consumed and whether she had taken drugs.

Galambos stressed that his sister does not use recreational drugs and that she had simply gone to the festival with friends. He also criticised the way he says the pair were treated by medical staff, arguing that his sister was treated as though she had voluntarily taken drugs.

The Hungarian National Ambulance Service shared his post and said it takes the claims seriously and will investigate the circumstances. The service also emphasised that professional medical care should be accompanied by appropriate and empathetic communication with both patients and their concerned relatives.

Reports of more women becoming unwell

According to accounts shared by festivalgoers, the incident may not have been isolated. Witnesses claimed that a number of women experienced similar symptoms and sought medical assistance during the event. One account circulating online claimed that 18 young women were treated at a single medical point.

However, this figure has not been independently verified, and it remains unclear how many people may actually have been affected or what caused their symptoms. Another festivalgoer, a 39-year-old woman named Enikő, also described becoming suddenly ill during the DJ show.

She said she had asked someone to bring drinks from a VIP area because of the long queues at the festival bars. She claimed that shortly afterwards she became severely unwell and lost control of her movements. According to her account, her husband and another couple who happened to be nearby helped her until medical assistance arrived. She later said she was convinced that her symptoms were not simply the result of drinking alcohol.

What is GHB?

Some of the social media reports have suggested that GHB, sometimes known as “Gina”, may have been involved. However, there is currently no confirmed evidence establishing that GHB was responsible for the reported incidents.

GHB is a synthetic psychoactive substance that is colourless and odourless in liquid form. It can cause drowsiness, confusion and impaired consciousness, while larger amounts can result in unconsciousness and potentially life-threatening breathing problems.

Combining GHB with alcohol can be particularly dangerous because both substances can depress the central nervous system. The drug has also been associated with sexual assaults and robberies because a person under its influence may become extremely vulnerable and unable to protect themselves.

Importantly, the symptoms described by festivalgoers alone cannot establish what substance, if any, was involved. Medical assessment and toxicological testing would be needed to determine the cause.

GHB can disappear from the body quickly

According to Blikk, one difficulty in investigating suspected GHB exposure is the substance’s relatively short detection window.

GHB can generally only be detected in blood for a few hours after consumption and in urine for several more hours. This means that if someone suspects they have been drugged, seeking medical attention as soon as possible can be important. A hair test may potentially detect GHB exposure much later, but such testing is more specialised and costly.

No official police complaint reported so far

Despite the growing number of social media posts, there has so far been no confirmed report of an official police complaint concerning drink spiking at Sziget, according to the reports available. The claims therefore remain allegations at this stage.

The Hungarian National Ambulance Service is investigating the circumstances surrounding the treatment of the reported patients, while the exact number of people affected and the cause of their symptoms remain unclear.

Festivalgoers are nevertheless being urged to take sensible precautions, including keeping an eye on their drinks, staying with friends and seeking medical help immediately if they or someone in their group suddenly becomes confused, severely drowsy, unconscious or otherwise seriously unwell.

If you missed it: Transylvanian villagers attack ambulance after seeing TikTok rumours about kidnapping children

Sziget not aware of drugging incidents

Sziget also responded to the above reports. In their response to Daily News Hungary, they stated that medical services were provided during the event in cooperation with the National Ambulance Service. Of the more than 60,000 visitors, fewer than 100 required medical attention; of these, 20 cases were alcohol-related, and there were no drug-related incidents.

“We, too, were deeply outraged by the reports that appeared on social media, and we encourage anyone affected by such an incident to contact the police. For our part, we will do everything we can to assist the investigative authorities in their work,” they wrote.

They also noted that their catering units have been working with the same tried-and-true, reliable subcontractors for years, who serve the public safely and to a high standard.

World.title: Ferencváros narrowly beaten by Real Madrid at packed Groupama Arena
World.content:
Ferencváros suffered a narrow 2-1 defeat to Real Madrid in a high-profile friendly at Budapest’s Groupama Arena on Saturday, but the Hungarian champions gave their illustrious opponents plenty to think about and found the net through Kenan Kodro.

Fradi impress against European giants

Real Madrid took control late in the first half when Mario Rivas headed the visitors in front, before Carlos Espí doubled their advantage shortly after the interval. Ferencváros responded through Kodro in the 57th minute and grew into the game, but could not find the equaliser.

The result nevertheless represented a memorable occasion for Ferencváros, who welcomed one of football’s most decorated clubs to their home ground.

Groupama Arena turns white and green

The match attracted an unusually large number of Real Madrid supporters, with fans wearing shirts bearing the names of stars such as Federico Valverde, Jude Bellingham, Kylian Mbappé, Vinícius Júnior and Rodrygo.

Inside the stadium, Real Madrid shirts were considerably more prominent than usual alongside Ferencváros’ traditional green-and-white colours.

On the pitch, however, the colours were reversed. Ferencváros wore a new pale-gold and off-white kit, while Real Madrid appeared in green. The atmosphere was lively from the start, with the stadium filling rapidly before kick-off.

Real Madrid dominate but Fradi stand firm

Ferencváros did not appear intimidated by their illustrious opponents and created several promising attacks in the opening stages, although their efforts failed to seriously trouble the Madrid goal.

As the first half progressed, Real increasingly controlled possession. Their quick passing and explosive movement forced Ferencváros deeper, with the visitors repeatedly attempting shots from distance.

The hosts’ first major defensive test came in the 36th minute, when Endrick found space in the area, only for goalkeeper Dénes Dibusz to keep out his close-range effort.

Real’s pressure finally produced a goal in the 41st minute. Arda Güler’s corner reached Alexis Ciria, who returned the ball into the danger area, allowing Mario Rivas to head Madrid into the lead.

Madrid’s stars make their mark

The second half brought a major change in personnel for the Spanish giants, with Vinícius Júnior, Dean Huijsen, Antonio Rüdiger, Trent Alexander-Arnold, Carlos Espí and Bernardo Silva among those introduced.

The arrival of several established stars immediately increased Madrid’s attacking threat. After an impressive passing move, Federico Valverde provided the final pass for Carlos Espí, who finished calmly to make it 2-0.

Ferencváros responded quickly. In the 57th minute, Kristoffer Zachariassen delivered an excellent cross from the right, and Kenan Kodro met it at the near post to fire the ball into the bottom-left corner. The Groupama Arena erupted, with even some Real Madrid supporters applauding the home side’s goal.

Fradi push for an equaliser

The goal changed the complexion of the match. Ferencváros began escaping the pressure that had characterised much of the first half and regularly worked their way towards Madrid’s penalty area.

Zachariassen came close again with a header, but his effort went straight into the hands of goalkeeper Andriy Lunin.

Real continued to threaten from set pieces, with Trent Alexander-Arnold, Federico Valverde and Güler among those around a late free-kick. Güler ultimately sent his effort over the crossbar.

As the final whistle approached, Ferencváros looked capable of finding an equaliser, with the flow of the game suggesting they were closer to making it 2-2 than Real were to extending their lead. The second goal ultimately failed to arrive.

Encouraging test ahead of European football

Real Madrid therefore left Budapest with a 2-1 victory, but Ferencváros can take considerable encouragement from their performance.

The Hungarian side competed well against one of the world’s biggest clubs, absorbed sustained pressure, scored against Madrid after the interval and created chances to level the match.

The friendly was nevertheless only part of a busy summer schedule. Ferencváros’ attention now turns to the return leg against Górnik Zabrze in Europa League qualifying.

That fixture will carry far greater competitive importance, but after their performance against Real Madrid, Fradi can approach it with plenty of confidence.

World.title: Romania banks 6 medals, first place among nations at U19 World Rowing Championships
World.content:
Romania finished the U19 World Rowing Championships held in Plovdiv, Bulgaria, with 6 medals, among which 3 gold, one silver, and 2 bronze, and first place in the nations' medal ranking.

On Sunday, August 9, the women’s 8+1 crew, made up of Teodora Sandu, Carolina Pănuţă, Elena Bianca Niţu, Maya Renata Bumbac, Elena Denisa Baciu, Mariana Casu, Angela Gabriela Cazacu, Mădălina-Dumitriţa Ursaciuc and Sarra-Maria Vasca, became Under-19 world champions, according to the Romanian Rowing Federation.

The silver medal was won by the mixed 8+1 crew: Anca-Andreea Culidiuc, Denisa Mihaela Vasilica, Răzvan Ioan Marin, Andrei Mihai Bălan, Radu-Andrei Enescu, Dumitru Cristian Pascari, Marina Ariana Balint, Jessica Popescu and Sarra-Maria Vasca.

The other two world titles were won by Radu-Andrei Enescu and Dumitru Cristian Pascari in the men’s coxless pair, and by Ana-Maria Bordanc, Alexandra Daria Crăciun, Anca-Andreea Culidiuc and Denisa Mihaela Vasilica in the women’s coxless four.

The two bronze medals came through Gabriela Costinela Ursu and Andreea Măriuca Dumitraşcu in the women’s double sculls, and through Ioana Gabriela Cristescu, Francesca Iulia Stejar, Sonia Teodora Biţă and Daria-Elena Maximiuc in the women’s quadruple sculls.

In total, 42 athletes represented Romania in the competition in Plovdiv.

World.title: Survey: 7 out of 10 Romanians expect higher expenses in August due to holidays
World.content:
Roughly 7 out of 10 Romanians estimate that they will spend more in August than in a usual month, and for almost half of them the difference is significant, as they anticipate expenses at least 26% higher, according to a survey conducted by Raiffeisen Bank Romania in partnership with Appinio.

Summer holidays, going out, and home projects weigh heavily on the budgets of Romanians. Around 61% of Romanians said they continued to allocate the most money to current expenses, while 40% say they spend more on outings and recreational activities, 39% on holidays in Romania, 33% on home renovations and improvements, and 32% on weekend trips and city breaks.

Even during the holiday season, current expenses remain the main source of financial pressure, as indicated by 18% of respondents. They are followed by holidays abroad or in Romania with 14% each, and home renovations or improvements with 13%.

However, respondents say holidays are the expense that brings them the greatest satisfaction. For 13%, the greatest satisfaction comes from investments in the home or personal comfort, while 19% mention recreational activities (organizing or participating in festive events, attending festivals).

When summer plans exceed the usual budget, Romanians primarily rely on money they have set aside. Around 32% say they will use savings made for this period, while 29% will reduce other current expenses.

Another 28% say they will give up some outings or activities, while 23% will postpone other important purchases. A total of 13% are considering using a credit card or paying in installments, and 7% a personal needs loan.

Among respondents who have close relatives or friends in the diaspora returning to Romania, 58% say these visits generate additional expenses to a large or very large extent, while 42% feel the impact to a small extent or not at all.

Asked how they would best describe their summer from the perspective of personal finances, Romanians indicated caution rather than financial exuberance. Around 21% say it is a summer without unusual expenses, while another 21% describe it as “the summer in which I keep the budget under control.” For 19%, however, it is “the summer of financial compromises.”

The research on Romanians’ summer spending is part of the Despre Bani 1:1 series carried out by Raiffeisen Bank Romania. The survey was conducted in collaboration with Appinio, on a sample of 1,300 people aged between 18 and 65, representative at national level, in July 2026.

World.title: Fitness club operator World Class Romania earmarks EUR 18 million for network expansion, upgrade
World.content:
World Class Romania announced a total first-phase investment of EUR 18 million to expand and upgrade its network of fitness clubs.

More than EUR 12 million has been allocated to the complete modernization of 17 clubs throughout 2026, while approximately EUR 6 million will fund the opening of two new clubs in the third quarter of the year: World Class One High District in Bucharest and World Class City of Mara in Timișoara.

The modernization works have already begun at World Class ParkLake and will continue in phases throughout 2026 across other clubs in the network, including București Mall, Plaza România, Mega Mall, Caro, Downtown, Otopeni, Titan, Incity, Jolie Ville, Militari, Promenada and One Cotroceni.

Each location will go through a transformation lasting approximately two months, depending on the size and complexity of the existing facilities.

The 17 clubs included in the 2026 upgrade program are only the first phase of a long-term transformation strategy that will continue across the entire network in 2027 and beyond.

The network transformation is the first step in a broader strategy “that will see World Class Romania evolve beyond the traditional health and fitness model toward the gym-as-a-clinic concept,” the company said.

"The future of our industry lies in delivering an integrated experience where health assessments, training, recovery, and nutrition work together in a personalized way. We want World Class Romania to become a lifelong partner in helping people live healthier lives. In the coming months, we will introduce a series of initiatives focused on longevity and on the role World Class Romania aims to play in bringing this concept to the Romanian market," Matei Filipidescu, CEO of World Class Romania and Deputy CEO of Vectr Holdings, said.

World Class Romania has an annual revenue of EUR 51.6 million, a network of 45 clubs, 29 swimming pools, and a community of over 80,000 members across seven cities. It also operates W, its premium fitness and lifestyle concept.

World Class Romania is owned by Vectr Holdings, an investment company with operations in Romania across sectors including agribusiness, agricultural equipment, real estate, and health&fitness. The company recently expanded its portfolio through the acquisition of the Befit brand of fitness clubs.

World.title: Seven Romanians placed in detention after attacking an ambulance in Cluj County
World.content:
Six men and one woman were placed in pre-trial detention after attacking an ambulance in Cluj County, central Romania, amid a backdrop of disinformation on TikTok regarding black ambulances that allegedly steal children.

The attack occurred in the village of Recea-Cristur, Cluj County, on Saturday, August 8. The incident began when the medical crew stopped after entering the locality to ask residents for directions to a patient's address.

Soon after, according to the Department for Emergency Situations, the ambulance that was transporting a patient to hospital was intentionally blocked by two cars. Several people reportedly got out carrying clubs and axes and began attacking the ambulance, accusing the crew of operating the alleged "black ambulance that steals children."

The police were called, and the ambulance crew managed to continue its mission and transport the patient safely to the Emergency Unit.

As a result of the assault, the driver of the ambulance suffered ocular trauma, which required specialist medical evaluation and a surgical intervention during the night

A day later, the Dej Court decided to place six men and one woman in pre-trial detention. The woman is being investigated for disturbing public order and peace and for assault or other acts of violence, while the men are being investigated for disturbing public order and peace.

In response to the attack, DSU drew attention to the danger posed by false information regarding the activity of ambulances and emergency services on social media. “Such claims are false and deeply dangerous,” the service said in the press release.

Also on Sunday, deputy prime minister Oana Gheorghiu said that Romania needs a strong law against online disinformation and manipulation. “Ambulances do not steal children, but TikTok steals brains,” she also wrote on Facebook.

Similarly, Romania’s Ministry of Interior noted that no cases have been recorded in Romania in which ambulances were involved in the kidnapping of persons. MAI warned that the videos and images on social media are modified or entirely created using artificial intelligence.

Last month, Romanian president Nicusor Dan argued that Romanian legislation should be adapted to resist the spread of false information.

World.title: Constanţa County Council advances with project of EUR 23 mln Aquarium
World.content:
The Constanţa County Council has entered the implementation stage of one of the most important investment projects in the field of tourism and education in the region, after signing the financing contract for the new Aquarium of the Constanţa Natural Sciences Museum Complex, according to Ziarul Financiar.

The project has a total value of RON 115.02 million (approximately EUR 23 million, including VAT) and benefits from financing through the South-East Regional Program 2021–2027. The works will have an estimated duration of 24 months, and the implementation deadline is set for December 2029.

The project includes the development of pools dedicated to the Planetary Ocean and the Black Sea, underwater viewing tunnels, a penguin habitat, thematic exhibitions, a conference room, a library, a café, and modern spaces for educational and scientific activities.

World.title: Ambulance attacked in Romania amid viral TikTok child-stealing hoax
World.content:
An ambulance crew was attacked with sticks, axes and stones in Recea Cristur, Cluj County, after false claims circulated on TikTok that an ambulance was being used to steal children, according to Romanian authorities and Curs de Guvernare.

The ambulance driver was injured in the eye by shards of broken glass after the vehicle was attacked and required emergency surgery in Cluj-Napoca. The doctors said he suffered corneal damage and would need at least three months to recover.

The incident began when the medical crew stopped after entering the locality to ask residents for directions to a patient's address. Police said the ambulance appeared similar to vehicles shown in TikTok videos spreading false claims that children were being abducted for organ harvesting and medical experiments.

After the medical team collected the patient and began travelling towards Dej Hospital, where the patient was due to be transported, their route was blocked by a car. Several people reportedly got out carrying clubs and axes and began attacking the ambulance, accusing the crew of operating the alleged "black ambulance that steals children".

The attack has prompted renewed calls from the government for legislation addressing disinformation and harmful content on social media.

Acting Defence Minister Radu Miruță urged Chamber of Deputies President Sorin Grindeanu to put forward for debate and rapid adoption a bill he submitted in March 2025 aimed at limiting the spread of manipulative and illegal content on social networks, according to Euronews.

"The law against disinformation must be adopted! I submitted it to Parliament in 2025. It passed tacitly in the Senate and is blocked in the Chamber of Deputies," Miruță said.

World.title: Romania’s Liberal Party ready to back government of technocrats with transparent majority
World.content:
Romania’s Liberal Party (PNL) would support a possible technocratic government, the party's president and acting PM Ilie Bolojan told RFI.

The interim prime minister, however, sets some conditions: the incoming government should have transparent majority parliamentary support, at least for a defined period of time, and it should come with a ruling agenda that maintains the strategy of controlling state spending and reducing deficits.

“The sooner we have a government, the better for this country, and each of us has a responsibility to seek solutions for this," PM Bolojan said.

The statement came after Social Democrat leader Ilie Grineanu announced an imminent ruling majority that his party will make public after August 15.

Ilie Bolojan has repeatedly stressed that it is the Social Democrats’ responsibility to come up with a new government, after it joined the Alliance for Unity of Romanians (AUR) in the no-confidence motion against the government.

Nearly 90 days after the dismissal of the government on May 5 and two unsuccessful appointments made by president Nicusor Dan, there is no consensus for the future government team.

PSD leader Sorin Grindeanu will have more discussions with the President by the end of the week, according to sources in the party leadership consulted by HotNews. Sources expect a prime minister appointment to be made next month at the latest. The Social Democrats are working on forming a majority to support a possible single-party PSD government.

World.title: Romania’s slot-machine sector shrinks sharply after new local rules
World.content:
Romania’s authorised slot-machine sector has contracted sharply following new regulations that transferred greater powers over gambling authorisation to local authorities, with only 2,337 slot-machine stations authorised between February and May 2026, compared with 18,981 in the same period of 2025, according to data cited by Profit.ro.

This seems, however, to be the indirect effect of the public debate rather than direct constraints of city halls that gained greater power: only a few of them have imposed restrictions so far.

The decline follows the entry into force of Emergency Ordinance 7/2026, which gives city halls greater authority to allow or prohibit gambling activities in their jurisdictions. The changes have also reduced the number of gaming devices currently operating and the associated tax revenues.

Of 45,659 gaming devices authorised across Romania in 2025, 29,014 remain in operation, according to the data. This represents around 64% of last year's authorised stock.

The reduction has occurred despite limited implementation of the new local rules. Only 90 of roughly 3,100 administrative-territorial units have so far adopted local council decisions on gambling, even though the 60-day deadline for issuing such decisions expired more than two months ago.

Of those 90 decisions, 35 prohibit gambling activities, while 55 allow them to continue, according to the data cited by Profit.ro.

The contraction has also affected public revenues from gambling authorisation fees. Operators paid RON 485 million in such fees between February and May 2025, compared with RON 300 million during the corresponding period of 2026.

The new rules have therefore reduced the number of authorised machines before most local authorities have formally decided whether gambling activities should be permitted in their jurisdictions.

The government introduced the changes as part of wider efforts to regulate the gambling sector and give local authorities greater control over where gambling businesses can operate.

World.title: In Solving World War II ‘Puzzle’, Young Greeks Help ‘Heal a Wound’
World.content:
After wading through the archives at Arolsen, municipal registers, the Internet and other documents, the tram was able to return a wristwatch to the family of Vangelis Kerasiotis, who spent time in a forced labour camp in Germany in 1944, aged 19.

Having worked at the camp as an interpreter, Kerasiotis returned to Greece in 1945, where he moved in with a Jewish woman and joined the police. He died at the age of 25.

“The objects are of zero value in terms of their literal value, but they are of enormous value in terms of mental upliftment,” said his niece, Chrysanthi Kerasotou, who received the watch with her sister and mother during an event organised by the Greek government in late June.

Hotzidis, a historian, said that between 50,000 and 60,000 Greek Jews perished in the Nazi camps and at least 10,000 other Greeks were sent to labour camps, including leftists involved in the resistance against the Nazi occupation of Greece.

“We do not know if Kerasiotis was engaged in any political activity,” Hotzidis said. “The relatives did not mention anything, but even if wasn’t, his name was certainly heard somewhere by Greek collaborators of the German battalion security forces and some gendarmes who collaborated with the Germans.”

“It is important to remember, because this way we know not only our recent history, but we can think that it is good that all these events do not happen again,” he said. “So, first we must know them and secondly remember them, ensuring they are never forgotten.”

In Arolsen, Meiwes said that some 2,000 envelopes remain. For some, they known neither the nationality nor the identity of the person whose belonging are inside.

“It is possible that some of these still belong to Greek nationals,” she told BIRN.

The Nazis turned people into numbers, Meiwes said, so it is important “to give them back their names and to tell their stories”.

World.title: A Decade After North Macedonia’s Deadliest Floods, Dangers Remain
World.content:
On August 6, 2016 torrential rain triggered a devastating flash flood in the north-east outskirts of Skopje, killing 22 people and causing more than 30 million euros in damage.

Suburbs of the capital like Singelic and Cento, villages like Stajkovci and Aracinovo, and surrounding areas were among the worst hit, as torrents of water and mud swept through streets and homes within minutes.

“We narrowly escaped death. The water was almost two metres deep. I have never seen this kind of weather,” one Stajkovci resident said at the time. “It was terrible. We had only half a minute to get outside [the house] and save ourselves when the water surged,” said another.

In the aftermath, experts pointed to several factors that had turned an extreme weather event into a disaster. Around 93 litres of rain per square metre fell on the heavily deforested southern slopes of Skopska Crna Gora Mountain in just four hours, allowing water and mud to rush towards the settlements below.

World.title: Albania Could Face Costly Arbitration Battle After Scrapping Vlora Airport Plans
World.content:
An international arbitration dispute is looming after Albania’s Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy announced last week that it has officially started the procedure to terminate the concession contract for Vlora International Airport.

The decision follows a bitter legal tussle between the two consortium partners, Mabco Construction and 2A Group, which began in the autumn of 2025 over a dispute concerning the division of shares between them.

There have also been large confrontations between workers from the two companies over access to the site, and a series of court rulings. The deadlock persisted even after the Supreme Court in May rejected 2A Group's requests for interim measures to secure its lawsuit. That decision was later followed by additional blocking rulings issued by the Court of First Instance Tirana.

World.title: Albanian Court Puts Turkish Activist in Custody After Extradition Demand
World.content:
Protesters rally with pictures of victims of the 2013 Gezi Park protests in Istanbul, April 2022. Photo: EPA-EFE/SEDAT SUNA.

The Tirana Court on Friday ordered a custody remand for Julide Yazici, who is wanted for extradition by Turkey to serve a prison sentence for aiding a terrorist organisation – charges that she claims are motivated by her political activism.

Yazici was arrested on August 4 at Tirana Airport while travelling from France to Albania after it was discovered that she was wanted for extradition to Turkey.

The judge granted the prosecution’s custody request despite Yazici’s lawyer’s arguments that his client “holds political asylum status in France and poses no danger”, and could be placed under house arrest instead.

The lawyer, Artan Shllaku, said that the decision will be appealed.

Shllaku added that Yazici, who teaches at an elementary school in France, had visited Albania a year earlier to see relatives and had encountered no issues.

Yazici is wanted by Turkish authorities to serve the remainder of a four-year prison sentence – three years, five months and 22 days – for providing logistical support to and participating in a terrorist organisation.

According to a decision by the French National Court of Asylum dated November 2020, a document obtained by BIRN, Yazici was involved in political activism in Turkey and participated in the Gezi Park mass protests in 2013 against the administration led by Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

She actively supported the former People’s Democratic Party, HDP, a left-wing political group that supported Turkey’s Kurdish minority, and which later became the DEM Party.

The French court decision granting asylum to Yazici stated that she was arrested in January 2016 “for having allowed a young woman she did not know, who had been introduced to her by a friend, to stay in her student room”.

The French court decision in the document that Yazici had “a well-founded fear … of being persecuted if she returns to her country due to her political activism”.

Yazici is not the first Turkish national to be arrested in Albania for extradition in controversial circumstances in recent years. Teachers and others linked to the movement previously led by the now-deceased cleric Fethullah Gulen, which is classified as a terrorist organisation by the authorities under Erdogan, have also been detained and then deported in line with Ankara’s demands.

World.title: Secrecy Surrounds Croatia’s Arrest of Alleged Serbian State-Linked Hacker
World.content:
Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH.

The Croatian and Serbian authorities are remaining tight-lipped over the arrest last week of a Serbian businessman named as Georgije V., 33, on suspicion of hacking into the computer systems of various Croatian state institutions and public agencies.

The Serbian man is reportedly suspected of hacking into the Croatian Interior Ministry, the Central Register of Pension-Insured Persons, the Croatian Health Insurance Fund, the Croatian Regulatory Agency for Network Activities, the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute, the Croatian Tax Administration and the Croatian Automobile Club.

Tomo Medved, the Minister of Croatian Veterans, was asked about the case on Friday but declined to provide details.

“I would like to commend the entire security and intelligence system for its responsible and vigilant monitoring and protection of the interests of the Republic of Croatia. Given the ongoing proceedings, I cannot comment further than that,” Medved told journalists.

Croatian daily Jutarnji list has reported that the arrest took place on July 28, when Georgije V. was on holiday in Croatia. He had arrived with his wife, two children and mother at a tourist resort on the Adriatic coast a few days earlier.

Following his arrest, police searched his electronic devices, vehicle and accommodation under court orders. They seized items and digital data allegedly linking him to criminal acts, including two mobile phones and a laptop containing a large amount of data.

The court ordered one month of pre-trial detention, despite the man offering 20,000 euros in bail money and his family home in Novi Sad as collateral.

Croatia’s Chief State Attorney, Ivan Turudic, initially sparked public interest on Monday when he made a comment about a case related to national security. It was then reported by Jutarnji list that Turudic was referring to the arrest of an alleged hacker linked to Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency, BIA.

It is not known whether the suspect’s alleged access to the computer systems of various institutions and agencies endangered Croatia’s national security in any way, or what he did with any data he may have obtained.

Nera Gajdarov Beg, the suspect’s lawyer, told Jutarnji list that the court’s custody order is being contested.

“An appeal has been filed against the decision to order pretrial detention because we believe that not all legal requirements for such a decision have been met. At this point, I cannot provide details of the defence because the proceedings are in the investigation phase, which is secret,” Gajdarov Beg said.

The Serbian authorities have not commented on the arrest so far. However, Serbian media have reported that Georgije V. is the owner of an active Novi Sad-based company specialising in computer programming and cybersecurity.

World.title: Croatian Serb Leader Deplores Hate Speech at Operation Storm Commemoration
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Milorad Pupovac, president of the Independent Democratic Serb Party, SDSS, and MP, on Friday said that slogans and chants heard on the streets of Knin on August 5, the day marking the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, represented a “serious attack on constitutional values and democracy”.

Pupovac, leader of the main party representing Serbs in Croatia, argued that “hatred and incitement to crime are incompatible with true patriotism”.

At a press conference, he showed a compilation of recordings from Knin, the town that was the headquarters of a rebel Serbian statelet crushed by the Croatian Army’s Operation Storm in 1995.

They included sports fans and army veterans singing songs glorifying the Ustasha – the army of the Independent State of Croatia, NDH, a World War II fascist puppet state operating under the patronage of Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.

The recordings also showed people chanting: “We Croats do not drink wine, only the blood of Chetniks [Serbian nationalists] from Knin”; “The battle is fought, it is fought, the Ustasha flag is flying”, as well as insults directed at St Sava, the patron saint of the Serbian Orthodox Church.

“Those who have been trying to pass this off as an act of patriotism for years are actually seriously violating the true values of patriotism. In peacetime, the greatest patriotic virtue is constitutional patriotism,” Pupovac said.

He added that such behaviour was a “vicious attack on democracy”.

The SNV cited articles of the Croatian Constitution that it believes were violated by the shouting of the Ustasha salute “For the Homeland, Ready” and other glorifications of the NDH. The violations came after, not during, the official anniversary celebrations, it said.

Every year, Knin hosts a commemoration of Operation Storm, which liberated about 18 per cent of Croatia’s territory from rebel Serb forces and was followed by the flight of around 200,000 Serbs from Croatia. Some of them later returned.

SDSS leader Pupovac also criticised the Croatian judicial authorities, questioning why the State Attorney’s Office often does not react to hate speech and incitement to violence, appealing for an end to what he called a policy of appeasement.

He warned that failure to condemn such phenomena represents a direct threat to the Serb community in Croatia, and to all citizens who advocate for a state governed by the rule of law.

World.title: Week in Review: The Electoral Merry-Go-Round
World.content:
Last week, a no-confidence motion in the Serbian government was held in the country’s parliament. A boisterous discussion ensued between ruling and opposition MPs, but the motion failed – as expected.

Its real significance was not so much the outcome as the fact that the holding the vote, tabled at the beginning of the year, cleared an important obstacle to calling early parliamentary elections.

President Aleksandar Vucic has fuelled speculation that polls are imminent. Our analysis takes a look a look at what will determine when they happen – and whether they will happen at all.

World.title: The Green Heart of Zagreb: Exploring the Croatian Capital’s Parks
World.content:
August the 10th, 2026 – Zagreb is one of the most heavily forested EU capitals, and the green heart of Zagreb acts as the lungs of the urban side’s beating heart.

Zagreb, much like Croatia as a whole, is very widely praised for its cafe culture, but you don’t need to be sitting in a busy city street to enjoy that coffee. Less celebrated, but equally defining, is just how green the city feels. Parks, gardens, lakes and densely forested hills weave through and around the capital, giving it (as touched on above) one of the highest concentrations of green space among EU cities.

For visitors, this means you can move from a museum, restaurant or old square to a lush, green meadow or park in mere minutes. Croatia is full of natural beauty, but when it comes to cities, these spaces are not an afterthought or somewhere forgotten by builders, they’re an absolutely central to the city’s identity and daily life.

The Green Horseshoe: Nature Woven into the City Centre

Sanjin Kastelan/TZGZ

Turning the clock back to the late 19th century, celebrated urban planner Milan Lenuci designed a U-shaped sequence of parks and squares that still frames the Lower Town (Donji grad). Known locally as Lenuci’s Green Horseshoe (or, if you want to get even more local: Zelena potkova), it connects promenades, blooming flower beds, monuments and grand public buildings into a continuous green corridor stretching for roughly 1.2 miles.

Zrinjevac is arguably the most atmospheric part of all. Just a short walk from the hustle and bustle of Ban Jelačić Square, an oasis awaits. It features towering mature plane trees, flower beds, fountains and a distinctive cast-iron music pavilion. During the summer, the pavilion hosts open-air concerts and free dance evenings; locals and visitors gather for waltz, swing or salsa under the trees. The scorching Croatian summer heat is calmed by the trees and thick plant life. The sequence continues near Strossmayer Square and King Tomislav Square, all the way to the main railway station (Glavni kolodvor), with statues, shaded walkways and seasonal colour. During the much cooler winter, Tomislav Square transforms into a ice rink; while swapping out its winter attire to serve as an open stage for classical concerts in summer.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

These central parks reward unhurried wandering. They are places to sit with a coffee, watch the city pass by, or simply appreciate how thoughtfully nature was integrated into Zagreb’s 19th-century expansion.

zagreb’s botanical garden

Marko Vrdoljak/TZGZ

At the southwestern end of the Green Horseshoe sits the Zagreb Botanical Garden (Botanički vrt). It was formally established back in 1889 by Professor Antun Heinz of the University of Zagreb, and opened to the public in 1891. Spanning about five hectares, it is both a scientific institution and a public garden of real charm.

The layout mixes English landscape style, long, winding paths, irregular plantings and a substantial arboretum with a more formal French-style parterre of flower beds. Collections include native Croatian flora, alpine and Mediterranean plants, aquatic species, conifers, and exotic trees and shrubs from all around the world. Estimates of the plant holdings range from several thousand to over 10,000 taxa, including many protected and endemic species. Small lakes with bridges, a rock garden and historic glasshouses (including a house for the giant Amazonian water lily Victoria amazonica) add to the allure.

Boska i Kreso/TZGZ

The garden is compact enough to explore in an hour or two yet rich enough to reward slower visits. It’s open seasonally (typically from April to early November, with limited winter opening in particularly calm, good weather) and charges a modest entrance fee. Located a short walk from the main train station, it is one of the easiest major green spaces to reach.

the legendary (and gorgeous) park maksimir

Julien Duval/TZGZ

East of the city centre lies Maksimir, the city’s largest, most famous, and most beloved park of all. Founded on the initiative of Bishop Maksimilijan Vrhovac and opened to the public back in 1794, it was the first large public park in all of southeastern Europe at the time. Spanning roughly 316 hectares (about 780 acres or so), it is comparable in scale to some of the grand European landscape parks and remains a protected monument of garden architecture and cultural heritage.

Originally conceived with baroque elements and later reshaped in the English Romantic style under Bishop Juraj Haulik, Maksimir combines broad meadows, mature oak and hornbeam woodland, five artificial lakes, streams, pavilions and long tree-lined avenues. Historic structures like the Swiss House, the Echo Pavilion and lookout points still stand. Wildlife of all kinds absolutely thrives here, with the park a well known habitat for birds, including rarer species.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Within the park sits Zagreb Zoo, one of the oldest in the region (opened 1925), home to lions and all kinds of other animals you (thankfully) wouldn’t bump into in a cafe.

Families come for the playgrounds and lakeside walks; runners and walkers use the extensive paths; picnickers claim the grass on weekends. Trams (lines 4, 7, 11 and 12 among others) make it straightforward to reach. Maksimir feels both historic and lived-in. It’s a genuine city park that has adapted to changing fashions while retaining its charming, grand 18th- and 19th-century character.

the city of lakes – meet bundek and jarun

Julien Duval/TZGZ

South of the centre, the winding Sava River corridor offers a different kind of green space with a distinctly more recreational and watery character.

Bundek Park in Novi Zagreb sits between the Liberty (Most slobode) and Youth (Most mladosti) bridges. It centres on two expansive lakes surrounded by walking and cycling paths, meadows, playgrounds, sports courts and barbecue areas. Significantly renovated back during the mid-2000s, it has become a beloved for families, picnics and summer swimming (with lifeguards on the larger lake during the hotter season). An open-air stage hosts events, including the Pop Up by the Lake festival. Its proximity to the city centre (a short bus ride from the main station) and relaxed atmosphere make it especially popular with locals.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Jarun sits further west and is often called Zagreb’s very own “sea”. This large artificial lake is ringed by paths popular with cyclists, runners and more. Islands, beaches, cafes, outdoor gym equipment and sports facilities give it a lively, active character. During the summer, it is a major venue for outdoor living; it also hosts the INmusic festival. Trams 5 and 17 serve the area. Where Bundek feels more intimate and family-oriented, Jarun offers scale and a truly energetic feel. Together, the two lakes give Zagreb something very few inland capitals possess: genuine waterside recreation within easy reach of the busy urban core.

bear mountain – medvednica has always had zagreb’s back (quite literally)

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Just north of Zagreb rises Medvednica, a densely forested mountain and protected nature park that functions as the city’s great outdoor backyard. Its highest peak, Sljeme, stands at 1,033 metres. The park is home to dozens of marked hiking trails of varying difficulty, mountain lodges serving traditional food, the medieval fortress of Medvedgrad, the Veternica cave, and viewpoints that look back over the entire city.

Miroslav Zadravec/TZGZ

Popular routes include the gradual Leustek trail and the steeper Bikčević trail toward the summit or lodges such as Puntijarka. Medvedgrad itself is a rewarding shorter destination, combining history with panoramic views. In winter the upper reaches attract skiers and sledgers; year-round the forest offers cool shade and clean air. Public transport (tram to Mihaljevac followed by bus, or the Sljeme cable car) and road access make it straightforward for visitors without a car. Few European capitals can claim a proper mountain nature park so close to the centre. For many Zagreb residents, “going to Sljeme” remains a ritual escape.

Though named after the populations of brown bears that once called it home (in Croatia, bear is medvjed), you won’t find them there now. As Zagreb expanded and grew, the bears retreated to more remote areas. If you do want to see them – head to Lika!

honestly, you can’t even name them all…

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Beyond these major sites, Zagreb is sprinkled with additional green spaces. Ribnjak Park near the cathedral offers a more intimate central oasis. Tuškanac and Cmrok on the northern slopes provide wooded walks and, in winter, popular sledging slopes. Mirogoj Cemetery, designed by Herman Bollé, is as much a landscaped park and open-air architectural gallery as a burial ground, with arcades, monuments and mature trees.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Most city parks are free to enter, but the Botanical Garden and Zagreb Zoo charge modest fees. Public transport (trams and buses) reaches nearly all the major sites efficiently; walking and cycling are excellent options for the central Green Horseshoe and the lakeside paths. Spring brings blossom and milder temperatures; summer is ideal for the lakes and shaded trails; autumn colours are spectacular in Maksimir and on Medvednica; winter has its own quiet beauty, especially after snow has fallen.

zagreb gets hot, but it would be far hotter without these green spaces

Julien Duval/TZGZ

The above photo likely doesn’t stir up mental images of sunscreen and t-shirts, but we won’t sugarcoat it – Croatia is extremely hot in summer. Zagreb, far from the sea breeze, can become absolutely stifling. This is where the functionality of these green spaces come to the fore. Zagreb’s green network is not merely decorative. It cools the city down, supports biodiversity, provides everyday recreation for residents and offers visitors an immediate sense of the city’s character.

Sanjin Kastelan/TZGZ

You can step out of a cafe on the main square and be under the protective shade of tall plane trees within minutes, or leave the centre and be hiking forest trails and bumping into deer an hour later. That accessibility is rare and worth experiencing deliberately when in Zagreb. Everyone can become sick of the sound, pace and stress of the city, but you can’t always escape it as easily as you can here.

Whether you prefer the grandeur and elegance of Zrinjevac, Maksimir’s sprawling trails and numerous lakes, the energy of Bundek and Jarun, Medvednica or anywhere else, Zagreb’s green spaces should enjoy much more attention than they get.

World.title: Big Changes Coming for Drivers in Croatia in Autumn
World.content:
August the 10th, 2026 – Big changes are on the horizon for drivers in Croatia this autumn, more specifically as of October the 1st.

The beginning of the roll out of this change has in fact already begun. As of the 1st of July this year, drivers in Croatia are no longer able to use their previous top up SMART cards. However, they’ve still been able to spend the existing balance on them and will be able to continue doing so until the end of September.

After October the 1st, the SMART card will cease to function entirely as a means of payment on the motorways managed by HAC (Croatian Motorways), as reported by Poslovni.

an overhaul of a system used for years

For drivers in Croatia who still have a remaining amount on the card, there are two possibilities available to them. Those who wish to continue using electronic toll collection can transfer the money from their SMART prepaid account to an ENC prepaid account. In the process of doing that, they can exchange their SMART card for an ENC device at Croatian Motorways sales offices.

The second option is intended for those who do not wish to switch to ENC. They can request the closure of the SMART prepaid account and a refund of the available money. The request can be sent to HAC by e-mail or submitted in person at one of their sales offices.

Some drivers have been using the SMART system for years, especially on the motorways previously managed by Autocesta Rijeka – Zagreb, so it’s fairly understandable that some cards are still sitting in cars. Precisely these users should pay attention to the deadline, because after 30 September they will no longer be able to spend the remaining balance in the usual way.

massive changes are afoot for the toll collection system

The change comes at a time of major interventions in the Croatian toll collection system and increasing reliance on electronic payment. For the SMART card user themselves, however, the most important question is much simpler – whether there is still money on the account and what to do with it before the card ceases to be valid.

That is why it is not a bad idea to check the balance already now, especially if you use the SMART card only occasionally. Until the 1st of October, it can still be used for payment, but topping up is no longer possible. After that date the options remain transferring the funds to ENC or getting a monetary refund.

World.title: Croatia is Losing an Industrial Giant After 106 Years of Operation
World.content:
August the 10th, 2026 – Croatia is very unfortunately set to lose an industrial giant after 106 years of operation in the country.

As Dubravko Grakalic writes for Index, Croatia is very sadly losing yet another symbol of its formerly rich industrial heritage. After over a century of continuous operation, the company Chromos, which became a “second name” for paints and varnishes on the domestic market, is ceasing production in Croatia. The decision was made by the Japanese owner, the company Kansai Helios, which announced that production will continue in Količevo in Slovenia and in the Serbian town of Gornji Milanovac, while only a sales network will remain in Zagreb.

The shutdown of production in Croatia marks the end of a tradition that began back in 1920, during which Chromos was the largest producer of paints, varnishes, plastics and resins in all of former Yugoslavia. Back during the mid-1980s, Chromos was an industrial giant that employed around 4,500 people. Today, about a hundred workers are employed at the Zagreb Chromos plant in Žitnjak – most of whom will tragically lose their jobs – while the company Kansai Helios still has around sixty employees in Croatia.

“Chromos is a brand with a deep tradition and an invaluable legacy in Croatia, based on decades of dedicated work by our employees,” said Goran Dolenec, director of Chromos boje i lakovi d.d. and KANSAI HELIOS Croatia d.o.o., in a media statement.

From a small workshop to an industrial giant

Today’s Chromos originated from a small paint-mixing workshop belonging to the wholesaler Bernard Moster in 1920. The plant with around thirty workers was located on Radnička Street, in premises that had previously housed a soap factory. In the first year they produced around 500 tonnes of paints and varnishes; production expanded with the construction of the main factory building in 1923. In the following years the factory complex grew to include around ten more buildings.

Both production and the number of employees increased – by 1940 there were 162 workers who produced more than 1,800 tonnes of paints – and new technologies and products were developed, such as plant-protection coatings. During the so-called Independent State of Croatia (1941-1945) the factory changed its name to Oil and Lacquer Industry, while after liberation in 1945, it received the name Perunika.

Alongside Bernard Moster’s company, Chromos is also the successor of the tradition of the company of the same name for the production of graphic inks, which the German company Springer-Moller from Leipzig founded in 1923 in Samobor. The Samobor Chromos produced graphic inks and rotary-press ink with which all newspapers in the then Yugoslavia were printed. Business went so well that at the end of the 1930s they also built a factory in Zemun.

Perunika and Chromos were merged in 1947 into a single enterprise, Chromos, Chemical Industry Zagreb. Altogether they had around two hundred workers in the Zagreb and Samobor plants. The Chromos Research Institute was founded in 1955 and worked on polymer synthesis.

Industrial development continued through links with the companies Katran and Pliva – which produced paints until 1962. A major amalgamation in 1964 created the Chemical Combine Chromos – Katran – Kutrilin, which became the leading producer in the former Yugoslavia. In the 1970s the companies Labud from Zagreb and Svjetlost from Slavonski Lužani joined the combine.

The largest producer in croatia’s entire immediate region

During its period of greatest growth the Chromos combine built a Graphic Institute, a production complex in Žitnjak that today spans 100,000 square metres, and several more laboratory plants. In 1979 they employed around 3,900 workers, produced around 180 thousand tonnes of various chemical products and exported to around twenty countries, primarily to the then Soviet Union.

Back during the 1980s, the Chromos-Katran-Kutrilin combine, with 4,500 workers, was the largest producer of its kind in the region, followed by Slovenian Helios and Zorka Šabac from Serbia, which today operates through several companies. At that time the Chromos business tower was also built on the corner of Vukovarska and Heinzelova streets, one of the symbols of the eastern part of Zagreb. It was erected in 1989 according to the design of architects Marijan Turkulin and Petar Vovk. It is considered the last skyscraper built in Zagreb before the Homeland War.

The Chromos tower is fifteen storeys high, or sixty metres. It was the main centre of the Chromos combine; today it houses offices of several dozen companies employing around 600 people.

Privatisation in 1993 divided the Chromos combine into 16 independent companies. Four firms collapsed in the following years, while the others still operate today under different owners. Chromos Tvornica smola operates as part of the Scott Bader group, while the Samobor Chromos d.d. produces graphic inks as an independent company. The former Chromos Aroma operates as Ireks Aroma in Jastrebarsko, while Chromos Argo, Katran, Kutrilin TPV, Komicro, Svjetlost and Hempel continue to operate normally.

general slobodan praljak purchased their land

The complex business structure of the vast Chromos and the privatisation of the 1990s still create confusion about what has survived of the former industrial giant. The story of the Zagreb Chromos real estate is also interesting.

From October 1995 to June 1996 the president of the Management Board of the company Chromos boje i lakovi d.d. was HV General Slobodan Praljak, later convicted in The Hague. Great public attention was therefore aroused by the sale of 27,000 square metres of land to the company Oktavijan d.o.o. in 1999, whose owner was precisely this same Slobodan Praljak. The land was sold for four million four hundred thousand German marks and today a business centre stands there.

In a 2003 report by the State Audit Office it is stated that the land was paid less than the estimated value: “The said real estate was valued in the conversion procedure at 5,198,383 DEM, and the cost of acquiring an additional 1,137 m² amounted to 1,102,039 DEM, which totals 6,300,422 DEM. The said real estate was sold for 1,900,422 DEM less than the estimated value and the cost of acquiring the additional area.”

the sale to helios and the end of the line…

The company Chromos boje i lakovi from Zagreb’s Žitnjak was sold back in 2001 to Helios from Domžale – its former main market competitor. It is not known how much that takeover amounted to, but the media estimate that the value of the remaining assets of Chromos boje i lakovi at the time was fifteen million euros.

It is known that Helios bought the shares of small shareholders and acquired ownership of the plant, brands and patents. The Austrian owners, Ring International Holding, sold Helios in 2017 for 572 million euros to the Japanese company Kansai Paint.

The story of the break-up of the Chromos combine and the recent shutdown of production of the largest company that emerged from its conversion is an interesting component of the history of privatisation and the collapse of national industry. Chromos boje i lakovi – a company that closed the last business year with a profit – after 106 long years is becoming a wholesale trading company. Just like the one from which Bernard Moster made a factory in 1920.

World.title: Major Croatian Projects Involve New Bridge, New Tunnel & Railway
World.content:
August the 10th, 2026 – Several major Croatian projects involving a new bridge on Krk, a 14 kilometre tunnel and a railway line to host high speed trains are underway.

By the end of 2029, the reconstruction of the 44-kilometre railway line from Karlovac to Zagreb should be completed. Snjezana Bicak/Poslovni reports that if you want to go from Rijeka to Istria, you will come across a major construction site; there are more and more excavators and tall cranes as you approach the Učka tunnel or exit it, all so that already next year we will have a full-profile motorway and a more comfortable and pleasant drive to the peninsula and along the entire Istrian Y.

You will also encounter works if you travel through Slavonia, especially around Požega. If you fly with Croatia Airlines, its pilots will bring you to your destination in new aircraft. And if you travel by train from Karlovac to Zagreb, for the next four years you will also watch the works from the train, given that, finally, four years after the first tender was announced, construction of the second track on the Hrvatski Leskovac – Karlovac line has begun these days. Thanks to this, passengers from, for example, Karlovac to Zagreb should reach their destination by train in about 20 minutes.

karlovac is going up in the world…

Karlovac Mayor Damir Mandić has said several times so far that this is a big thing for the development of Karlovac, given that a large number of Karlovac residents work in Zagreb, children go to the metropolis to study, and a number of business activities are linked to Zagreb, writes Večernji list.

Karlovac thereby becomes an even more desirable place to live – outside the hustle and bustle of the big city, yet only about 20 minutes away by train, and the same after the construction of the third lane of the motorway connecting the two cities, which is also planned.

Karlovac will truly become a suburb of Zagreb with an excellent transport connection to it, but also to the rest of Croatia, especially towards the Adriatic, which makes it even more attractive for business investments that lead to the opening of new jobs, and then also for living and the arrival of new families.

The start of construction of the lowland railway, at least on this part of the corridor, delights everyone it concerns. This is no small investment; the contractor, the Spanish company Comsa S.A., which signed a contract with HŽ Infrastructure in July for the execution of the project, will reconstruct the existing track, build the second track, carry out the electrification of 44 kilometres of railway, build new bridges, viaducts and power facilities, arrange stations and stops, and construct five facilities for the needs of HŽ Infrastructure in Karlovac. After the works are completed, train speeds of up to 160 km/h are planned. The value is not negligible either: it amounts to 348.5 million euros including VAT, and the deadline for completion of the works is 36 months, i.e. by the end of 2029.

The Hrvatski Leskovac – Karlovac section is only part of the entire lowland railway project that will connect Zagreb and Rijeka on a section 56 kilometres shorter than the current railway connecting the two cities, and the procedures for contracting works on certain sections are underway. The project is complex; the new double-track and fully electrified railway is designed for speeds of up to 160 km/h for passenger trains and 120 km/h for freight trains.

With a total length of about 175 kilometres – 56 kilometres shorter than the existing line – this will drastically reduce travel time. The biggest challenge on the section after Karlovac is overcoming the demanding mountainous terrain, which is why the construction of more than 30 viaducts and tunnels is planned.

a brand new tunnel through velika kapela

The star of the project is the future tunnel through the Velika Kapela massif, 14 kilometres long, which will become the longest in Croatia. For comparison, the Sveti Rok and Mala Kapela tunnels together are a little less than 12 kilometres long. The route also provides for the construction of five new stations and one stop. All of this should be completed by 2036. From just these few points it’s very clear that Croatia is in a major infrastructure boom that has been going on for some time and will last at least another ten years, which is the period planned for the construction of the entire lowland railway corridor that will connect the largest port of Rijeka with the Hungarian border.

“Croatia is currently implementing one of the largest investment cycles in its existence in transport infrastructure, which covers all types of transport, as well as the development of public urban transport and new forms of mobility. Through European sources of financing within the financial periods 2014–2020 and 2021–2027, projects with a total value of around 5.57 billion euros have been contracted and are being implemented in transport infrastructure, of which around 3.45 billion euros relates to non-refundable EU funds.

The stated amount refers exclusively to projects implemented with the support of European funds and financing instruments, through the Operational Programme Competitiveness and Cohesion, the Competitiveness and Cohesion Programme 2021–2027, the National Recovery and Resilience Plan and the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF). The largest part of these investments is directed towards the modernisation of railway infrastructure, followed by the road sector, maritime transport and public urban transport,” the Ministry of the Sea, Transport and Infrastructure told us.

They add that, in parallel with the already contracted projects financed with the support of European funds, the Government is implementing a broader investment cycle of modernisation of the transport system that includes EU funds, the state budget, loans and other sources of financing.

more railway and train projects are in the works

The railway sector stands out in particular, where investments in railway infrastructure worth more than 1.7 billion euros are underway, while an investment cycle worth around 6 billion euros is planned over the decade to come.

This is the total value of planned investments in the modernisation and renewal of the railway network, which will be financed by a combination of different sources, including EU funds. The goal of the investments is to increase the safety, capacity and quality of railway transport and to strengthen Croatia’s connectivity with European transport corridors, the competent ministry adds.

Minister Oleg Butković said that never before has so much been invested in local and regional railways as now, thanks to part of the loan from the European Investment Bank that the Croatian Government secured. He emphasises that Croatian Motorways invest around 50 million euros annually in investment maintenance of motorways, along with investments in the development and modernisation of the motorway network and the introduction of a new electronic toll collection system.

Croatian Roads, for example, have invested around 1.6 billion euros over the past ten years in the construction of new and the reconstruction of existing state roads, while a series of projects with a total value of more than 1.2 billion euros is currently in preparation and implementation.

port infrastructure investments

“We also have a major investment cycle in port infrastructure worth more than 500 million euros, the largest part of which is financed with EU funds. From the Ministry’s budget alone last year, 14.7 million euros was allocated for port infrastructure and the rehabilitation of maritime domain in general use, and a total of more than 118.4 million euros during the terms of this Government. Investments in inland navigation are aimed at increasing navigation safety, improving the navigability of rivers and developing port and berth infrastructure. In the period 2014–2027, more than 200 million euros was invested in inland waterway projects through European funds and other sources of financing, with the largest part of the investments relating to the development of infrastructure on the Danube River and in the Port of Osijek,” the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure adds.

roads and expressways

When it comes to investments in road transport, among the most important projects currently underway is certainly the completion of the construction of the Istrian Y in full profile, including the section from the Učka tunnel to Matulji, with a total value of around 200 million euros.

A network of expressways is also being built across Croatia, among which the most important is the Podravina Y (from Vrbovec – Bjelovar – Virovitica – the border with Hungary), then the Varaždin – Krapina expressway, the Požega expressway with an exit to the A3 motorway, the Solin – Stobreč – Dugi Rat – Omiš expressway, the Nuštar – Vukovar expressway, the Okučani – Stara Gradiška expressway, and the Zlatar Bistrica – Marija Bistrica expressway as part of the Zagreb Ring.

New bypasses are also being built across Croatia: Fužine, Nedelišće, Pušćine, Orebić, Drniš, Zaprešić, Čakovec and other towns, and reconstructions of state roads are underway: the new entrance to Split, the Sisak junction – Sisak, Donja Zdenčina – the bridge on the Kupa, Veli Vrh – Pula, the narrower city ring of Karlovac, the Širina intersection. The introduction of a new toll collection system is underway, and the Križišće – Selce section on the A7 motorway is being built, while the procedure for signing a contract with the consortium of bidders is underway for the Jadranovo – Selce subsection.

A contract has been signed with the contractor for the Križišće – Jadranovo subsection, the first phase of the Selce – Novi Vinodolski section is being built, and project documentation is being prepared for the Novi Vinodolski – Senj and Senj – Žuta Lokva sections. The Rudine – Osojnik section on the A1 motorway is being built, and additional lanes are being added on the Zagreb – Karlovac section of the A1 motorway and the Zagreb West – Lučko section of the A3 motorway. These last two projects in particular will significantly contribute to reducing congestion, especially in the summer months.

For decades, for example, investment in connecting Požega to the A3 motorway was awaited. Požega-Slavonia County Prefect Antonija Jozić said at the signing of the contract with the contractors that the construction of the expressway and the Požega junction will be of decisive importance for the transport accessibility and economic development of Požega-Slavonia County.

“For many years there was talk of a project that is now being realised. Our county will no longer be the appendix of Croatia; we are becoming more accessible by transport, and what we are most looking forward to is that these projects will be a strong driver of the economy,” Jozić said.

Brod-Posavina County Prefect Danijel Marušić emphasised that this project is proof of cooperation and common interests of neighbouring counties. “In my municipality, along this road, economic zones are already slowly being prepared; of course there will be greater circulation of both people and goods, and it is truly a completely different perspective,” Marušić said.

modernisation of the railway system

In addition to roads, the Croatian Government is also investing in the modernisation of the railway system through the renewal of infrastructure and rolling stock.

“In the recent period, the procurement of new trains for HŽ Passenger Transport has been realised, and 70 new low-floor trains are in operation: 55 electric multiple units, 13 diesel multiple units, and one electro-battery and one battery train each. The total value of the procurement amounts to 363.4 million euros,” the Ministry adds.

And they are not stopping there, because a new procurement has already been contracted. Specifically, 6 electro-diesel trains for the Zagreb – Split route, worth 57.3 million euros, which will be put into service this year; then 5 electro-diesel, 4 electro-battery and 4 battery trains with two charging stations, worth €117.9 million, with delivery during 2027 and 2028. There are also 6 electro-battery trains and a hybrid charging station in Kotoriba, worth 53.6 million euros, with delivery during 2028 and 2029. Additionally, by the first quarter of 2029, 228.8 million euros will be invested in the procurement of an additional 25 trains, the competent authorities note.

Preparation is also underway for potential financing of the procurement of an additional 30 new trains from the Social Climate Fund. The new trains will run on more modern tracks, given that major investments in railway infrastructure are also underway.

Specifically, the reconstruction and construction of the second track on the Dugo Selo – Novska line is underway, a project worth around 900 million euros; the modernisation of the Dugo Selo – Križevci and Križevci – Koprivnica – state border with Hungary sections is being completed; and, as mentioned, the modernisation of the Hrvatski Leskovac – Karlovac section worth 280 million euros has begun.

Numerous projects for the renewal of local, regional and international lines are also underway, including the Pitomača – Kloštar, Generalski Stol – Oštarije, Ogulin – Moravice, Karlovac – Ozalj, Knin – Zadar, Osijek – Koška and other sections.

that isn’t all…

“When it comes to investment in port infrastructure, in the previous period 25 projects were contracted through which 14 ports were built or reconstructed, including the ports of Tkon, Crikvenica, Cres, Unije, Sućuraj, Korčula, Baška, Žigljen, Zadar, Split, Stinica, Vela Luka and others. In the new financial period, investment in port infrastructure continues through projects with a total value of 267.64 million euros. These include projects for the reconstruction and expansion of the ports of Novi Vinodolski, Rovinj, Murter, Krk, Rab, Prvić Šepurine, Perna, Prigradica, Split, Kaštela, Vrsi, Ika and others,” the Ministry of Maritime Affairs revealed.

Among the more important projects related to inland navigation, the completion and development of the bulk cargo terminal in the Port of Osijek, the arrangement and improvement of the waterway of the Danube River, and the construction and development of port infrastructure for inland freight transport stand out. The leaders of Slavonian cities and counties are particularly looking forward to these projects, given that they will contribute to the development of economic activities across Slavonia.

Minister Oleg Butković also said that the goal of these significant investments is to increase the share of river transport in total freight traffic, connect Croatian ports with European transport corridors and further relieve road traffic.

World.title: Will New Toll Collection System Reduce Croatian Traffic Jams?
World.content:
August the 9th, 2026 – Will the new toll collection system set to come into force next year actually manage to reduce the infamous Croatian traffic jams on the motorways?

As Poslovni reports, the much anticipated installation of more than 220 portals on motorways across Croatia is currently underway. Appearing on HTV’s programme Studio 4, the director of the Traffic Sector at HAC (Croatian Motorways), Hrvoje Ordulj, touched on the new toll collection system, which is expected to become operational during 2027.

More than 220 portals are currently being installed on motorways throughout Croatia, and a large part of the infrastructure has already been put in place, reports HRT. “We expect all the portals to be installed by October, and the system could go live during next year,” he said. However, he did warn that not even the new system will be able to completely eliminate the country’s well known summer congestion. “Regardless of barriers or the new toll collection system, traffic will stand still if the load is too high,” Ordulj stated.

Major projects: Učka, Novi Vinodolski and Matulji

Speaking about future projects, Ordulj announced the continuation of construction of the Novi Vinodolski bypass, the completion of the Matulji junction, and the connection of Istria and Kvarner with a full-profile motorway.

“We expect that in the first quarter of next year Istria and Kvarner will be connected by a full-profile motorway,” Ordulj said. He added that works on the sections between Križišće, Jadranovo and Selce will intensify after the end of the summer tourist season.
