World.title: Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.content:
Outside an unassuming three-story building in downtown Kangyi Town, in the eastern Shandong province, hangs a sign that reads: “Striving to be the cheapest internet café in China.”

With charges as low as 0.6 yuan ($0.09) an hour, it’s certainly not false advertising. Yet step inside and you will find not just gamers chasing rock-bottom prices, but also a mix of locals and out-of-towners with myriad tales of misfortune, many looking to rise from their own rock bottom.

Here, customers can bathe and do laundry for free, enjoy a lunch of meat and vegetables for just 10 yuan, and even sleep in reclining esports chairs. For those looking to get back on their feet, it’s the ultimate low-to-no-cost option.

Like many of its patrons, the café’s owner, Wang Zhongkai, is also just trying to survive. After struggling to keep the doors open for more than a decade, the 38-year-old decided to slash his prices last year to attract more foot traffic.

The move certainly accomplished that — although it’s also inadvertently created a shelter for people in hard times.

After seeing a video about the internet café on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang’s first out-of-town customer traveled 800 kilometers from neighboring Jiangsu province to “seek refuge” — and ended up staying for eight months.

Changing fortunes

China had roughly 122,600 licensed internet cafés last year, up 12% from 2024, according to the Internet Access Service Association of China. However, data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism shows that average annual revenue fell from 216,000 yuan to 197,000 yuan over that same period.

Hardware is the biggest investment. With ever-changing technology, a new computer costing 15,000 yuan can lose a third of its value within a year, with software requiring constant paid-for upgrades.

Wang’s is one of only two surviving internet cafés in Kangyi. The business today has more than 150 computers of various specs, including 35 priced at 0.6 yuan an hour. The other machines in the main hall range from 0.9 yuan to 3 yuan an hour, while private one-person rooms are available for 99 yuan a day.

From nearly empty every day, Wang has seen occupancy increase to about 90%. At nighttime, the second floor is illuminated by the shifting colors of the PC screens, with the faces of customers — almost entirely men — aglow with yellow, green, red, and blue hues. Some are fast asleep, wrapped in summer blankets, headphones dangling from their neck.

Over the years, Wang, a father of three, has tried many ways to increase his income. He tried opening a grocery store on the side, which saw him lose 500,000 yuan in about six months. To recover, in 2023, he moved to Beijing — leaving his wife in charge of the café — to become a daijia, a designated driver for hire, working 15 hours a day. One day, he was so exhausted that he fell asleep while riding his electric bike and crashed.

He knows all too well that sometimes people just need to get through a rough patch. While living in the capital, he would pay 15 yuan to spend the night at an internet café where he could charge his e-bike and get hot water.

Wang returned to Kangyi in 2025. Today he helps his customers find low-cost rooms in town for as little as 200 yuan a month, with no deposit. For those who can’t even afford that, he lets them sleep for free in the café’s luxurious esports chairs.

He also advertises day-labor gigs available nearby, such as sorting packages at a courier depot or casual shifts at a machinery plant. Most of his customers decline, however, either because they’re not fit enough to handle manual labor or can’t stomach the idea of being bossed around.

His wife and mother-in-law are responsible for preparing lunch every day at the café, with one meat dish, one vegetable dish, and mountains of rice and steamed buns. Most diners pay 10 yuan, but those without a penny eat for free.

The showers and an industrial-size washing machine are also free to use — Wang even provides soap and detergent.

Despite the increased foot traffic, Wang’s profit margins remain wafer-thin. He says his family has invested more than 700,000 yuan in new computers, yet their revenue streams comprise only the cut-rate internet fees, sales of food and drink, and the occasional livestream on Douyin, during which some viewers will send virtual gifts. Except for relatives, the business has only one employee — an elderly male cleaner.

Boosting opportunities

Qiang Yu, a 30-something from Huaibei in the eastern Anhui province, has spent every day and night in the “0.6-yuan zone” for nearly a year. Like many others here, he makes money as a “game booster,” which involves playing video games to level up someone else’s account. His specialty is the online role-playing game Legend of Mir 2.

High-level accounts in popular games are worth tens of thousands of yuan, and cheating can lead to a permanent ban by game developers. Account owners are usually unwilling to hand their username and password to strangers, but Wang has built a reputation among several clients, offering a personal guarantee for any losses. He regularly farms out orders to the boosters at his internet café — and doesn’t even take a cut.

In the past, Qiang did manual jobs — digging gravel by the railway tracks, getting paid by the meter, his hands raw and blistered at the end of a shift, as well as toiling at factories making garments, lights, and electronics. It left him with a “crushing depression,” he says.

Qiang now earns just over 100 yuan for 12 hours’ work and survives on just 25 yuan a day. If, in a year, he has 10,000 yuan in his pocket, he plans to go home and clear the weeds that have taken over his courtyard.

Cao Ti Lie, a gamer who asked to be identified only by his username, arrived in Kangyi from Foshan, in the southern Guangdong province, in June. He grew up in video arcades, and now regularly livestreams to 60,000 subscribers on Douyin as he competes in the classic King of Fighters ’97.

Gaming used to be fun, he says; now it’s a full-time job. “The heart of the boy I was is dead. When you have to face life, it gets erased.”

The 41-year-old previously ran a business in Foshan and was making 30,000 yuan a month, but bad investments and a gambling habit saw his debts pile up. His wife left with their children, and then his mother suffered a stroke and broke her hip, losing the ability to care for herself.

Soon after spotting a video about Wang’s internet café, he hopped on a train here. His only goal is to save enough money to cover the costs of his mother’s nursing home.

Future is now

Wang’s day starts at 8 a.m. He scrubs five toilets, restocks the fridge, wipes down the keyboards, picks up any trash from the night before, and then takes his spot at the front counter.

He sees plenty of local faces come and go, but many of the out-of-towners are now permanent fixtures. In February, the café hosted about 40 people on Chinese New Year’s Eve, an important day on the calendar for family reunion.

Mao Lifen, a gamer from the northern Shanxi province who arrived in May, says he tries not to think about the future. He used to have a plan — work at a factory for five years, save up, and open a fruit shop. This was derailed when he and his colleagues had a falling out with the factory management and quit.

He went to work in food delivery and partnered with a friend to open a restaurant, maxing out several credit cards to the tune of 100,000 yuan and losing it all. Mao then tried starting a business with another friend, who ran off with all their money. A string of bad investments appears to have killed his interest in making plans.

His only thought now is to get through this year. “I’ve got food and drink — what is there to be unhappy about?” he says. At Wang’s internet café, he takes boosting orders for the first-person tactical shooter game Delta Force. When he’s not playing, he likes to walk up to the rooftop to look at the trees in the distance.

Mao likes this life that requires next to no human contact: everyone stares at their screen, submerged in the game. With his headphones on, there is no “outside world.”

This year, a wannabe entrepreneur from out of town visited Wang with a view to copying his business model elsewhere. Wang laid it out for him: 150 computers plus renovations, licensing, and other expenses mean at least 2 million yuan upfront; profits will unlikely keep pace with the equipment’s depreciation; and a minimum of three or four employees are needed to run 24/7. The visitor listened patiently and immediately abandoned the plan.

Wang knows he’s too deep into the industry to pull out. When he was young, he dreamed of making a fortune and owning a luxury car, but now “I know my limits,” he says. With a 30-year mortgage and still owing 110,000 yuan for equipment, his only wish is to draw customers and stay afloat.

(For privacy reasons, Qiang Yu and Mao Lifen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Customers sleep in the esports chairs, at Wang’s internet café in Kangyi Town, June 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.title: A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.content:
A Chinese city has launched a new residential cooling program using water from abandoned coal mines, a low-carbon initiative that could replace traditional air conditioners.

The initiative in the eastern Jiangsu province’s city of Xuzhou routes water from the now-defunct Woniushan Coal Mine to apartments in a nearby neighborhood, domestic media reported this week. The water maintains a consistent temperature of 19 degrees Celsius year-round.

Disused mines often fill with water via rainwater accumulation and groundwater seepage — water that can then be used to heat or cool nearby homes.

Xuzhou, a former coal-producing center with a decades-long mining history, has previously used abandoned mine water for clean heating, including a system installed last winter at its former Hanqiao Coal Mine. With annual average temperatures climbing and China’s “dual carbon” initiative — where the country aims to peak its carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 — a national priority, the cooling initiative, which began June 1, has been a focus for the city.

“After heat exchange (with the homes), the water returns to the mine, without having consumed any energy or produced any carbon emissions,” Zhang Tao, leader of the cooling project and a worker at Xukuang Heating Company, told state media outlet CCTV. Compared with traditional air conditioning, he said, this technology lowers carbon emissions and aligns more closely with China’s energy conservation and emission reduction policy.

According to domestic media, such closed-loop geothermal systems reduce energy consumption by approximately 50% compared with traditional methods. It is also estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions for the 100 homes in the pilot program by about 50 tons annually.

The city offered residents in the pilot program two free months of cooling, after which they’ll be charged quarterly at 4 yuan ($0.60) per square meter.

Wang, a resident in the pilot area, said that in previous summers her monthly electricity bill often exceeded 400 yuan due to air conditioner usage. In contrast, the pilot program has allowed her to cool her home for four months this summer for only 410 yuan. She said her home now maintains a constant temperature 24 hours a day, and the system is quiet, unlike air conditioners.

Zhang, the heating company researcher, noted the great potential of the pilot program. “This year we only used a part of Woniushan Coal Mine’s capacity, and since the mine has significant potential, in the future we plan on using it to capacity, extending it to more neighborhoods.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.title: [Rappler’s Best] Absentee judge
World.content:
LOREN LEGARDA. Senator-judge Loren Legarda questions National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 22, 2026.

The impeachment court last week saw one additional empty seat aside from three already vacated by others — proof of the utter misfortune of Filipino voters who elected these senators

Metro Manila and 23 other provinces have been under depressing skies the past days, as rain dropped like there was no tomorrow, triggered by the southwest monsoon and enhanced by Typhoon Dolphin that battered Japan and China over the weekend. Expect more rainfall in the coming days.

Two people died and eight others were hurt in the Cordillera, with heavy rain cutting off at least 20 road sections, uprooting crops, and forcing hundreds of residents to flee their homes. Images of flooded communities spilled into our social feeds, a grim reminder of humanity’s self-inflicted wounds: the climate crisis and a flood control corruption scandal in our part of the world.

Add to this the latest report on the economy.

The country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) fell to its lowest quarter-level growth in nearly two decades (with the exception of the COVID-19 years) at 2.3%. What dragged it down, aside from the Middle East crisis, is slow government construction which, according to this story, plunged by 32.4% year-on-year. The cause is obvious: government agencies have been extra-cautious in implementing public works given the intense scrutiny of spending on infrastructure following the flood control scandal.

The World Bank said that “uncertainty around infrastructure procurement” has dampened not just public spending but also private investments.

The government had already trimmed down its growth targets for the remainder of the Marcos administration’s term in 2027 and 2028 to around 5 to 6%. But even that seems like an uphill climb now.

Inflation woes will persist throughout the year.

Unemployment is at 4.9% as fresh grads scramble for few job options. Worse, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s promised “historic” P85 a day minimum wage increase has also been put on hold.

But Filipinos badly in need of a break got some last week.

The feisty Lorna Kapunan, prosecutor in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, put some spice in an otherwise ho-hum trial that has become too technical — showing some courtroom masterclass.

The question now is, will the senator-judge who was absent last week show up at the resumption of the trial this week? We refer to Senator Loren Legarda, who left the country on August 2 with her son Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste. (The impeachment court canceled the scheduled trial on Monday, August 10, due to bad weather.)

The senator-judge skipped all the three trial days last week, but until the immigration bureau announced her travel, the Senate leadership was mum about her absence. It later said she filed for medical leave.

Thus last week, the impeachment court saw one additional empty seat aside from three already vacated by others — proof of the utter misfortune of Filipino voters who elected senators Bato dela Rosa, now a fugitive; Rodante Marcoleta, now in jail for alleged plunder; and Jinggoy Estrada, also behind bars on a plunder suit.

Legarda, on the other hand, is being investigated for plunder along with her son over the latter’s failed solar energy franchise.

Here are some of Rappler’s bests that you shouldn’t miss:

Jasmine Payo talks about Alex Eala’s rabid fans who are now defying some of tennis’ unwritten rules. But sports is never about sports, writes Vince Rodriguez, as he tells us about what Alex, Manny Pacquiao, and Alyssa Valdez can teach us about community.

Our Brandrap team shows you a visually delightful ube, the much loved Filipino crop.

Jairo Bolledo reminds us that the US asked for the extradition of detained Pastor Apollo Quiboloy a year ago. What happened between then and now that the justice department finally received the request from the US? Herbie Gomez narrates how the guilty plea of Los Angeles-based Maria de Leon helped strengthen the case against Quiboloy.

Lance Spencer Yu reports that big banks are gearing up this year for Apple Pay, which launched last week in the Philippines.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Which ‘Flavor Clap’-ready Potato Corner moment resonates with you?
World.content:
PotCor, please! How our craving for our favorite fries helps us create exciting memories

Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by Potato Corner and was produced by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the production of this piece.

My Potato Corner craving is a frequent visitor in my headspace, and I always welcome it.

In fact, even Gen Z TikTok star Niana Guerrero and your favorite online personalities aren’t spared from this phenomenon. Something new I noticed thanks to them, though, is that there’s actually a name for how my hands form – my middle finger and thumb gently colliding – whenever my favorite fries are on my radar: the “Flavor Clap”.

Play Video

The gesture looks pretty much like how many of us grab each piece of our PotCor order – and it’s the same thing that shows the happy aftermath of our snacking (a.k.a. powder-covered fingers). But this gesture doesn’t only signal craving, but also summon Poco, the brand’s official mascot.

When the summoning is successful, this friendly neighborhood potato-employee poco-bombs the most random spots – think a mall meant for sidequest maxxing or even the chill office pantry.

This reminds me of the many mundane moments that Potato Corner can easily brighten, just by existing. Which one of these examples resonates with you the most?

The commute that wraps up your day

The “treat yourself” mantra just gets too real when it’s EOD o’clock, whether you’re a student, a working adult, or just someone who had a very eventful day. Now that stressors are (temporarily) gone and the day’s adrenaline has died down, snacking is more tempting.

To those dealing with long and winding commutes, a bag of Potato Corner can instantly make the travel time less bleak and boring. Good thing PotCor kiosks are everywhere – you may spot one in your go-to train station, the crowded terminal, or even just the street you pass by daily.

That rare cinema hopping weekend

Catching a Homer adaptation twice (with different movie buddies) or maximizing a film festival’s promising roster? Just when you think this once-in-a-blue-moon activity can’t get any more thrilling, this hangout can easily transform into a full-blown core memory with Potato Corner in your cinema arsenal. Pro tip: Get the Tera Fries with multiple flavors so your group stays in harmony.

That spontaneous work desk break

No, this isn’t exactly a lunch break. I’m talking about that genuine (and often random) urge to de-chain from your work desk and have a little walk; companions optional. During moments like this, you’re likely to feel the monotony of everyday life, especially if your daily tasks tend to be similar, or you follow the same routine.

But it’s also the perfect time to exercise that free will and add a little whimsy – like getting your bag of PotCor anytime. Just pick your poison: extend the fun walkathon so you can order at the nearest branch, or just have your favorite flavor delivered.

Your action-packed barkada catch-up sesh

POV: Finally, the plans have made their way out of the group chat!

In the mood for a friendly fire with your besties in a newly-purchased RPG or via a nostalgic card game, while attempting that long overdue catch-up? Don’t skip the snacks. While moments like these are already fun as they are, you can further solidify the hype by asking the room, “PotCor, g?” to which you receive a resounding “Yes!” mid-battle. That little moment of distraction that leads to losing? Worth it.

Whether you’re a cheese enjoyer, sour cream fan, or a loyalist of other Potato Corner flavors, you’re sure to flip any ordinary scene into one for the books – and share-worthy, too!

World.title: PhilHealth president Edwin Mercado appointed as new DOH chief
World.content:
OATH. Edwin Mercado takes his oath as the new Philippine Health Insurance Corporation president and chief executive officer on February 4, 2025.

The Department of Health gets a new secretary again, just a month after Jose Pujalte Jr. replaced Teodoro Herbosa

MANILA, Philippines – Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) President and Chief Executive Officer Edwin Mercado is now the new secretary of the Department of Health (DOH), replacing recently appointed Jose Pujalte Jr., Malacañang announced on Monday, August 10.

Mercado had been serving as the head of the state insurer since February 2025.

Palace Press Officer and Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a press briefing that Pujalte, a veteran orthopedic surgeon who was appointed to the position last July 13, just a month ago, has submitted his resignation to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. due to health reasons.

Pujalte’s predecessor, Teodoro Herbosa, also cited health concerns when he resigned in July.

Pujalte has faced allegations since taking the helm of the DOH. On July 31, a complaint letter addressed to the Palace claimed that he has been gambling at casinos, which is illegal for government officials.

Last Wednesday, August 5, a complaint filed with the Office of the Ombudsman accused Pujalte of delaying the bidding for tuberculosis medicines to allegedly favor a certain bidder.

When asked whether Pujalte’s resignation was linked to these allegations, Castro said: “Sa ngayon ay hindi pa po natin masasagot. Siya naman po ay boluntaryong nag-resign…. Nasa kamay na po ng Ombudsman ang pag-iimbestiga kung ano man po ang naireklamo laban kay dating secretary Pujalte.”

(We cannot answer that at this moment. He resigned voluntarily. The investigation into the complaint filed against former secretary Pujalte is now in the hands of the Ombudsman.)

New PhilHealth chief

Castro also announced that Dr. Beverly Lorraine Ho, a former undersecretary and assistant secretary of the health department, will succeed Mercado as the new president and CEO of PhilHealth.

Ho is currently the chief health officer of Ayala Healthcare Holdings, a subsidiary of Ayala Corporation.

She also served as DOH deputy spokesperson during the COVID-19 pandemic, from 2020 to 2022. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who is Lordan Suan, public prosecutor in Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial?
World.content:
Coming from an island where loyalty to the Duterte family remains strong doesn't deter the Cagayan de Oro 1st District lawmaker

Congressman Lordan Suan is among the few Mindanaoans who are part of the public prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

He comes from an island where loyalty to the Duterte family remains strong, but this fact doesn’t deter the Cagayan de Oro 1st District lawmaker.

“My being a Mindanaoan is precisely why I take this duty very seriously. Because we’re not just talking about the people’s money, we’re also talking about the taxes that Mindanaoans are paying,” Suan said during the first press briefing of trial prosecutors in May.

“No region, wherever it is — Luzon, Visayas, Mindanao — no family, no officials should be elevated above the Constitution or even above the investigations of the Commission on Audit,” he added.

The articles of impeachment assigned to him are those related to allegations that Duterte misused her confidential funds worth P612.5 million, and amassed unexplained wealth from the time she entered public service as Davao City vice mayor, until she became vice president.

The 43-year-old CDO native is the son of free mason Agapito Suan Jr. and businesswoman-broadcaster Girlie Gualberto-Suan. His brother, Aga Suan, is a Cagayan de Oro councilor.

Congressman Suan obtained his undergraduate and law degrees from Xavier University-Ateneo de Cagayan. His LinkedIn profile says he is a member of the fraternity Scintilla Legis.

Before entering public service, he had been chief executive officer of out-of-home media and billboard company Ultracraft Advertising Corporation. His family is also said to own Ultracraft Broadcasting Corporation, the company that operated DXRU Radio Ultra, now called Gold Radio.

Suan entered politics in 2016, successfully securing a seat in the Cagayan de Oro City council. He served two terms, then ran for congressman in 2022.

Suan won that race with a single-digit percentage-point margin against Joaquin Uy, son of then-term-limited congressman Rolando Uy.

In the 19th Congress, Suan became one of the members of the Young Guns, a House bloc led by the President’s son, Sandro Marcos, and who, at the time, were public talking heads supportive of the leadership of then-speaker Martin Romualdez. He was also an active member of the quad committee, which investigated the controversies that hounded the Rodrigo Duterte presidency, from gambling operators to his drug war.

In 2025, Suan sought a second term, winning in his rematch against the younger Uy, although it was a razor-thin race that ultimately came down to just 3,000-plus votes over Uy.

The Mindanaoan prides himself as an advocate of education, infrastructure development, and social welfare. Today, he serves as chairman of the House public information committee, tasking him to defend the freedom of information bill and the highly criticized anti-disinformation measure on the plenary floor.

In May, he emphasized the dangers posed by disinformation in the impeachment process involving Duterte.

“Our biggest challenge in this impeachment process is really ‘fake news.’ Because we’re talking about accountability here, and accountability does not respect regional bias. The truth should prevail, and hopefully everyone can come together and decide whether what we’re sharing is actually news or ‘fake news,'” he said. – Rappler.com

Patricia Fontilar is a journalism student at the University of the Philippines Diliman and the managing editor of Tinig ng Plaridel, the official student publication of the UP College of Media and Communication. She is a Rappler intern.

World.title: Weeks after Marcos SONA, House panel OKs higher income tax exemption ceiling
World.content:
CHRISTMAS SEASON. Filipino shoppers flock to the Divisoria Market to buy gifts for their loved ones on December 14, 2025.

MANILA, Philippines – The House ways and means committee approved on Monday, August 10, a bill seeking to expand tax relief for workers and small businesses, two weeks after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signaled it as a priority during his State of the Nation Address (SONA).

The panel passed House Bill No. 10345, filed by Speaker Bojie Dy and Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, which aims to amend the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 and allow individuals earning up to P350,000 annually to be exempt from income tax.

Currently, only workers earning P250,000 or less per year are exempt from paying income tax.

“We want our tax system to keep pace with the realities faced by Filipino families and workers. If incomes have not kept up with the rising cost of living, then we have to make sure that taxation does not further erode their purchasing power,” ways and means chairman Miro Quimbo said.

Dy and Marcos’ second tax-related bill, which seeks to abolish the minimum corporate income tax of 2% for small businesses, also cleared the committee on Monday.

“The objective…is to create breathing room for entrepreneurs and businesses so they can spend, invest, hire, and grow,” Quimbo said.

Marcos drew thunderous applause during his penultimate SONA when he promised to pursue tax relief measures “to ensure the continued progress of the middle class” on the heels of the oil crisis.

Play Video

– Rappler.com

World.title: What’s a precautionary hold departure order and when can it be issued?
World.content:
A PHDO has the power to prevent a person from leaving the country. Here's how it works.

The Supreme Court (SC), in a decision made public on August 7, reiterated when a precautionary hold departure order (PHDO) may be issued.

Generally, it’s not easy to prevent a person from leaving the country. This has to go through a process that involves authorities like the Department of Justice (DOJ), Bureau of Immigration, and the Philippine courts.

For example, Senator Loren Legarda and Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste both left the country on August 2, amid the pending plunder and graft complaints against them.

There’s nothing irregular here because there are no pending orders that could prevent them from flying.

Another case: former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque.

The former Duterte official, who was implicated in the Philippine offshore gaming operators, was able to leave the country because again, there was no court or immigration order that could have prevented him from leaving at the time.

Here’s where the PHDO enters because through this, Philippine authorities may prevent a person from leaving the country even if a case has yet to be filed before courts. Here’s how it works.

Immigration mechanisms

By rules, there are two orders that can ban a person’s travel abroad: a hold departure order (HDO) and a PHDO.

An HDO can only be availed of by authorities when there’s a case pending in court. A judge might issue this, apart from an arrest warrant, once the charge reaches the court.

Meanwhile, a PHDO may also be issued by courts even if the legal action is only at the complaint level.

Prosecutors may apply for the issuance of a PHDO if the complaint is at the preliminary investigation stage or the phase when the prosecution checks if there’s enough evidence for the complaints to become cases and be filed with courts.

After the application for PHDO, a judge assesses if there’s probable cause and if there’s a high probability of flight to evade arrest and prosecution.

Another mechanism, the immigration lookout bulletin order (ILBO), is used for monitoring purposes only and is not as strong as the HDO and PHDO.

Through ILBO, the BI can check if there are any pending warrants against subjects and if they have any violations or infractions. Immigration officers can monitor the subjects’ itineraries and whereabouts if they attempt to leave the country through this, but cannot prevent them from flying.

PHDO rules, clarified

A PHDO is a relatively new mechanism that started only in 2018.

It was triggered by a tussle between then-DOJ secretary Leila de Lima and former president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo. De Lima issued an HDO against Arroyo, citing DOJ Circular No. 41 signed by former justice secretary Alberto Agra, which empowered DOJ chiefs to issue HDOs and watchlist orders.

The SC, however, stopped the HDO, but De Lima still succeeded in preventing Arroyo from leaving the country. Seven years later, in 2018, the SC introduced the PHDO.

Then, the SC explained that a PHDO applies to cases where the minimum penalty is at least six years and one day. It may be issued by a tribunal that has jurisdiction over the place where the alleged crime was committed.

In a ruling on August 7, the SC reiterated that PHDOs may also be issued in cases where a respondent is a foreigner, regardless of the penalty. The Abad v. People ruling, penned by Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh, however, reiterated that a PHDO may only be issued in the aforementioned instances.

“The SC also clarified that PHDOs are intended to apply while the preliminary investigation is still pending. Once completed and an information is filed in court, the rules governing regular Hold Departure Orders apply,” the High Court said.

“The PHDO may be temporarily lifted upon the filing before the issuing court a verified motion based on meritorious grounds — that is, based on the complaint and the evidence that the respondent will present, there is doubt that probable cause exists to issue the PHDO or it is shown that the respondent is not a flight risk,” it added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Ramon Ang buys his way into Lopez Inc., which owns what he already builds
World.content:
So far, what has actually changed hands is one family branch’s stake in the private company at the very top of the Lopez empire. Whether it leads to a direct ABS-CBN rescue is a question about what Ang, and the Lopez family, do next.

Ramon Ang has been trying to own a piece of Philippine media for more than a decade. This week, he finally got a piece of something Lopez, just not the piece anyone expected.

He has chased a broadcast network, been rumored to be behind a cable news channel, and once got close enough to a newspaper deal that the price was already being haggled over. None of those closed. What closed instead, on Monday, August 10, was a 25.68% stake in Lopez Inc., the private company that sits at the very top of the Lopez Group, bought from the family branch led by Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III rather than negotiated with any media owner at all.

It is not the entry point expected, and it is not the first time Ang has shown up near a Lopez-controlled business either. Media is the chapter people remember, but it is not the oldest one.

Not his first time near a Lopez asset

In October 2008, San Miguel Corporation (SMC), then a food and beer conglomerate in its early years of diversifying under Ramon Ang, bought the government’s 27% stake in Manila Electric Company (Meralco) out from under Manuel V. Pangilinan, who believed he had already secured it. Ang had flown to Cebu the weekend before the deal closed to meet GSIS president Winston Garcia directly, after GSIS’s long, public fight with the Lopez family over control of Meralco’s board. (READ: The Lopezes, presidents, and the cost of dissent)

A separate entity, Global 5000 Investment Corp., staffed by people close to San Miguel’s leadership, picked up another chunk of government shares soon after, splitting the total purchase in a way that kept it under the threshold that would have required offering the same price to Meralco’s other shareholders.

Around the same time, Ang had also gone after another Lopez asset directly, offering a late, above-market bid for the family’s stake in Manila North Tollways Corp. after Pangilinan’s group had already all but closed that purchase. The Lopez family’s own advisers dismissed the offer as not genuine, arriving too late to be taken seriously, and turned him down.

Once the Meralco deal closed, San Miguel’s board representatives sat for a period alongside directors from the Lopez family’s own branches, including the Manolo Lopez branch, the same branch known within Lopez Inc. today as Mantes Corporation.

Power, not media, is also where the Ramon Ang and the Lopez family’s current empires actually collide at scale. Ang runs his energy business mainly through San Miguel Global Power Holdings Corp. (SMGP) and Petron Corporation, together controlling roughly 5,057 megawatts (MW) of installed and contracted generating capacity, close to a fifth of the entire Philippine grid and more than a quarter of Luzon’s. That capacity leans heavily on coal, Masinloc, Limay, Davao Greenfield, and Mariveles among the plants SMGP owns outright, plus a contracted share of the Sual coal plant, alongside the Ilijan gas plant, now running on imported LNG, and a 1,000-MW-hour battery storage rollout across 32 sites. Petron adds the country’s largest oil refinery, in Limay, and a nationwide retail network on top of that.

Federico “Piki” Lopez, Gabby’s cousin who focused on the energy side, built First Gen Corp. (First Gen) and Energy Development Corp. (EDC) in the opposite direction, and did so publicly. First Gen’s installed capacity ran to roughly 3,500 to 3,600 MW before the family sold 60% of its gas business to Prime Infra and redirected the proceeds into pumped-storage hydro. Its pure renewable capacity today stands at about 1,764 MW, with a stated target of 13 GW by 2030. EDC alone carries 1,302.8 MW of geothermal capacity, which the company describes as the largest vertically integrated geothermal operation in the world, plus roughly 300 MW of conventional hydro and a 2,000-MW pumped-storage pipeline still under development. In 2016, under Piki, First Philippine Holdings Inc. (FPH) adopted an explicit “No to Coal” policy, ruling coal out of the group’s power strategy entirely in favor of geothermal, hydro, gas, and renewables.

That makes the two men’s energy strategies close to opposites: Ang’s coal-and-gas-anchored, multi-fuel grid operator built for scale, Piki’s renewables-first platform built partly as a rejection of exactly the fuel mix Ang’s business depends on. Ang’s Lopez Inc. stake does not merge the two companies, or give him any direct say over First Gen’s fuel choices; the ownership sits several layers above First Gen’s own board. But it puts him, for the first time, inside the ownership structure of a power company whose entire public identity has been built in opposition to the kind of power company he runs.

The media chase: four attempts, zero completions

Ang’s pursuit of a media company has followed the same rhythm every time: serious talks, a near-agreement, and then no deal. In January 2014, he confirmed personal talks with the three founding families of GMA Network for a stake in the country’s second-largest broadcaster, offering at least 30% at a premium price. The talks stretched past a year and collapsed in June 2015. GMA’s majority shareholders had said Ang kept revising terms after they had already accepted his proposals, while Ang insisting the opposite was true. It was, by GMA’s own account, the fifth time the network had walked away from a suitor.

Before GMA, Ang had said in 2012 that he wanted a personal stake in Radio Philippines Network (RPN-9), a partly government-owned broadcaster. That did not happen either, though he reportedly built a personal investment in Solar TV Network, a blocktimer that later became a minority RPN owner. When Solar TV was renamed Nine Media Corporation and struck a deal to carry the CNN brand in the Philippines starting 2015, rumors circulated that Ang was behind the new channel. Nine Media’s own SEC filings showed no trace of him: its parent company was wholly owned by five individuals with no visible Ang connection.

The Philippine Daily Inquirer looked, briefly, like the one that would finally close. In July 2017, the Prieto family confirmed it was in talks to sell its 85% majority stake in the Inquirer Group of Companies to Ang, in his personal capacity rather than through San Miguel, and by November that year Ang told reporters the deal was done, pending clearance from the Philippine Competition Commission. It wasn’t done. Due diligence turned up receivables Ang’s team considered uncollectible, and the price was renegotiated down from an initial indicative figure before the Prietos pulled the group’s real estate out of the deal entirely, cutting the offer further to a level the family ultimately judged too low. Talks broke down for good in 2018, and the Inquirer has remained under Prieto and Pangilinan-linked ownership ever since.

That gives Ang an unbroken record across four separate media pursuits, GMA, RPN, CNN Philippines by way of Solar TV and Nine Media, and Inquirer, in which serious, sustained negotiations never once converted into actual ownership. The political backdrop to the Inquirer talks is still worth noting for context: then-president Rodrigo Duterte spent 2017 attacking the paper over its drug-war coverage, and Ang was, by his own account and Duterte’s, a friend and campaign donor, which is part of why the near-deal drew so much attention even though it never closed. Duterte would later cite Ang’s name anyway when he told ABS-CBN it should simply sell rather than fight for its franchise renewal, apparently unaware, or unconcerned, that the Inquirer precedent he was gesturing at had fallen apart.

What makes the Lopez Inc. stake different from the media chase is that Ang did not need it to gain exposure to the Lopez Group’s businesses. His own empire already sits across nearly every sector the Lopez companies operate in.

In power generation, First Gen and EDC compete in the same broad space as SMC Global Power’s gas, hydro, solar, coal, and battery storage portfolio, and Petron’s fuel refining and retail business runs alongside First Gen’s own energy interests.

In real estate, Rockwell Land and First Philippine Industrial Park sit in the same market as San Miguel Properties and San Miguel’s large-scale reclamation and aerotropolis projects around Bulacan. In construction and infrastructure, First Balfour and ThermaPrime’s drilling business compete in a space where SMC runs Eagle Cement, Northern Cement, and a tollway and airport portfolio that includes Skyway, SLEX, TPLEX, and the new Bulacan airport.

In media and telecommunications, ABS-CBN and Sky Cable sit opposite a San Miguel history that once included Liberty Telecoms and Vega Telecom before those assets were sold to PLDT and Globe, alongside SMC’s sports broadcasting interests. Even in manufacturing, First Philec‘s transformer business and San Miguel Yamamura’s packaging operations occupy adjacent industrial ground.

The two groups have been, in effect, neighbors across almost the entire Philippine economy for years before this week.

Held against that backdrop, a 25.68% stake in Lopez Inc. reads less like an outsider buying his way into unfamiliar territory and more like the latest entry in a long-running relationship between two of the country’s most diversified conglomerates, one that has included open rivalry (power), at least one failed courtship of a Lopez asset (NLEx), a shared board table (Meralco, 2008), and now a shared shareholder registry (Lopez Inc).

Control at every level

Lopez Inc. sits above two very different kinds of empire, media and energy alike, and it holds voting control over nearly all of both, even where its economic stake has thinned to a fraction of that.

On the media side, Lopez Inc., directly and through ABS-CBN Holdings Corp., which it owns 59.5% of, commands 78.5% of ABS-CBN’s voting shares. That is close to outright control. Lopez Holdings carries a separate 53.55% economic claim on ABS-CBN through Philippine Deposit Receipts (PDRs), but no vote unless those PDRs are exercised, since the Constitution reserves voting control of mass media for Filipino owners, and Lopez Inc. is the fully Filipino entity that qualifies. Lopez Inc. holds the vote. Lopez Holdings gets most of the money.

On the energy and property side, the arithmetic runs differently. Lopez Holdings owns 60.67% of FPH outright. Lopez Inc.’s own indirect economic stake in FPH, run through its 54.74% of Lopez Holdings, comes to roughly 33%, though its practical control of FPH’s board remains total. FPH owns 67.84% of First Gen; carry the dilution one layer further and Lopez Inc.’s indirect economic stake in First Gen lands at roughly 22-23%. First Gen’s Red Vulcan vehicle holds 65% voting and 45.8% economic interest in EDC; carry it a fourth layer and Lopez Inc.’s ultimate economic interest in EDC, the asset now drawing a reported multibillion-dollar offer from an Indonesian conglomerate, comes to roughly 10%. Outside capital already fills most of what the family’s chain does not reach: PREHC, a Macquarie-and-GIC-linked vehicle, holds close to 55% of EDC’s economics; KKR holds a 19.9% economic and 14.1% voting interest inside First Gen itself; and Prime Infra, Enrique Razon’s company, already controls 60% of First Gen’s gas businesses and 67% of its new pumped-storage hydro venture, leaving First Gen a minority, non-controlling partner in both.

Control, in other words, survives every layer of this structure. Money does not. The family’s actual economic claim on its own crown jewel, the asset outsiders are currently competing to buy into, is down to roughly a tenth.

LOPEZ INC. The Lopez empire shareholder tree. Graph by Lala Rimando

The rift was always about ABS-CBN’s money

The dispute that has consumed the Lopez family since February traces back to a single question: whether Lopez Inc. should inject roughly P2 billion into ABS-CBN to stabilize its finances after its 2020 franchise denial under the government of Rodrigo Duterte. Gabby’s branch and allied cousins pushed for the infusion; Piki opposed the plan as structured, arguing more than half the money would go to executives and insiders rather than a clear turnaround.

The urgency behind that fight is documented in ABS-CBN’s own numbers. A complaint Piki filed with the SEC put the network’s immediate liquidity gap at roughly P1.5 billion, pointing to P8.5 billion in interest-bearing loans classified as current liabilities and due within 2026, against liquid assets of only about P7 billion. (READ: Family friend to referee? SEC’s Francis Lim has peace plan for Lopez war.)

ABS-CBN’s own 2025 annual report describes ongoing loan refinancing talks with its creditor banks and management’s assessment that it can meet its obligations over the next twelve months, without disclosing a specific rescue figure of its own.

FPH, First Gen, and Rockwell carry none of that strain. Their businesses, power generation and real estate, have continued largely undisturbed by the family fight. The disruption has stayed concentrated at the top, in Lopez Inc.’s boardroom and courtroom filings, and at ABS-CBN, the one asset in the group that needs money it does not have.

So far, what has actually changed hands is one family branch’s stake in the private company at the very top of the pyramid, nothing more. Whether it becomes anything closer to a direct ABS-CBN rescue is a question about what Ang, and the family, do next, not about what has been confirmed so far. As of writing, whether any portion of what Ang paid for the Crème stake is meant to reach ABS-CBN,t through a future capital call, a loan, or some other mechanism, is not yet known.

ABS-CBN’s own disclosure, filed also on August 10, backs up the “nothing more, for now” reading. After a news report on the sale prompted the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) to direct ABS-CBN to confirm or clarify the transaction and disclose any effect on its business, ABS-CBN responded that it is not a party to the transaction and is unable to comment on it, and that because the sale sits at the Lopez Inc. level, the company does not foresee any impact on its business, financial condition, operations, or ownership structure. That is the company’s own words, not this piece’s inference: as things stand, the sale has not touched ABS-CBN at all.

The vehicle, and who approached whom

San Miguel Corporation’s own disclosure to the exchange, filed the same day as the sale, names the vehicle: Illumina Investment Holdings Inc., a corporation wholly owned by Ang, executed a Deed of Assignment with members of Gabby Lopez’s family for the Crème Investment Corp. shares. The filing also settles a question the earlier reporting had left open: the deal was struck “upon the invitation of the ELopez Family,” San Miguel’s own language for it. Meaning, Gabby’s side approached Ang, not the other way around.

ILLUMINA INVESTMENT. San Miguel Corp. discloses to the Philippine Stock Exchange Ramon Ang’s personal investment in ultimate Lopez parent firm, Lopez Inc., on August 10, 2026. Screenshot from SMC disclosure

San Miguel’s board itself was not briefed on the details until a meeting scheduled for Thursday, August 13, three days after the deal closed, consistent with how Ang has handled his previous media-adjacent investments: personally, outside the conglomerate’s own governance process, with the board informed after the fact rather than asked beforehand.

What Ang actually bought into

Strip away the family names and the press statements, and what Ramon Ang bought on August 10 is a seat at the top of a pyramid that controls almost everything beneath it and owns less and less of it the further down the shareholder tree. He now holds a piece of a media company whose votes the family guards completely and whose bank accounts are running dry, sitting atop an energy empire the family still commands from the boardroom while owning, in real terms, a shrinking sliver of its most valuable asset, an asset a foreign conglomerate is already circling with an offer measured in billions.

Razon is already inside the gas and hydro businesses. KKR is already inside First Gen. An Indonesian bidder is already asking about EDC. Ang did not buy his way past any of them. He bought a seat at the table one level above all of it, in a private company where the vote still belongs entirely to the family, for now, and where the money increasingly does not.

Eighteen years ago, Ang flew to Cebu on a weekend, not to take the company from the Lopez family, but to beat now Meralco chair Manuel Pangilinan to GSIS’s hostile stake before the Lopezes could broker their own exit for it. This time, he did not have to fly anywhere, or beat anyone to it.

A family feud did the work for him. One cousin wanted out, and Ramon Ang, who has been circling this family’s businesses for 18 years, was there to buy. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

World.title: Negrense web developer proposes AI-powered transparency portal for gov’t projects
World.content:
FOR TRANSPARENCY. Japheth Gonzales, a young educator from Kabankalan City and creator of K-Tracer, promotes transparency in government spending.

‘I also want to prove that it’s not only big cities that can develop innovative applications. People who grew up here in Kabankalan can do it too,’ says Negrense web developer Japheth Gonzales

NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines — At a time when the Philippines is grappling with controversies over failed government projects and corruption in trillions of pesos in flood control spending, a young Negrense web developer is pushing for greater transparency through a digital platform that allows ordinary citizens to track where every taxpayer’s peso goes.

In just eight hours over a weekend during the third week of July, Japheth Gonzales, a 25-year-old instructor at Southland College and a resident of Barangay 1 in Kabankalan City, turned a moment of boredom and inspiration from the public’s increasing demand for greater transparency in government spending into an innovative response.

K-TRACER. The transparency portal that features government projects allows users to view their corresponding budgets and track the status of the projects.

Drawing on years of expertise in artificial intelligence (AI) — a field he began studying in 2021 — Gonzales developed a prototype transparency portal he called K-Tracer.

“It’s not about politics. It’s about transparency and accountability. As taxpayers, we have the right to know where our money goes and whether projects are actually being implemented,” Gonzales told Rappler in a mix of Hiligaynon.

The developer clarified that the current prototype uses dummy data for demonstration purposes. Even so, the platform showcases how users can monitor government projects, view their corresponding budgets, and track whether projects are ongoing, delayed, pending, or completed.

“It can help reduce doubts and misunderstandings because people can directly see how government funds are being used and where taxpayers’ money goes. It also gives people easier access to information. They can see which projects are being implemented by the government and where the budget is allocated,” Gonzales said.

“For every project, the application can display detailed information such as the budget, project items, suppliers, engineers involved, and other relevant data. It also has an AI feature that helps people quickly verify whether the government has officially approved a project,” he added.

The dashboard also includes a price comparison feature that shows each item’s prevailing market price alongside its awarded bid price, enabling users to identify any price variance.

Immutable data

To ensure records remain secure, he envisions integrating blockchain technology should any government unit adopt the platform.

He said that local government units (LGUs) do not need to seek approval from an outside organization to use blockchain, describing it as part of the software infrastructure that can be built into the system.

“Once it’s integrated, every time an authorized LGU employee enters a new project or budget, the portal can automatically encrypt and record that information on the blockchain,” he said. “The staff won’t need to do anything differently because the system handles everything in the background.”

According to Gonzales, blockchain technology would make project records traceable and significantly reduce the risk of unauthorized editing or deletion, strengthening public trust in government data.

Kabankalons can deliver

The developer also hopes the invention would send a message that great innovation can also come from communities outside major cities.

“I also want to prove that it’s not only big cities that can develop innovative applications. People who grew up here in Kabankalan can do it too. I also hope the government will continue supporting students because many of them have the potential to contribute to technology, especially those studying computer science, computer engineering, and related fields,” Gonzales said.

“That’s one of the reasons I became a teacher — to help students develop their skills, learn new technologies, and think beyond Kabankalan toward the international level,” he added.

“I want students to realize that they don’t have to leave Kabankalan to achieve great things. They can study here, learn from their teachers and mentors, and still create technologies that can make a difference.” – Rappler.com

A version of this story was first published in Brigada News.

World.title: Comic Con Astana 2026: How Kazakhstan Turns Pop Culture into Creative Industries
World.content:
ASTANA — Comic Con Astana 2026 drew more than 76,000 visitors from 40 countries over four days, underscoring the growing popularity of pop culture in Kazakhstan and the festival’s expanding international profile.

Held from Aug. 6 to 9, the festival brought together fans of films, TV series, comics, gaming and cosplay across two venues: Barys Arena and Alau Ice Palace. The program included meetings with international stars, Q&A sessions, an international cosplay competition with a 20 million tenge prize pool, gaming tournaments, workshops and other activities.

This year’s international headliners included “Game of Thrones” star Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, “Peaky Blinders” actor Paul Anderson, and “One Piece” stars Iñaki Godoy and Taz Skylar.

International stars discover Kazakhstan

For several international guests, Comic Con Astana marked their first visit to Kazakhstan.

Mexican actor Iñaki Godoy, known for playing Monkey D. Luffy in Netflix’s “One Piece” adaptation, shared his first impressions of Astana.

Godoy said he was particularly impressed by Astana’s distinctive architecture, mentioning the Nur Alem pavilion at EXPO and Khan Shatyr.

“I haven’t seen much of Astana yet. But when I went into one of the shopping malls, I saw this huge sphere right next to it. I also got to see the giant tent. It’s really impressive. I’d love to see even more interesting places,” the actor said.

During his Q&A session, Godoy also spoke about working on One Piece and said he would like to see Kazakhstan become one of the filming locations for the series. He noted that some storylines in One Piece feature nomadic themes, which could make Kazakhstan an interesting location for future productions.

“I would really love to come back here, and I would really love to film here,” Godoy said.

British actor Paul Anderson, known for his role as Arthur Shelby in “Peaky Blinders”, also visited Kazakhstan for the first time.

“I was really impressed when we drove in from the airport to the hotel. What I saw outside the window… I honestly thought I’d landed in Los Angeles,” Anderson said.

One of the festival’s main headliners was Danish actor Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, internationally known for playing Jaime Lannister in “Game of Thrones”.

His visit to Kazakhstan was also his first.

“This is my first visit to Kazakhstan, to Astana. I have to say, it’s a very big country. Wonderful food, especially the meat. Today I ate more of it than I have in the last three years,” Coster-Waldau said.

When asked where Kazakhstan might fit into the world of “Game of Thrones”, Coster-Waldau drew a parallel with the two powerful sides of the fictional universe.

“If we’re thinking in “Game of Thrones” categories, Kazakhstan would probably be kind of in the middle between two very powerful neighbours. So it would kinda be somewhere between the Lannisters and the Dothraki lands, like very diplomatic. And making each side believe that they are their best friends,” he said.

Coster-Waldau also expressed interest in discovering Kazakh cinema and praised the landscapes of the Mangystau region. His conversation with fans also touched on artificial intelligence, a technology that is increasingly becoming part of Kazakhstan’s creative landscape.

When asked about the use of AI in filmmaking, Coster-Waldau said he sees it primarily as a tool rather than a replacement for human creativity.

“I think AI can be used as a tool, and it should be used as a tool,” the actor said.

At the same time, he stressed that key creative decisions should remain in the hands of artists.

“When we talk about filmmaking, the entire creative process should remain in the hands of the creators, in the hands of artists,” Coster-Waldau said.

That discussion found a practical continuation at Comic Con Astana 2026 with the presentation of “Tengrida: Cyber Steppe”, a Kazakh art film created with AI as one of its production tools.

Tengrida: from a cosplay character to a new universe

The festival hosted the first public screening of a three-minute AI-animated episode titled “Arena,” which introduces a new original fictional universe.

The story follows Tengrida, a young woman who enters a techno-clan arena to fight for justice. In a future where technology has replaced much of human memory and brutal fights have become mass entertainment, she faces a warrior named Kanjar while trying to help people see the truth again.

The character was created by Almaty-based cosplayer Aruzhan Zhunusova, known as Aruvibez. Tengrida’s story began in 2025, when Zhunusova presented the original cosplay character at Comic Con Astana, combining elements of Kazakh national style with a futuristic aesthetic.

According to Zhunusova, the audience’s reaction was the moment she realized the cosplay character could become something much bigger.

“So many people came up to me, took photos and wrote to me. And I realised that I had found some kind of response in people’s hearts. I didn’t want to limit it to just one festival. I wanted to create something much bigger, ” Zhunusova told The Astana Times.

This led to the idea of developing an entire universe around the character.

“In the end, we decided to start with an animated video using AI, as we want to take part in the AI film festival, and then gradually reveal the character and her universe. It could be comics, games, feature films. So I think this is only the beginning,” she said.

Zhunusova describes Tengrida as a “Kazakh warrior from the future” who fights for justice and truth.

The production of “Tengrida: Cyber Steppe” took around four to five months. For the directors, the project was also their first major experience working with AI animation and a fantasy aesthetic. According to Zhunusova, the first two months were spent developing the project’s visual language and experimenting with the technology.

Despite the use of AI, the film was not created with a single automated process. Individual scenes were generated in short fragments, after which the team manually reviewed and approved the material.

“We didn’t generate it all at once. We worked in five-second fragments. Then we approved everything, put it together, edited it and worked on the sound design,” Zhunusova explained.

Zhunusova believes AI does not replace the creative team in the project, but expands its possibilities.

“I believe that if AI is in the hands of a professional, it can be used as a great tool,” she said.

From fan festival to creative industry platform

The festival has steadily expanded its international profile, welcoming stars such as Mads Mikkelsen, Andy Serkis, Pilou Asbæk, Scott Adkins, Esai Morales, Michael Rooker, Sean Gunn, Percy Hynes White and Alexander Kuznetsov over the years.

Its international cosplay competition has also become a major part of the program, attracting participants from more than 20 countries. This year, 64 finalists competed across 20 categories for a total prize pool of 20 million tenge.

According to the festival’s General Producer Natalia Abrashkina, Comic Con Astana is increasingly becoming a platform for the development of the creative industries.

“Comic Con Astana is much more than a festival. It is an international platform that brings the industry together, creates new opportunities for talented people and contributes to the development of Kazakhstan’s creative economy,” Abrashkina said.

She stressed that the festival aims not only to attract international stars, but also to promote Kazakh authors, artists, cosplayers and content creators internationally.

The story of Tengrida offers one example of this shift. A character created for a cosplay competition has, within a year, evolved into a screen project using AI and the foundation for a potential universe that could eventually extend beyond animation into comics, games and film.

For Comic Con Astana, that trajectory points to a broader evolution: from bringing global pop culture to Kazakhstan to giving local creators a platform to build stories and intellectual properties of their own.

World.title: Abai’s Legacy Endures as Nearly 19,000 Kazakh Citizens Carry His Name
World.content:
ALMATY – Nearly 19,000 people in Kazakhstan bear the name Abai, according to the Bureau of National Statistics, as the country marks Abai Day on Aug. 10, commemorating the 181st anniversary of the birth of Abai Kunanbayev, who was born in 1845. The figures highlight how the name of the country’s renowned poet, philosopher and thinker continues to resonate across generations.

A total of 18,961 people in Kazakhstan are named Abai. The largest number live in Astana, with 2,186 people, followed by the Turkistan Region with 2,008 and Almaty with 1,740.

The name remains in use among younger generations. During the first half of 2026 alone, 91 newborns were given the name Abai. Although traditionally regarded as a male name, national statistics also record nine women named Abai.

The oldest Kazakhstan resident with the name was born in 1932, while the largest age group is people aged 30–34, numbering 3,267. The name is also reflected in Kazakhstan’s geography. One region, one city, three districts and 26 villages are named after Abai.

Abai’s legacy in national identity

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, in his message marking Abai Day, described the poet’s intellectual and creative heritage as an important part of Kazakhstan’s cultural legacy. He also linked Abai’s ideas about knowledge, diligence, responsibility and unity to contemporary efforts to strengthen social values and national identity.

Abai’s influence has also extended beyond the country’s borders. Monuments dedicated to the poet have been erected in more than 20 cities, including Beijing, Budapest, Istanbul, Moscow, Tashkent, Baku, Tehran and Vitebsk.

In 2016, monuments were unveiled in Cairo and Rennes, France, further expanding the international presence of the Kazakh thinker. In 2021, President Tokayev took part in the opening of a 2.2-metre monument to Abai in Seoul during his official visit to South Korea.

Abai’s international recognition also has a longer history. UNESCO declared 1995 the Year of Abai to mark the 150th anniversary of his birth, placing his literary and philosophical legacy within a broader international cultural context.

For Kazakhstan, the continued spread of the name Abai, from newborn children to towns and cities and monuments abroad, reflects how a historical figure has become part of both the country’s cultural memory and its contemporary identity.

World.title: Kazakhstan Emerges as Firebird AI Market With Data Center Valley Project in Ekibastuz
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has emerged as the second market for US-based AI infrastructure company Firebird, which is developing a 125-megawatt computing facility in Ekibastuz as part of the country’s broader effort to build domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure and attract a larger share of the global AI economy.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev announced the development during the official opening of the first phase of Firebird’s AI campus in Hrazdan, Armenia, on Aug. 8. The event brought together Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang, NVIDIA Vice President Rev Lebaredian, US government representatives, technology companies, investors and industry experts.

Firebird’s Armenian facility is described as the region’s largest operational AI factory based on NVIDIA’s DSX architecture. The company plans to expand its Armenian infrastructure to more than 70,000 NVIDIA Rubin and Blackwell GPUs and 300 MW of computing capacity by the end of 2027.

Kazakhstan is becoming the company’s second major market. In Ekibastuz, Firebird, together with Kazakhtelecom as project operator, is developing the Data Center Valley, with an initial capacity of 125 MW.

The project has received the necessary approvals from the Kazakh government as well as an export authorization from the US Bureau of Industry and Security for the supply of relevant technologies.

Kazakhstan targets global AI infrastructure market

Huang highlighted Kazakhstan alongside Armenia as part of Firebird’s expanding infrastructure network.

“Together with Firebird, we are building AI infrastructure in Armenia and Kazakhstan that will provide researchers, startups and industry with the computing foundation to develop artificial intelligence within their countries, attract international innovators and participate in the global AI economy,” Huang said.

According to Madiyev, the project forms part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop domestic computing capacity rather than rely exclusively on external infrastructure.

“Kazakhstan has the necessary energy base, territory and developed digital ecosystem to host large computing capacities. Our task is not only to attract global technology partners, but also to create a complete environment within the country for the development of artificial intelligence, research, startups and new digital services,” he said.

The Data Center Valley builds on plans announced earlier this year to develop a large-scale computing hub in Ekibastuz. Kazakhstan has been discussing the project with major international technology and investment companies, including Microsoft, OpenAI, G42 and Mubadala. The project has been envisioned as capable of eventually scaling to up to one gigawatt of computing capacity and attracting around $30 billion in investment.

Why Ekibastuz matters

Kazakhstan’s energy resources therefore provide one of the main potential advantages for developing large computing facilities. At the same time, the government is seeking to upgrade the digital infrastructure needed to connect these facilities to international markets.

One such project is the Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable, which is being built between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. The new submarine connection is expected to establish an additional high-speed data route toward Europe, strengthening the infrastructure supporting international cloud and AI services.

Together, the projects point to a broader approach in which Kazakhstan is attempting to develop several layers of an AI ecosystem simultaneously: electricity and data centers on one side, international connectivity and computing capacity on the other, and regulation, talent and startups to build applications on top of that infrastructure.

Firebird plans to continue expanding internationally and aims to bring its total global AI infrastructure capacity to 2 gigawatts across Armenia, Kazakhstan and other markets by the end of 2028.

The company has also announced plans for NVIDIA to invest in Firebird, while CoreWeave has previously invested in the company. The new funding is expected to support the accelerated development of Firebird’s global AI infrastructure.

World.title: AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov on How AIFC is Preparing for Next Era of Finance
World.content:
ASTANA — When Renat Bekturov first joined what would become the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), the institution existed only as an idea. There were no success stories to point to and no guarantee that an international financial center could take root in the heart of Eurasia. Nearly a decade later, the conversation has shifted. The AIFC has grown into an ecosystem with its own exchange, court, arbitration centre, business-friendly regulatory framework and growing international reputation.

“It was just an idea. Now this is a real jurisdiction with real working institutions,” he recalled.

That philosophy of institution building runs through nearly every initiative the AIFC pursues. Whether discussing Islamic finance, critical minerals, creative industries or digital assets, Bekturov repeatedly returns to one belief: institutions matter because they outlive the people who create them.

“I believe people create institutions, institutions create policy or culture, and culture affects people again. We’re trying to create an institution that will live beyond us and serve the economy and investors for many years ahead,” he said.

The vision has since translated into tangible results. Nearly a decade after its launch, the AIFC hosts more than 6,000 companies from over 90 countries, including companies from the United States, the United Kingdom, China, Türkiye, Singapore, and the UAE, has attracted more than $25 billion in investment, and has ranked as the leading financial center in Eastern Europe and Central Asia for three consecutive years in the Global Financial Centres Index. Those milestones reflect not only the center’s growth but also the institution-building philosophy Bekturov believes is essential for long-term success.

That long-term perspective also shapes how the AIFC identifies new areas for growth. Rather than focusing exclusively on traditional banking or capital markets, the center is building financial infrastructure around sectors where Kazakhstan has long-term competitive advantages.

Islamic finance is one example. While still developing in Kazakhstan, Bekturov believes it represents a significant opportunity for both the country and the wider Central Asian region, where many practicing Muslims remain underserved by conventional financial products.

“They have fewer opportunities than people who are not practicing Muslims. They can use current accounts and bank cards, but they cannot use deposits, which means they cannot earn returns on their money. And they cannot leverage financing to buy assets or make investments in the same way that others can,” he said.

Critical minerals are another strategic priority. As global demand rises for rare earth elements used in renewable energy, electric vehicles and advanced technologies, Kazakhstan’s vast mineral wealth is attracting growing international interest. But natural resources alone are not enough.

“The opportunities and ideas are nothing if they don’t have capital,” Bekturov said.

To connect promising exploration projects with investors, the AIFC will launch a dedicated Junior Mining Pitch Day during this year’s Astana Finance Days, taking place inSeptember and borrowing a format familiar from the venture capital world.

“We’ve learned it from the venture capital industry. The founders present their projects to investors. We want to organize the same kind of pitch day for junior miners,” Bekturov explained.

The same approach is now extending to Kazakhstan’s creative economy. Rather than financing films or music directly, the AIFC is building the legal and investment framework that allows private capital to support creative businesses.

“One of the biggest assets Kazakhstan has is its people — the talent and creativity of its people,” Bekturov said.

This year’s Astana Finance Days will also feature a Creative Pitch Day, bringing together filmmakers, producers and investors as part of the AIFC’s broader effort to open new sources of financing for the country’s creative industries.

Looking ahead, Bekturov believes the next transformation of finance will be driven by technology, particularly digital assets. While cryptocurrencies often dominate public discussion, he argues that the real breakthrough lies in tokenization: turning physical assets into digital ones that can be traded more efficiently. He illustrates the idea with a simple example. Gold is a physical asset that requires storage and security, but its ownership can be represented digitally through tokens, making transactions faster and easier.

“I really believe that digital assets will be transformative for the financial industry,” he said.

The technology, however, is only part of the equation. According to Bekturov, the problem is not technology but its adoption. Financial institutions and regulators, he said, will ultimately determine how quickly these innovations become part of the global financial system.

Artificial intelligence presents another challenge. Rather than focusing on whether AI will replace people, Bekturov is more interested in where responsibility should remain.

“We’re already discussing at what time we will give AI the role of a decision-maker and should we ever give that role?” he said.

For him, technology should strengthen financial markets rather than replace human judgment. That balance between innovation and institution building reflects the broader vision behind the AIFC. While the center continues expanding into new areas, from Islamic finance and critical minerals to creative industries and digital assets, its long-term objective remains unchanged: creating a trusted platform that connects global investors with Kazakhstan and Central Asia.

Bekturov often describes the AIFC as a bridge rather than a destination in itself.

“We’re basically a bridge that connects the world with the island of Kazakhstan, or Central Asia wider. People don’t use the bridge because it’s there. They use it because they want to get to a particular location,” he said.

For now, that bridge serves investors seeking opportunities in Kazakhstan and the wider region. Over time, Bekturov hopes it will evolve into a financial hub where international transactions are structured regardless of geography. Ultimately, however, his definition of success extends beyond financial indicators.

“For me, if in 10 years the AIFC is recognized among the world’s top 30 international financial centers, that would definitely be a success. Equally important is seeing a new generation of leaders moving the center forward, ensuring that the institution lives beyond its founders and the people who started it,” he concluded.

World.title: How PSG Academy’s Arrival Reflects Kazakhstan’s Rise as Football Talent Hub
World.content:
ALMATY – Paris Saint-Germain’s decision to open its first football academy in Kazakhstan this September is more than another international expansion for the French club. It reflects Kazakhstan’s growing attractiveness as a destination for elite youth football development, following a series of milestones that have elevated the country’s profile.

Located in Astana, the new PSG Academy Kazakhstan will welcome up to 300 boys and girls aged six to 14 during its inaugural season. Training will follow the official Paris Saint-Germain methodology, modeled on the club’s renowned youth academy in France and emphasizing technical excellence, game intelligence, discipline and teamwork.

While the academy’s opening marks Kazakhstan as the 24th country in PSG’s global network, it also fits into a broader pattern that has accelerated over the past two years: the country is increasingly positioning itself not only as a participant in international football, but as a place where future talent can be developed.

A broader football ecosystem is taking shape

The arrival of PSG follows several developments that together suggest Kazakhstan’s football strategy is evolving beyond isolated infrastructure projects or individual success stories.

Earlier, Atlético Madrid announced the creation of its football academy at the Akbulak Olympic Center in the Almaty Region. The project aims to introduce the Spanish club’s training methodology while improving the qualifications of Kazakh coaches and developing young players capable of competing at the highest international level.

Institutionally, Kazakhstan also reached an important milestone when the Kazakhstan Football Federation’s national academy became only the ninth association in the world and the second UEFA member to receive official FIFA Talent Academy recognition. The designation confirms that the country’s youth development system meets international standards and places Kazakhstan among a small group of national federations participating in FIFA’s global talent development initiative.

From exporting talent to building pathways

The growing interest from international clubs coincides with increased visibility of Kazakh football talent abroad. Earlier this year, teenage player Dastan Satpayev completed a record transfer to Chelsea, becoming one of the country’s most promising young exports.

Kazakhstan’s domestic football also enjoyed a breakthrough season. FC Kairat became the first Kazakh club to qualify for the UEFA Champions League group stage after eliminating Scotland’s Celtic FC in a dramatic penalty shootout in Almaty.

The club was later ranked among the world’s top 500 football clubs by the International Federation of Football History and Statistics (IFFHS), becoming the only Kazakh representative on the list.

Another milestone came when goalkeeper Anarbekov became the first Kazakh footballer to be named UEFA Champions League Player of the Match following his performance against Olympiacos. UEFA awarded him a 9.2 rating, while two of his saves were selected among the competition’s best moments of the round.
