World.title: Donald Trump, ‘Toxic Bob’ and the $3.1b patch of dirt near Dubbo
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMining Donald Trump, ‘Toxic Bob’ and the $3.1b patch of dirt near Dubbo Simon Johanson August 10, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A billionaire American mining financier, once known as “Toxic Bob” because of his environmental record, is nearly $124 million richer after US President Donald Trump backed a little-known Australian mining explorer with a $560 million loan. The paper wealth of the colourful and wealthy American-Canadian mining identity Robert Friedland soared $124.5 million over a 1½-hour period on Australia’s stock exchange on Monday morning after Australian mining company Sunrise Energy Metals revealed details of the US government’s support for its Syerston Scandium Project in NSW. US President Donald Trump (second left) speaks at an event at the weekend with Robert Friedland (second right). Bloomberg via Getty Images Sunrise shares jumped 19 per cent, from $15.93 to peak at $19.63 before midday, increasing the value of Friedman’s holding to $660.63 million. The stock ended trading at $18.49, up 16 per cent, giving the company a market capitalisation around $3.1 billion. That is a useful paper increase for Friedland, who built his estimated $US3.2 billion ($4.5 billion) fortune through helping to develop mines such as Rio Tinto’s gigantic Oyu Tolgoi copper field in Mongolia.



Friedland and Sunrise chief executive Sam Riggall were at a televised roundtable with Trump and numerous other mining executives at the US State Department on Friday when the president announced the Pentagon’s support of the miner’s venture, which the White House described as “the world’s first primary scandium mine”. “Mr President, this is a truly historic occasion to bring America back to the leadership of mining,” Friedman said at the event. “We’re going to use Yankee ingenuity to prove that we can dominate the supply chain again, rather than have that used by other nations against us.” Friedland is the chairman and biggest investor in Sunrise, joining the board in 2016. The billionaire founded a company called Ivanhoe Mines, which owns major copper mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Ivanhoe Capital, a Singapore-based investment firm with large holdings in Sunrise.



He reportedly was friends with Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, spending time with Jobs at Reed College in Oregon and on an apple farm owned by Friedland’s uncle that gave some inspiration for the name of the tech entrepreneur’s company, Apple Inc. Related Article Critical minerals Pentagon ploughs $560 million into ‘world-first’ Australian mining project Friedland’s early foray into mining was marred by scandal, earning him the “toxic” moniker. A US mine owned by the company of which he was chief executive leached sodium cyanide into a nearby river system, killing fish for miles downstream and requiring millions of dollars to clean up. Some profiles of Friedland contrast the episode with his reputed role as the MC of the famous countercultural festival Woodstock, but that appears to have been born of confusion. Friedland had served on a charitable board with a hippie activist known as Wavy Gravy, who was the MC at the festival. America, and other Western countries, are urgently diversifying their supply chains for rare earths to circumvent China’s stranglehold on many of the rare minerals that are key to critical defence technologies, electric vehicles and the clean energy transition.



Sunrise’s as-yet-unexploited patch of dirt near Fifield, south-west of Dubbo, contains one of the world’s largest and highest grade deposits of scandium, a rare metal largely produced by China, Russia and Ukraine, which is primarily used to strengthen the lightweight alloys used in high-performing fighter jets. “The project hosts one of the largest and highest grade mineable scandium deposits within the Five Eyes jurisdiction and is being advanced as scalable, long-life and low-cost source of primary scandium outside [of] China,” the company said. The US Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital committed $US400 million ($560 million) in conditional loans to help develop the project. World.title: The official David Crisafulli calls direct (just don’t say he bypasses Dale Last)
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: the Fraine Train, emerging external recruitment allergies, Core bargaining heats up, and more tea on 1WS coffee. David Crisafulli has been busy courting public servants since ascending to the premiership in a bid to shut down Labor’s supposed scare campaign warning of Newman-like mass sackings. But beyond his own department chief Damian Walker, there’s another bureaucrat the premier has a close working relationship with – Natural Resources and Mines director-general Graham Fraine. Queensland Natural Resources Minister Dale Last, Premier David Crisafulli, and Last’s department director-general Graham Fraine. File / Supplied Circus whisperers, who spoke anonymously to discuss internal matters, said Crisafulli is known to call Fraine directly when it comes to the resources and mines portfolio.



Some experienced government staffers said it was unusual for a premier to speak with a DG directly rather than going through the minister, who in this instance is Dale Last. However, multiple contacts said they weren’t surprised, given Fraine is widely viewed as an effective operator. Public servants and former government insiders have dubbed him as a Mr Fixit, though current colleagues have said “Ideas Man” is perhaps more apt. Circus likes the ring of “Fraine Train”, and our analysis of cabinet diaries outlines the significance of his role. Fraine appears in Crisafulli diary entries three times without Last. The full trio have clocked up 12 formal entries together. A spinner for the Premier denied Crisafulli bypasses Last. Their only attributable response to questions was: “Labor’s siloed way of working is why we ended up in so many crises; we are absolutely all working together to deliver better outcomes for Queenslanders.”



But the reliance on the experienced Fraine comes at a pivotal time for Crisafulli – and Last – who are aiming to kick-start the critical minerals mining and production industry, which will be a focus of trade talks when the Premier travels to the US later this month. Related Article Critical minerals The Nordic country’s pitch to Queensland for multibillion-dollar industry And what of Fraine’s meeting with Dave Davies from Gina Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting and Last’s chief of staff Ally Foley back in December, discovered during our recent diary crunching efforts? The department regularly engages with stakeholders in its role helping the sector, a spokesperson said. Given this often involves commercially confidential matters, they declined to say more. An allergy to listing top roles? Mackie appears to make it two from two



Friday delivered news of maybe the worst-kept secret since State Development chief John Sosso’s departure – the appointment of Public Sector Commissioner David Mackie as his successor, again. Another recurring element, just one month after Sosso’s move was made public? This government’s apparent newfound allergy to independent external recruitment for directors-general. Under directives for the recruitment and selection of these roles, Premier David Crisafulli is responsible for deciding the process, including whether a competitive advertised approach is taken. Queensland Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie and Public Sector Commissioner David Mackie at the latter’s wedding in April, in which Bleijie acted as a celebrant in a “private capacity”. Facebook / Jarrod Bleijie This is despite the landmark 1989 Fitzgerald Inquiry report suggesting all director-general appointments be conducted through an external, transparent, merit-based recruitment process.



A number of initial post-election appointments were, as was that of Local Government Department boss Bronwyn Blagoev after the departure of predecessor Linda Dobe. Related Article Public service Misdirected or misleading? Health boss in hot water over estimates show But, with Michael Drane’s permanent elevation at Youth Justice in July, Mackie’s sideways shift seems to make it two from two recent department head hirings to not have involved a wider search. From August 17, Mackie will lead the major department driving infrastructure projects and economic development under Deputy Premier (and his wedding celebrant) Jarrod Bleijie. And despite suggestions from some of our columnist comrades, word reaching the Circus tent – along with annual report crunching – says there’ll be no skin off his $700,000-plus salary.



We’re certainly not suggesting Mackie (or Drane) are not suitable. But without hearing from a wider range of applicants, who knows if they’re the best. We sent questions to Crisafulli’s office and have heard only crickets about the process taken – but we’ve seen no evidence it was externally recruited. At estimates hearings last month, Mackie said direct appointments allowed consideration of “whether or not it would be wasteful to go to market”. During that same line of questioning, Crisafulli said they could save tens of thousands of dollars – “a lot of money”. All eyes now are on the recruitment of a permanent police commissioner, and the now acting heads of the Public Sector Commission, Queensland Corrective Services, and Customer Services. State and union Core Agreement talks approaching the pointy end



Among the remaining workplace deals still being wrangled by the Crisafulli government, the State Government Entities Certified Agreement is a big one. It’s politically sensitive, with 13 unions at the table, representing a large proportion of the public sector workforce. Hence, the “Core Agreement” label. Another factor likely to complicate Core Agreement talks for the workplace deal covering a vast array of public servants across the state: the looming State Wage Case. Matt Dennien Circus has been keenly awaiting any hints of things heating up, which emerged in the form of a brief July 31 update posted online. In its telling, after 15 central meetings and 40 entity-specific ones, the government floated an offer on June 30 “to achieve early resolution” and replace the deal set to expire that day.



“On 31 July 2026, Together Queensland, Industrial Union of Employees, advised it did not accept the fair and reasonable Offer Government made to unions,” the update read. “As a result, the Offer has now lapsed and negotiations will continue.” Also lapsing, according to the government, is the offer of backpay to July 1. Circus has sung out to Together for their side of things, but is aware of another factor likely to complicate things: the State Wage Case which sets minimum wage and award rates a number of collective agreements can’t drop below. With some of those already overtaking or nipping at the heels of workplace deals, the QCU and Together are again chasing a repeat of the federal Fair Work Commission’s 4.75 per cent June lift to awards it oversees, to apply from September 1. The state is trying to inject as much context into the case as it can, to ensure the “fair and reasonable” increase is a little closer to the up-to-3.5 per cent year-one lift in its wages policy.



In one affidavit filed for the state, Office of Industrial Relations executive director Shane Donovan said while a 4.75 per cent lift to awards would directly benefit the less than 2000 workers reliant on awards or the minimum wage, it would also indirectly boost pay for those in up to 29 of the state’s collective agreements – including six in arbitration. In another, deputy under-treasurer Matt Bonaventura put the cost of any such lift at about $93 million in the 2026-27 financial year. Bonaventura warned this could lead to further cost implications through next year’s boost to awards then applying to a higher base, and used boilerplate talk copied from last year about the pressure such wage increases place on government service delivery and fiscal objectives. There was also a nod to the precarious position of the state’s credit rating. Circus wonders if the curtain of secrecy drawn over an uncertain $6.8 billion in planned savings might play more of a role in that than a slight ripple in the $40 billion wages bill. New coffee machines landing, but 1WS tea supply answers still in the mail



Brewing news last week about the lack of tea stock in the Tower of Power, perhaps unsurprisingly, has seen many more Circus folk come forward to spill the proverbial hot beverage. By all accounts, it’s been a masterclass in muddled messaging from all involved – but we’ve used our powers for good to try to get to the bottom and read the leaves on what’s really going on here. Electronic payment options? In 2026? After fielding an image of one laminated sign warning of the removal of tea, milk and sweeteners from all 1 William Street kitchens as of August 1, we’ve now also seen one all-staff departmental email saying similar. Both informed readers they would need to supply their own from here on, and sheeted blamed for the decision on the building – not the department.



This had all been explained as related to a changing of the automatic coffee machine guards from the old coin-operated fleet whose funds fed the supplies, to new ones with electronic payments enabled. Technology! (One director-general even told staff last week not to panic and pointed them to the sole remaining relic on level 40. Luckily, we hear, a stampede did not ensue.) Well, Circus has now seen photographic evidence of the fancy new machines installed, along with signs seemingly from 1WS building management thanking people for their patience. We’ve also dropped them a line to see if they can’t shed more light on the situation – and had to push back when we were pointed to the Right to Information website. Best put the kettle on. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.title: The art of the deal: Victoria to pay millions more than host cities overseas to bring NFL to Melbourne
World.content:
Exclusive SportNFLCity life The art of the deal: Victoria to pay millions more than host cities overseas to bring NFL to Melbourne Bridget McArthur August 10, 2026 — 8:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victorians could pay up to 11 times more than other international host cities to bring American football to Melbourne next month after beating NSW and Western Australia for the sporting privilege. The state government announced in February last year that it had secured the first ever in-season NFL game, signing a “two-plus-one” multi-year contract – two confirmed games over four years, with the possibility of a third. Sports Minister Steve Dimopoulos has called the deal “one of the biggest returns on investments Victoria has ever seen”. However, figures obtained by this masthead suggest Victoria is expected to pay between $10 million and $15 million per NFL game, substantially higher figures than what was paid for matches to be held in Germany and Brazil. Berlin paid about $7.4 million per NFL game, with the first taking place late last year. Getty Images Speaking in parliament earlier this year, shadow industry minister Richard Welch put the cost at $15 million a game – a figure that aligns with what the NSW government said the NFL put to it, according to a source familiar with negotiations who spoke to The Australian Financial Review last year – which would see the state spend $45 million in a three-game scenario.



The government has not confirmed or denied this figure, but comments made by Dimopoulos in a recent podcast interview indicate it is in the ballpark. Referencing the commercial benefits of the deal, he told the Armchair Experts podcast last month: “If you were to buy that advertising on digital and media right across the world, [it would be] over $32 million. Now that’s well and truly a great head start to our investment”. Related Article Exclusive

NFL 2026 ‘Here to stay’: The numbers behind the NFL’s major Australian gamble If $32 million is a great head start to covering Victoria’s investment, the total amount spent is likely to be higher. However, if one assumes that figure as an absolute minimum, and divides it by three games – though only two are currently assured – Victoria must be paying at least $10.6 million per game. When this masthead contacted Dimopoulos to confirm these figures, a spokesperson said all financial details were commercial in confidence and could not be discussed. By comparison, the German city of Frankfurt paid just $1.3 million a game, while Berlin paid $7.4 million, and Sao Paolo in Brazil paid $7.5 million. The only overseas host to pay more than Victoria was Ireland, which paid $17.8 million for a single game in Dublin.



A spokesperson for Berlin’s department of sport said it estimated the NFL was contributing about €48 million ($78.5 million) of its own money to take the games to Germany. The department spokesperson and a spokesperson for the Frankfurt mayor’s office said no additional financing for the events had been provided by the German federal government to either city. Sao Paulo’s municipal government was contacted for comment. In Ireland, a government spokesperson confirmed it had approved an allocation of up to €9.95 million ($AU17.8 million) to host a single game in Dublin last year, and said the investment had covered the licence fee, infrastructure works, security, transport services, city-activation events and a once-off contribution to venue-related costs. When this masthead put the public spending estimates to the NFL and asked why Victoria is set to pay significantly more per game than other international host cities, a spokesperson for the league did not dispute the figures, saying only it did not comment on financial matters. “The NFL has a growing presence in Australia and is committed to investing in the development of the game year-round,” the spokesperson said. “Through grassroots participation including our national flag football program, youth development, strategic partnerships, and now the historic first-ever regular-season NFL game being played at the MCG this September, Australia represents a key market in the league’s global expansion plans.”



There is no doubt there is significant appetite for the game to come to Melbourne, with 100,000 fans expected to turn out to watch the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers at the MCG. Related Article NFL 2026 On one of the AFL’s biggest weekends, 10,000 US fans will paint Melbourne red When the game was first announced, more than 151,000 people registered interest, and the first tranche of tickets sold out in less than half an hour. All four foreign hosts said the economic benefits of hosting the games far eclipsed the amount they had spent on them, with net profits estimated to be between $90 million and $190 million per game. While that will likely be the case in Victoria, the higher government input could reduce the expected return on investment.



Germany and Brazil have more-proven NFL markets. However expanding the sport to new markets is a key tenet of the league’s long-term strategy, and Australia has long been in its purview. NSW had previously been considered the most likely candidate to host the NFL’s Australian debut due to its sizeable fan base and ties to current players, such as former Rabbitoh-turned-Philadelphia Eagle Jordan Mailata. It was also the only state to have hosted an exhibition game in 1999, and was later assessed to host another pre-season match-up, according to the NFL’s former executive vice president of international Mark Waller, though plans were ultimately dropped. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell (middle right) commended then premier Jacinta Allan (left) for convincing him to hold Australia’s first in-season NFL game in Melbourne. Simon Schluter The NFL visited sites in 2024 and met representatives across various states, with NSW, Victoria and WA on the ultimate shortlist. States were given about three months to put together a proposal that covered hosting rights, investments, value-in-kind contributions, venue hire, and stadium operations. In October of that year, representatives from each state flew to London for a meeting to discuss their respective bids. When Victoria was confirmed as the winning host city, NSW Premier Chris Minns described the NFL’s asking price as “a king’s ransom”.



“We said no, it was just too expensive,” Minns said. “I’ve got a lot of pull on the government dollar – I didn’t have enough for the NFL game. I can only speak to my government’s priorities and where we spend your money, your tax money. We have to spend it wisely.” Dimopoulos has on multiple occasions said then-premier Jacinta Allan was eager to secure the deal, while NFL commissioner Roger Goodell commended her for having “the vision and the strength and the leadership to convince us this was the right place to play” – suggesting Victoria was chasing the league, not the other way around. A mural of an American footballer in Sao Paulo, Brazil, which has hosted two in-season NFL games to date. Getty Images Speaking in Melbourne this year, Goodell said the money offered was not as important as Victoria’s strong record in major events. “This community knows how to do big events,” he said in April. “They’re pros, and we felt very comfortable that they were going to deliver not just what they said but everything that was necessary to make this event successful.”



Goodell also cited the size and “tremendous reputation” of the MCG as another key factor in choosing Melbourne. Mark Waller, who laid the groundwork for the NFL’s international expansion, said Melbourne’s wider infrastructure – including public transport, accommodation and the proximity of the stadium to the CBD – was also likely to have played a part. It is a massive, tightly run logistical exercise for all involved. A local security company, which did not wish to be named due to the sensitivity of corporate dealings with the NFL, said the league was bringing over its own security detail – although the Victorian government said there would still be security jobs created here. On game day, fans will be required to bring their belongings in clear bags – per NFL policy in the US. Local company HG Turf will be under the pump to get the pitch set up and packed away between AFL games, with a final potentially on the cards for the MCG the following day. In a statement provided on Monday, a spokesperson for the sports minister’s office said the NFL partnership had been transformational for Victoria, and a rise in visits by Americans and hotel bookings had already been recorded.



“The September game will be beamed live to millions of US viewers during prime time, delivering significant economic returns through the $239 million American visitors spend annually in Victoria and attracting record interest from international fans and business leaders,” the spokesperson said. “Our multi-year NFL partnership is cementing Victoria’s status as Australia’s major events capital, with Delta Airlines now offering three new direct flights per week from Los Angeles, creating year-round tourism growth and business opportunities. The LA Rams will play the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne in September. Getty Images “This multi-year partnership is creating hundreds of jobs across Victoria – from security and hospitality to transport co-ordination and event management. The vast majority of staff delivering the game and surrounding fan activities will be local workers contracted by the MCG and MOPT [Melbourne and Olympic Parks Trust], supporting Victorian jobs and businesses throughout the event.” The NFL’s media team has been restricted in its communications. An interview previously organised between this masthead and the NFL’s Asia-Pacific head, Brett Gosper, was cancelled after questions were put to the league. A reason for the cancellation was not provided.



A lot is on the line for the American sports giant. If it can grow a loyal fan base in Australia, it will unlock significant potential earnings from media broadcast rights, sponsorships and merchandise deals. It is also seeking to grow flag football, handing out kits to every school in Victoria, as it looks to cement the non-contact sport on the global stage, including ensuring it remains in the 2032 Brisbane Olympics after its debut in the 2028 LA Games. World.title: ‘I felt a little bit of impostor syndrome’: How a sandwich guy claimed the MasterChef title
World.content:
Melbourne nurse Vinnie Gibaldi says it was his day job that helped him handle the pressure of the MasterChef Australia kitchen.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Sunday night, Vinnie Gibaldi was crowned the winner of MasterChef Australia’s 18th season. The 25-year-old transplant nurse from Melbourne beat Petro Papathomas in an intense two-round cook-off that included a mystery box challenge and then a five-hour Chinese Afternoon Tea pressure test set by world-renowned pastry chef Cherish Finden. He tells national TV editor Louise Rugendyke how he made the move from “sandwich guy” to champ, being a hit in the hospital and the meaning behind his necklace. Congratulations, Vinnie! How are you feeling? Pretty good, pretty, pretty good. I’m very grateful, and I’m just so appreciative of everyone. I don’t really have that many words because I’m still lost for words at the moment. Winner Vinnie (centre) and judges (from left) Poh, Andy, Jean-Christophe and Sofia. Ten How long ago did you film the final? How long have you been hanging on to this for? We filmed the final in May. I was in a bit of a limbo for a while. I know how I cooked, but you don’t see what happens at the other bench, and you don’t see the tastings. I got a call yesterday [Sunday] morning from the producers, and that was when I found out. So I only had to hold on to it for a little bit of time, but it was nerve-wracking just trying to wrap my head around everything. How did you feel last night when you got to see everyone’s reactions to your dishes in the pressure test? Cherish was pretty happy.



Related Article Exit Interview

Australian TV ‘Hate on my colleagues’: The brutal feedback Race Around the World contestants faced It was crazy because when that dish [Chinese Afternoon Tea] was revealed, I was like, “Oh no, this is the end for me.” Not only were they desserts, but they were also this big [makes tiny shape with fingers], and these hands aren’t really meant for things like that. So I was pretty scared. But hearing that feedback was really, really nice. All that work that I’d been doing, and all that time, and all that practice led up to this, and it was awesome to do everyone proud, including Cherish. I know you were nervous, but my theory with you and fellow contestant Annabel Lloyd is that you both have nursing backgrounds, which means you’re able to follow processes and not get flustered. Am I right – did nursing help? One hundred per cent. I feel like that’s me, but it’s also nursing, and I feel like those type of people go into nursing as well. So it’s hand-in-hand. But it’s definitely staying calm under pressure when something goes wrong, instead of hyper-fixating on it, just being able to brush it off was definitely a skill that I feel like came from nursing, and it was very, very helpful to me. Vinnie Gibaldi with judge Jean-Christophe Novelli and Cherish Finden during the MasterChef Australia final. Do you get flustered over anything? To be honest, not really. I’m usually quite calm. I feel like there’s never a time where you should dwell. I’ve been like that in general, just as a person, but especially at work. When something’s going wrong, you can either focus on it or you can just get it done.



In that final pressure test, did you notice how much Petro was struggling? He was getting quite emotional. Honestly, that cook was a blur to me. Being over five hours, but it felt like 45 minutes. Everyone was yelling, but it was just muffled. I was really locked in and focused. But after the cook, I could see he was pretty emotional, and you don’t want to see that. He’s still my mate. I never once thought that we were competing against each other. I thought it was always us cooking together, so that was sad for me as well. MasterChef Australia finalist runner-up Petro Papathomas. This year’s group seemed really collegiate. Was that the experience you thought it would be? What was a surprise was the fact that other years haven’t been like this. Talking to the judges, they were like, “You guys are really close, and you seem like genuine friends”, and we’re like, “Yeah, is that not normal?” I’ve met like a lot of people on that show who have become my friends for life, which is pretty special. I thought it was weird that that wasn’t the case for other seasons. At the beginning, you were “the sandwich guy”. Did you feel like that let you fly under the radar, even though you got the apron right at the beginning?



I felt a little bit of impostor syndrome. I’m not discrediting my audition dish because I did make every single element, but then I was looking at what everyone else did, and what everyone else would cook. I’m like: “Well, I don’t know how to do that”, or “I don’t know these fancy words”. I was very much a rustic Italian home cook. I felt a little bit out of my depth, but that just made me practise more and work harder to get up to scratch and do my absolute best every single day. Related Article ★★★★

Review What to stream this week: Netflix’s new take on an Australian classic, plus five more picks I did notice in the grand final episode you said, after the Josh Niland cook, you bought a whole lot flathead so you could practise filleting and deboning. Is that what it was like every single night? You just finish the cook, go home and keep cooking. Every time I had a cook, and I didn’t do too well, I would listen to what the judge’s feedback was as gospel, and I would go home and improve, and would work and work and work, and I would practise anything. So, for example, Josh Niland, I remember going to the Vic Market, and I was like, “I need to get up to scratch with this” because this is a really good tool to have in my arsenal, and it proved well [Vinnie won the first round of the final cook with his grilled flathead]. But, yeah, everyone did go home afterwards and would practise, and you’re always in each other’s room tasting something: “Oh, what do you reckon of this? What do you reckon of that?” MasterChef Australia winner Vinnie Gibaldi said all of the contestants were quite close. In our house, we all have a crush on Jean-Christophe Novelli. He has no poker face. You always know when he likes something.



John-Christophe is the loveliest man ever. Off camera, you don’t see a lot of it [on TV], but he is so lovely and caring and just a genuinely nice person. We would always look at him [during judging] because he would always let it loose. I don’t want to get too political here, but when I watch MasterChef Australia, I think of comments from Pauline Hanson, where she says she wants a monoculture. For me, MasterChef is just the best example of what being a multicultural country is all about. Your family is from Italy, Petro’s family is from Greece and so many of the other contestants had such a variety of backgrounds. It’s pretty awesome that we live in a country that’s so multicultural, and there’s so many different cultures here, and they all bring something new. When I was brought up, my grandparents would tell me stories of when they came to Australia and the food that they brought. And I feel like now it’s even changing again, and I feel like we’re very, very lucky to have this food scene here, especially in Melbourne, that’s so different, and you can go out and have cuisines from around the world, and they’re all top-notch. There’s a lot of places you go, you don’t get that. Vinnie with his good luck Sicilian corno necklace. Can I ask about your necklace – is it a red chilli? It’s a Sicilian thing. They call it a corno, which is like a horn. It’s like the evil eye in Greek culture, and it’s meant to bring protection and good luck. Well, it worked!

World.title: The 44-year-old working mother soon to lead the union movement
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceAustralian Council of Trade Unions The 44-year-old working mother soon to lead the union movement Millie Muroi August 10, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melissa Donnelly, the new face of the country’s peak body for unions, has pledged to tackle cost of living while pushing for greater workplace flexibility, but says she will not support an unlimited right for every employee to work from home. On Monday afternoon, the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) executive appointed Donnelly as its secretary-elect, replacing Sally McManus who will step down on August 30 after a decade of leading the union movement. Melissa Donnelly with her children Ellie, 11, and George, 8. Peter Rae Sydney-based Donnelly, who has been the national secretary of the Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) for seven years, said in an interview with this masthead that her sights would be firmly set on ensuring wage growth kept up with inflation, but was more ambiguous on the recent scandals affecting the union movement. “I know that workers, every time they go to Coles and Woolworths, [are finding] it costs more,” she said. “People are making decisions about whether their kids can go to an excursion or not, or when they get the new school shoes.”



But Donnelly would not go into detail on how she would handle some of the biggest challenges facing the movement including one of the biggest unions, the CFMEU, being put into administration following corruption scandals. Nor would she be drawn on the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) finding that United Firefighters Union secretary Peter Marshall had engaged in threatening and backroom misconduct. Related Article Analysis

Political leadership Sally McManus shook up the union movement. The question now is what she leaves behind Asked whether the union would cooperate with the Victorian Royal Commission into the CFMEU, and her views on the IBAC findings, Donnelly said she was not yet across the detail but that the union movement had “zero tolerance” for corruption and violence. “That’s not going to change under my leadership,” she said. “Construction workers deserve a strong and clean union ... and there’s more work to do. The administration is working towards those goals, but we need to ensure that the construction industry as a whole is free of corruption and violence as well.” Professionally, Donnelly said her job was to “continue to address the real cost of living pressures that working people are facing every day”.



The OECD last month noted that Australians’ real wages have fallen by 5 per cent since early 2021, meaning price growth has outpaced pay rises over that time. Donnelly, whose tenure begins on August 31, was the only person nominated for the secretary role and will be, at 44, one of the youngest secretaries of the council. Former ACTU leader Bill Kelty was 35 when he was appointed secretary in 1983. McManus said Donnelly had strong, overwhelming support across all unions and represented “generational change” for the peak body. “The average union member is a 44-year old working mother and so is Melissa,” McManus said. “She’s a year younger than I was when I took up the office. With two school aged children and having led a large union she well knows the pressures working people are under.” Donnelly is also a member of the Labor Party, representing the Left faction on its national executive.



Asked how often she speaks with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Donnelly said she had a “range of dealings” with the government and government ministers and that conversations had generally been respectful. Related Article Building Bad Labor, the CFMEU and a $109b question Victorians want answered During her time at the CPSU, Donnelly has overseen the reversal of the outsourcing of government advice and services to big consultancy firms, secured work from home rights and delivered eight weeks paid parental leave for both parents, according to the ACTU. While Donnelly said flexible work would continue to be a priority for the union movement, she said there was not a “single answer” on workplace flexibility. “What we achieved in the federal public service is not an unlimited right for every worker to work from home whenever they want,” she said. “There is a clear process and clear rights around how that can be requested, and what works for one worker, or for one workplace or industry, is going to be different. That’s why it’s really important we have a raft of options that allow employees flexibility.”



Figures from the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner showed one in five employees at some federal government agencies worked remotely full-time in 2024 despite research broadly suggesting such practice can lead to worse mental health and worse productivity outcomes. McManus warned last month that the new secretary would have to tackle issues such as the rise of One Nation and the far right, AI and billionaire influence in politics, along with the decades-long decline in union leadership. The share of Australians holding union membership has fallen dramatically since the 1970s with only a small uptick in 2024, although the CPSU’s membership numbers have grown by 23 per cent over Donnelly’s tenure, in part reflecting an expansion in the public service. World.title: Bias-free academia a nice idea, but mostly just that
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Bias-free academia a nice idea, but mostly just that August 10, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Vintage Cathy Wilcox To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. CULTURE WARS Re ‴⁣⁣Philanthropy is not neutral’: Debate swirls at university over controversial $35m scholarship program″⁣, 9/8.

Your correspondents (Letters, 10/8) in response make persuasive arguments for accepting scholarship money from conservative bodies like the Ramsay Centre for Western Civilisation. They may not be as open-minded about money from Marxist or Islamic foundations. Or those from Russia or China.

It’s easy to espouse academic liberty in the context of bodies that align with one’s own views. The very concerns about Ramsay are its processes to influence academic liberty.

It was only later in life I realised how cleverly bias was inserted into much of my university studies decades ago. Bias-free academia is a great idea but mostly just that. Ideally, our universities would only accept scholarship money with no strings attached. This rarely happens because the money is usually intended to buy influence.

Mark Freeman, Macleod Beware Trojan horses bearing money

Your correspondent (Letters, 10/8) states that rejecting $35 million in scholarships from the Ramsay Centre is a lost opportunity for Melbourne University.

So, if another “philanthropist” were to offer Melbourne University to create a course that climate change is “crap” (as Tony Abbott once declared), or that renewable power was a waste of money, then they should accept it?

Trojan horses have not fared well in history.

Alan Inchley, Frankston



Risk of inculcating a partisan political agenda

Your correspondent, (Letters, 10/8), is correct in warning against the ‘ideological paradigm’ inherent in the ‘Ramsay Centre for Western Civilisation’ putative scholarship program overseen by the University of Melbourne.

This tendentious proposal relates directly to the Anglosphere agenda promoted in recent years by Tony Abbott, which has seen him taking up quasi-academic roles in both the UK and Hungary.

As pointed out in Sean Kelly’s article, (″⁣How political enemies help Hanson″⁣, 10/8), our ex-PM has directly supported the recently defeated Hungarian PM, Viktor Orban, in stridently warning of migrants swarming Europe and perpetrating ultra-conservative populist population theories around immigration.

Interestingly here, in relation to the Ramsay Centre course proposal, Orban has long framed his arguments in the context of Western Christianity being threatened by Muslim invaders in the historic Crusader campaigns.

Universities of repute should indeed be wary of teaching cultural courses which, effectively, are inculcating a partisan political agenda.

Jon McMillan, Mornington Academic freedom without fear or favour

That the University of Melbourne Academic Board has voted against funds for student scholarships from the Liberal-linked Ramsay Centre, a centre dedicated to “western culture” is consistent with the principles of academic freedom.

Money can buy most things, including political votes and influence, as we have clearly seen in international and local politics. But it should not be used to fund the dissemination of a particular ideology in an academic setting.

As universities become more like corporate entities, they face more internal and external influences that can undermine freedom of expression.

A core value of universities is to preserve, defend and promote academic freedom. This includes engagement in critical enquiry and public discourse without fear or favour.

The University of Melbourne Academic Board is acting consistently with these principles in questioning funding linked to an organisation dedicated to “western culture”.

Leigh Ackland, Deepdene THE FORUM Plan for people

Re ″⁣7 million litres of diesel just 250m from homes: The data centre plan locals didn’t know about″⁣ (10/8): Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny should know that we need to grow human intelligence over artificial intelligence.

Plan for people and their real lives rather than the massive data centre proposed in Campbellfield by Singaporean-backed developer Zerra DC. This is such a drain on a fragile environment and an imposition on the neighbourhood. Kilkenny should not let it proceed.

Quality and dignity of human life must be paramount over company profits. Otherwise, the human race will be dominated by digital, soulless technology, and the environment trashed.

Julia Donnelly, Surrey Hills FOMO foolishness

We are now told that we must allow more resource gobbling data centres to be built in Melbourne, or risk “missing out”. What we will “miss out” on is never clearly articulated – job losses, excessive water consumption, spreadsheets with pictures, the ability to hack into unprepared internet sites? And what else?

FOMO (fear of missing out) is the latest way of persuading the naive to spend their money and other scarce resources. The billionaire captains of industry have perfected the art of exploiting FOMO.

AI didn’t exist three years ago for most of us, and there’s no indication so far that there is any great benefit to general society.

What benefits does Melbourne gain by having more data centres? To date, all the benefits have been flowing back into the AI industry and into the very large pockets of the wealthy.

Bruce Bowden, Preston



Enact Murphy report

Re “Albanese, Taylor hedge their bets on gambling reform deal” (10/8): According to an Australia Institute poll in May, more than three in four Australians support a ban on gambling advertising — including 81 per cent of Labor,

78 per cent of Coalition and 66 per cent of One Nation voters.

Surely, the government has more than enough political cover to withstand the wrath of the gambling lobby and implement the Murphy report’s bipartisan recommendations for a comprehensive ban.

Brian Marshall, Ashburton Nanny status

Nannies are lovely people and care for us, so why on earth is Anthony Albanese so afraid about taking tough action on gambling reforms, fearing One Nation gibes about a ″⁣nanny state″⁣?

Peta Colebatch, Hawthorn Global and local

″⁣We’d rather chuck another prawn on the barbie,″⁣ writes your correspondent (Letters, 10/8) capturing the spirit of global inaction admirably while environmental and social disaster unfolds – pollution, climate, disease, overpopulation, migrations, crime and violence through to habitat loss and

species extinction.

And on our doorstep, as an excuse to inflict Box Hill high-rise on the eastern suburbs, we have the Suburban Rail Loop: Two 26-kilometre tunnels of seven metres diameter yielding in excess of 2 million cubic metres of excavation needing to be dumped.

The energy required to undertake such tunnelling and the diesel fuel, air pollution and disruption of transporting spoil off site is an abomination.

The Greens, teals and independents’ silence astonishes, given the SRL’s 1.6-kilometre ″⁣exclusion zones″⁣ have removed residents and councils from planning realms to allow a concrete heat island stretching to Cheltenham. Is the ″⁣voice″⁣ of last resort Pauline Hanson?

Ronald Elliott, Sandringham Ticked off

I would like to help your correspondent (Letters, 10/8) who is concerned about the misuse of the terms “uptick” and “going forward”.

We give a tick to something that is correct or good. Thus, to describe the increase in something that is undesirable as an uptick gives two faux pas for the price of one. This is not to be sniffed at.

Many speakers tack a redundant “going forward” to the end of a sentence when they have run out of anything useful to say but wish to seem both “with it” and authoritative.

To be fair, they may be concerned for the understanding of any science fiction fans, and so they are making it clear they are not expecting to be time-travelling backwards.

Alister McKenzie, Lake Wendouree Not just semantics

I sympathise with correspondents (Letters, 10/8) who complain about degradation of the English language. For much of my 60 years in journalism, I was a sub-editor – one of a long line of dedicated grumps that once comprised the ″⁣sub-conscience″⁣ of newspapers.

My excellent Scottish education taught me about parsing, tautology, gerunds, semantics, non-sequiturs, etc. I also learned a lot on the job.

At times, it felt as though I were the doctor in The Plague, the allegorical novel by Albert Camus. Each day, the good doctor chooses to battle an epidemic that seems unstoppable because resistance is what makes life meaningful.

These days, I just relax in my regional village, drinking coffee, listening to jazz and polishing

my musical skills.

Ken Turnbull, Maldon



Melbourne so fine

I was sorry to read that your correspondent (Letters, 10/8) does not feel safe in Melbourne. I am 80, and I, too, visit Melbourne on a regular basis to go to the theatre, and I stay in hotel.

I have never felt unsafe walking around the CBD or catching trams, although I’m always vigilant and don’t go out too late at night.

He is missing so much. I wonder whether he has had a bad experience in the city or whether he is just overwhelmed by what he sees in the media? Come on in ... the water’s fine!

Mary Lyon, Camperdown Criminal behaviour

Australia’s new anti-money-laundering laws are expected to deter criminals from using their ill-gotten gains to buy real estate, “particularly in higher-value or more complex transactions” (“What happens when crime stops paying for real estate”, 10/8).

It follows then, in the absence of other alternatives, that cashed-up criminals laundering money will probably gravitate to lower-value, simpler real estate transactions. Those are transactions that are less likely to attract attention.

Crime-based price distortion will thereby shift from the upper, to the lower end of the property market. I don’t know whether to laugh or cry.

Lawrie Bradly, Surrey Hills Doctors’ time

Your article on more doctors bulk-billing their patients is inspiring; however, my doctor still charges an exorbitant fee. While I have been seeing my GP for many years and have been very well cared for, lately I have been advised that I am due for a health check with a nurse before I see my doctor.

This process covers things like mobility, vaccinations and general health. The health checks occur twice a year and are covered by the government.

I then go into the doctor who has a 15-minute window to discuss the health check.

Last time I visited, I had a specific problem that needed to be addressed by the doctor and was told that I needed to make another appointment for that, which would incur a cost.

I am over 70 and healthy, but I am concerned that my doctor’s visits will start to be needed more often as I age. The health checks sound wonderful, but I am confused with how the medical system works, and am wondering if I need to change my doctor.

Julie Ottobre, Brunswick East Fertility also men’s issue

I was surprised The Age named only women in the title of its article on recent IVF success rates (“IVF success rates are rising, but women still face a high-stakes numbers game”, 9/10).

As the article itself made clear, infertility affects men as well. And men (alongside people of all genders) also participate in IVF.

I understand that the title pointed to the decreased success rates for IVF as women’s age increases reported in the new research, but much research and reporting alike in the past decade have thankfully shifted from framing infertility as a “women’s issue” – and women as falling off a fertility cliff – to one faced by anyone who hopes they or a partner will become pregnant, including men.

Sarah Teasley, Thornbury Deduct club’s points

Fines for Geelong Football Club would not deter them with their wealthy backers.

What would really hurt is the English Football League sanctions of deducting match points.

Ask Southampton, who start the upcoming season on minus points following their spying on their opponents training, and also being disqualified from the Championship play-off for entry into the Premier League.

Sheffield Wednesday and Leicester City have also suffered from these point deductions.

Such punishments would act as great future deterrents for any football club.

Roger Revens, Shepparton



Clubs’ hard lessons ahead

Peter Ryan (″⁣Kolodjashnij told me about his ‘tough conversations’. His case reveals much bigger issues″⁣, 10/8) has written a must-read article on the concussion protocols that AFL players and clubs go through.

Rather than trying to pick Geelong off as a serial offender who is cheating their way to success, Ryan has done some work to reveal what clubs go through when a player with a history of concussion, but passed medically fit to play, wants to go on and see out his contract.

Geelong will most likely pay a fine and learn a hard lesson. They will not be the last club to face this difficult position. The next club will most likely just re-negotiate the player’s contract and retire

the player.

Murray Horne, Cressy AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Politicians

There’s no greater example of the addictiveness of having “a punt” than Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor “hedging their bets” (10/8).

Jenny Bone, Surrey Hills “As politicians, we don’t look at them much” was Mark Butler’s comment on Labor tanking in the polls. Really?

James Ogilvie, Kew



Well said to your two correspondents (Letters, 10/8). I don’t recall Jess Wilson saying anything sensible about the climate crisis either.

Greg Curtin, Nunawading I hope we have a refund policy on our AUKUS venture, but I expect not.

John Rome, Mt Lawley, WA Furthermore

I reported a pothole, and Moonee Valley Council fixed it within a week.

Susan Scalise, Ascot Vale Although Dorothea Mackellar wrote, ″⁣I love a sunburnt country″⁣, we might not love it for too much longer, while news footage of London’s sunburnt Hyde Park would have William Blake mourning his ″⁣green and pleasant land″⁣.

David Johnston, Healesville Another mystery: Why does no one ″⁣die″⁣ these days? They all “pass” or “pass on”.

Jacki Burgess, Port Melbourne



The US State Department sees Cuba as an existential threat to democracy because of its links to Russia and China (10/8)? The United States has had its knee on the throat of Cuba for more than

70 years. It is no surprise Cuba looks elsewhere for support.

Peter McGill, Lancefield Air Services Australia attributes the two aircraft near misses within a very short time at Sydney Airport to ″⁣operational challenges″⁣. What does that even mean, if anything at all?

Mick Hussey, Beaconsfield Finally

The Saints should negotiate a final-year payout for Ross Lyon and appoint Corey Enright now.

Peter Walker, Black Rock The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Takaichi will brush off Albanese’s melon joke. She shouldn’t have to
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaWorld politics Takaichi will brush off Albanese’s melon joke. She shouldn’t have to Lisa Visentin August 10, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi knows how to roll with the punches. She is not just a hard-nosed political operative, but a self-made one. With no political pedigree of her own, she has ascended to the top of Japan’s famously dynastic and patriarchal system, which has typically reserved its elite positions for the sons of important men. One can be fairly confident that in the three decades she has spent toiling in Japanese politics, she has brushed off all manner of innuendo that has typically plagued women in pursuit of power. Sanae Takaichi, with Anthony Albanese in May, is not just a hard-nosed political operative, but a self-made one. Alex Ellinghausen Whether he intended to or not, Anthony Albanese has forced her to brush off another one.



“She brought two. As you do,” the Australian prime minister said in a now surely regrettable podcast interview in July, accompanying the remark with an unfortunate cupping gesture. Related Article Political leadership Taylor demands PM apologise for comment about Japanese ‘melons’ He was referring to the expensive crown melons Takaichi gifted him during her visit to Australia in May – a gift he initially called “strange” despite the fact that Japanese fruit is widely regarded as the most elite across Asia. Bush Deep podcast host Nikki Osborne filled in the gaps with a jibe about Takaichi “smuggling” the melons in and looking like Pamela Anderson, which Albanese let sail through to the keeper. This interview, by the way, took place in a sitting room at The Lodge, the prime minister’s official residence in Canberra.



Taken in its broader context, it’s difficult to ignore the optics of the Australian leader disparaging the gift of a close ally in a conversation that clearly conjured links between melons and breasts. Even if Albanese wasn’t the chief conjurer, it was his house, his standards. Incidents like these often become political Rorschach tests, refracted through the endless tedium of culture wars and political point scoring. People tend to side with their political teams about whether this type of thing is a gratuitous beat-up or something befitting an apology. Loading On Monday – a full month after the podcast aired – Opposition Leader Angus Taylor framed it as an act of hypocrisy by a left-leaning prime minister, while Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek rejected the innuendo suggestions and called on people to make up their own minds. To be sure, the Coalition only began clamouring for an apology after former Japanese ambassador Shingo Yamagami denounced Albanese’s remarks as an “insulting joke” that “casually mocked” Takaichi in an editorial in The Australian. Yamagami tied his point to a political one, leveraging it to repeat his semi-regular criticism that Labor has been too meek in the face of China’s aggression, and its bullying of Takaichi.



This incident has received a paucity of coverage in the Japanese press. It’s a silence that Japanese journalist Waka Ikeda noted extended across the country’s political divide. Related Article Opinion

Podcasts It’s possible for the PM to be casual and jocular – and also respect women Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist “The Australian prime minister made a sexual joke about the Japanese prime minister. And in Japan, both right and left, men and women, feminists too, the LDP and the Communist Party – all stayed silent,” she wrote in July. As an arch-conservative who holds traditional views of gender roles, Takaichi is hardly an ally of the feminist movement. She won’t be expecting their support, nor be surprised when it doesn’t materialise. Equally, Japanese officials have declined to publicly weigh in on the issue when approached by the Australian press.



This is not the type of gaffe that will shake the bilateral relationship, but nor should the diplomats’ silence be interpreted as an absence of dismay about the framing of their leader in such a cavalier and jocular way. Multiple things can be true at once. Albanese may not have intended offence. He is a stronger advocate of women’s causes than Takaichi. The issue has been spun through the political wringer. Takaichi will brush it off. She shouldn’t have to. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Sydney council plans to make English compulsory for all shop signs
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life Sydney council plans to make English compulsory for all shop signs Cindy Yin August 10, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney council passed a motion to make English compulsory on business signs in an attempt to foster unity, sparking backlash from critics who say it has overstepped its authority. This is Strathfield Council’s second attempt to regulate shop signage – the idea was first floated at a council meeting eight years ago but attracted significant public resistance. Strathfield Council passed a motion that would make it compulsory for all shops in the LGA to clearly display English on all signage. Wolter Peeters The move mostly affects businesses and shops in the area that don’t have English on their signage, but it doesn’t ban other languages from being on shop signs. There are more than 7300 businesses in Strathfield, and about 73 per cent of the local government area’s 45,000 residents speak a language other than English. Mandarin, Nepali, Cantonese, Korean and Arabic are among the most common.



Liberal councillor Esther Kim, who put the motion forward, said some shops did not have English translations and were exclusively written in languages people could not recognise. “I’m a migrant too; when people come as migrants, living in Australia, we have to respect that English is our common language,” she said at the council’s July meeting. Federico Carucci has worked at Strathfield’s Italian cafe Barone for more than a year and has received no customer complaints about signage. Wolter Peeters Labor councillor Rory Nosworthy said it was “a little bit of overreach” for councils to determine what shops should display. “I’m not sure it’s an issue we have in Strathfield. I think it’s up to the store owner ... I’m not sure it’s for us to say what language they should put their signage in,” he said.



Federico Carucci, a worker at Italian cafe Barone, was unconvinced that non-English signs were an issue. He pointed to the numerous bilingual and trilingual signs along Strathfield’s main commercial street, near the railway station. “They [the council] have to fill their time by doing these things,” he said. Diana Son, owner of a salon in Strathfield, said customers had more than enough common sense to work out what services shops were offering. Wolter Peeters Diana Son, who has owned FM Beauty Salon for more than three decades, agreed, adding that customers had more than enough “common sense”. “People of all cultures come here. Strathfield used to have a big Korean community here, that’s why we put Korean words here, but we always use Korean and English [on signs] together,” she said.



It is unclear how or when the motion will be enforced, how much notice businesses will receive, and whether ratepayers or individual owners would be responsible for costs to fix noncompliant signs. Editor's pick Opinion

City life I swam in the newly reopened North Sydney pool. Was the 1986-day wait worth it? Cindy Yin Urban affairs reporter The council is preparing a report outlining existing council policies on multilingual signage, with recommendations to “promote clear and accessible communication for all residents”. “Until such time as the report has been prepared, we are unable to provide a response to the detailed questions posed,” a council spokesperson said. The council did not clarify how many complaints it had received about the matter in the past year. Independent councillor Matthew Blackmore said the move was in line with existing council policies, but he conceded he had only seen a handful of shops that did not comply.



Four councillors voted in favour of the motion, while two voted against it. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Huge impact’: Thousands of Sydney cancer patients pushed out of work each year
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCancer ‘Huge impact’: Thousands of Sydney cancer patients pushed out of work each year Rachel Rasker August 10, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At 19, Elizabeth Funa dreamed of a career in exercise and sport science. Then, doctors told her they would need to amputate her leg. “It felt like my whole world stopped,” the now 28-year-old Bankstown resident said. “Suddenly my focus shifted from building this career ... to simply trying to survive.” Elizabeth Funa would like to see better support for employees with cancer. Janie Barrett Funa is one of the estimated 3000 people in NSW pushed out of the workforce each year due to cancer, according to a new report from Cancer Council NSW and the McKell Institute. After being diagnosed with stage four Hodgkin’s lymphoma, Funa quit her dual role as a personal trainer and membership officer at a gym and dropped out of university. She said she could have continued her administrative role during treatment if she had been offered more flexibility.



“If I did have the support from management to be able to work from home or at least reduce the working hours, then it would have definitely helped,” Funa said. About 56,000 people in NSW are diagnosed with cancer each year, and about 40 per cent are aged in their prime working years. NSW has no dedicated policy to help patients keep their jobs during treatment, or help them return to work. In Victoria and Queensland, employers can access subsidies for hiring jobseekers from disadvantaged groups, including those recovering from illness. Professor Bogda Koczwara, who leads the Australian Research Centre for Cancer Survivorship, said the report was a “sign of the times” as rates of cancer survival increase. “It’s really important for us to consider what life is after cancer,” she said. “Not just through the prism of medical aspects ... but rather what does it mean for your livelihood.”



The report estimated the workforce exodus created major economic losses, including more than $240 million in lost wages annually, as well as reduced tax revenue and increased demand for social security payments. Related Article Exclusive

Cancer This cancer is rising in young people like Nathan. There are ‘exquisite’ reasons not to despair Recent Australian Institute of Health and Welfare analysis highlighted that cancer diagnoses among young people (under 65s) had risen, with incidence rates for Australians in their 30s and 40s about 11.6 per cent higher in 2025 than in 2000. “Often they can work, just in a reduced capacity, but we feel the system just hasn’t quite kept pace with the reality,” Cancer Council NSW policy and advocacy manager Brad Gellert said. “This has huge impacts on both their mental wellbeing and the financial stability of themselves and their families.” While some workers can access income protection insurance through their superannuation, government income support for under 65s with cancer is virtually non-existent. They do not qualify for the NDIS and are ineligible for aged care, and Gellert said that JobSeeker’s mutual obligation rules – which require numerous job applications – make it unsuitable for people with cancer.



“There really isn’t an alternative welfare route for these people, and they do slip through the cracks,” Gellert said. McKell Institute chief executive Ed Cavanough said the basic policy principle of the report was to “incentivise a retaining of the employer-employee relationship throughout the duration of a cancer treatment”. Elizabeth Funa had to leave her job after a cancer diagnosis. Janie Barrett Its key recommendation was a targeted wage-subsidy scheme that could “pay for itself”. It proposed the employer, the state and federal government directly fund up to 60 per cent of the cancer patient’s salary for up to a year while their capacity is reduced. “It would essentially enable people to stay connected to their workplace, stop that long-term welfare reliance, and it would give ... employers the ability to retain a person who’s a valued staff member,” Gellert said.



The report also suggested payroll tax concessions for employers that maintain the employment of their worker, a donated or government-funded “cancer and chronic illness leave bank” that employees could access after their sick leave is exhausted, as well as an expansion of flexible work and carer’s leave under the Fair Work Act. Related Article Exclusive

Health The innovative program that helped this couple beat cancer NSW Industrial Relations Minister Sophie Cotsis said the government would review the report’s findings and recommendations alongside Commonwealth counterparts. “We understand the devastating impact cancer can have on workers and their families, including being unable to work due to treatment,” she said. “I have experienced this myself, and I am committed to ensuring employees with cancer are supported.” A federal government spokesperson said the Fair Work Act’s National Employment Standards were under parliamentary review by a committee, which will consider if any minimum workplace entitlements – including personal and compassionate leave, unpaid carer’s leave and flexible working arrangements – should be updated to meet the needs of workers, employers and the economy.



For Funa, who did not need an amputation and is now in remission, the feeling of being “just one employee [in] thousands” after her cancer diagnosis propelled her to change career and switch her university major to human resources, so she might help others in a similar situation.
